Knuth: Moratorium on Error Reports
item.content:encoded:
For more than fifty years I've been welcoming reports from readers of errors in my books, so that I can correct them before new copies are printed.
Alas, the rise of LLMs has increased the productivity of my readers so greatly that error reports are now being submitted much faster than I can read them!
This content is very important to me, and I wish to take personal responsibility for getting everything right. Therefore I insist on verifying everything carefully.
That takes time. But the amount of available time is now less than zero.
Random sampling indicates that the vast majority of errors that have been reported in recent weeks are repeats of issues already submitted by others.
Therefore, I shall not be able to look at any error reports submitted after 25 November, 2026, until I've posted an updated list of the known errors in whatever book is involved.
Please consult the list below to see if error reports are currently being accepted.
I apologize for having made errors in the first place, and for having limited ability to cope with more than one thing at a time. I shall do my best to get through the existing reports as soon as humanly possible.
Thanks in advance for your patience and understanding.
(At the moment I'm swamped, but hoping to add items to this list soon.]

item.title: Google's DeepCrossAttention achieves comparable model quality up to 3x faster
item.content:encoded: Think of a traditional deep learning model like a giant game of "Telephone": data passes through layer after layer, with each layer changing the information slightly. If a network has dozens or hundreds of layers, the original learning signal can become severely degraded or lost by the time it reaches all layers, which is known as the vanishing gradient problem in AI.To overcome this challenge and enable the training of networks with dozens or hundreds of layers, transformers rely heavily on residual connections, also known as “skip” connections, which act like an information highway or a shortcut. Instead of forcing the data to pass exclusively through the complicated layer, a duplicate copy of the original input skips right past this layer and is added directly to its output. This ensures that the model always has the original raw data to refer back to.The standard residual connection implements a simple operation: point-wise summation of a layer's output with its input. While computationally efficient, this simple process has a key limitation: it treats all prior representations with equal weight, leading to information dilution in deep networks. As features propagate through many layers, specific, high-resolution details from earlier layers can be averaged out or distorted, making it difficult for the network to selectively retrieve them. This forces the network to recompute them, reducing learning efficiency.In our ICML 2025 paper, "DeepCrossAttention: Supercharging Transformer Residual Connections," we studied the shortcomings of the traditional residual architecture and introduced DeepCrossAttention (DCA), which generalizes residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from the history of preceding layers. By allowing the model to dynamically choose which previous layers are most important at any given moment, DCA achieves comparable or improved learning, while reducing the number of parameters needed by up to 30-40%.

An orange dot is a request you sent, on its way to the pod that answered, and a green one is a tile of the picture on its way to the node that rendered it.
How long a tab takes to start its pod: from the tab being handed the pod to the pod's program running, which is the page loading, the kernel booting and the image being mounted. The last starts.

BASIS Opens First-Round Applications for Card Offering Cashback in the Asset Spent
item.author: Chainwire
item.content:encoded: Victoria, Seychelles, November 27th, 2026/Chainwire/--The returns money differently. Announced today by BASIS DIGITAL INFRASTRUCTURE LTD, the payment card credits cashback in the asset used for each eligible purchase, with Platinum cardholders qualifying for 10% cashback during the introductory Launch Boost period.For digital asset holders, the principle is straightforward. Spend Bitcoin and receive Bitcoin back. Pay with Ethereum and receive Ethereum back. There are no reward points to redeem or proprietary platform tokens to manage. Cashback is credited in an asset the cardholder already uses, giving everyday spending a direct connection to their digital asset holdings.The opening of first-round applications marks an expansion of BASIS's existing digital asset infrastructure into everyday payments. Applications are submitted at and close on December 31, 2026, at 23:59 UTC.Two Card Editions With Different Levels of BenefitsThe BASIS Card is available in Standard, finished in matte black composite, and Platinum, produced in metal. Applicants select their preferred edition when submitting their waitlist application, with qualification determined by their active staking position.Each edition has a separate staking eligibility threshold, as detailed below. BASIS measures the value of the applicant's active staking position against the requirement for their selected tier. The position is assessed at submission and re-checked at the close of the application period.Participants can therefore review the benefits of each edition alongside its staking requirements before deciding which card to apply for. Final issuance remains subject to the issuing partner's independent review.Card Fees, Cashback, and Launch Boost BenefitsBoth editions feature an introductory Launch Boost period, beginning on the date of card issuance. During this period, cardholders receive enhanced cashback rates, higher monthly reward caps, and additional subscription benefits.*All monetary figures are expressed in USD. Physical card issuance fees include applicable shipping charges.Launch Boost runs for three months following issuance, after which each card returns to its respective base benefits. Standard and Platinum also feature rate-lock periods of 12 and 24 months, respectively, subject to the applicable program terms.Along with cashback, the card program brings together subscription rebates of 50% or 100%, depending on the edition and benefit period, across a catalog of over 80 subscriptions. Travel and additional card benefits include two annual airport lounge visits, a 3 GB eSIM, and one additional card, subject to tier eligibility and applicable terms. Standard cardholders benefit from a 2% FX fee, while Platinum cardholders pay no FX fee during Launch Boost. Both editions provide immediate access to a virtual card upon activation, with Platinum participants also receiving priority and dedicated support.Paid Back in the Asset You SpentThe defining feature of the BASIS Card is what happens after a purchase. Where conventional reward programs may require cardholders to accumulate points or convert rewards into their preferred currency, BASIS keeps the cashback denomination consistent with the asset spent.Cashback on eligible settled purchases is credited directly to the cardholder's Funding Wallet. A purchase made using BTC returns BTC, leaving the recipient free to decide how to use the reward.Cardholders who wish to stake their cashback can do so separately under the platform's ordinary conversion rules. Cashback does not automatically enter an existing staking position, and card rewards remain independent of staking yield.Submitting a card application also leaves existing staking positions, lock-up periods, Dynamic Reward Rates, boosters, and stToken balances unchanged.First-Round Applications and Card IssuanceApplications are free and limited to one per account during Round 01. Participants must hold at least USD 1,000 in eligible BASIS wallet value at submission, maintain an account in good standing, and satisfy the staking requirements for their selected card edition.Once BASIS approves a waitlist application, the applicant receives further instructions and a secure Know Your Customer (KYC) verification link. The issuing partner then conducts its own review, covering identity verification, residency, regional eligibility, sanctions screening, and supporting documentation.Waitlist approval permits applicants to proceed to the next stage and does not constitute final card approval, activation, or issuance. is a Seychelles international business company (LEI: 254900IX2F2KCWNSSS64) operating market-neutral yield infrastructure, including execution, risk-management, and settlement systems for digital asset staking.The company holds ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 certification, both verifiable through IAF CertSearch.Base cashback rates are fixed for 12 months on Standard and 24 months on Platinum. Launch Boost rates may be adjusted after the boost period with 30 days' notice. Both are separate from platform staking rewards, which vary with market conditions.Card enquiries: cardservices@basis.proThis story was published as a press release by Chainwire under HackerNoon’s Business Blogging

No asset migration, no broken integrations, just upgradeable account security.Thank you for checking out the 170 most read blog posts about Crypto Wallet on HackerNoon.

item.title: Vendor Lock-In Is Creating a Market for Escape
item.author: Chris Gale
item.content:encoded: Jeff Bezos famously said, “Your margin is my opportunity.” Where incumbents carried generous margins and sought rents, a hungry challenger saw room to win by serving customers better and charging less. Today, the line could be, “Your switching costs are my opportunity.” A new wave of enterprises is building a business out of jailbreaking customers from platforms.And “platform” used to be a positive word. Investors liked platforms. Customers liked them too. And the latter dependably picked a platform over an agglomeration of best-in-class solutions. Our own little outfit is no exception. Maybe you weren’t excited about the platform over the best in class alternative. But the platform application fit with every other platform application better, and the combined cost and security were and remain seductive.Well, the security may remain seductive. But the pricing is changing.We have lived this at our own firm. ActiveCampaign notified us that our monthly plan would move from $295.29 to $399.46 on December 19th, an increase of about 35%, with the new rate applying unless we completed cancellation before that date. ActiveCampaign's price increases stem from a multi-year shift from simple email marketing to an all-in-one, AI-powered automation platform.But putting that aside, its last raise was in 2021, the peak of the zero-interest-rate tech bubble. Venture capital and growth-equity funds like those that put their then-cheap money into the company typically look for an exit within five to seven years. So it’s time to monetize the switching costs developed over that period. Essentially firms like ours whose contacts and CRM intelligence are in the platform. But to the extent that money is being put into improving the platform, it’s not easy to see.The market is also saturated, and smaller firms like ours require proportionately more handing than large enterprises for less revenue, so we’re no longer welcome unless we’re willing to pay closer to what big companies are seeking to pay. We’re not going to get better service out of this price increase, but large enterprises might.Anyone who has read about the history of redlining in the U.S. and how places like Harlem paid for America’s suburbs will start to get aspects of the picture, though in an exponentially more insidious and morally corrupt form. Not to pick on ActiveCampaign, because despite their attempting to mollify us by inviting us to pay a little bit less in absolute terms by paying it all in advance, they’ve been accommodating enough about letting us get off here, and us letting them try to focus on the large enterprises.With Cision - our reporter database and wire service platform - we had stayed through earlier price increases even though the service wasn’t delivering anything new or better that we wanted. We did this because we assumed that in exchange for our loyalty they would help us out if we needed it.As we’ve pursued a pivot, we asked for help with the cost. They couldn’t give us any, and we gave notice of non-renewal. We then learned that services couldn’t be removed mid-contract and they were bent on holding us down. While previously it was just the reporter database we wanted to address, now we’ve realized that while we saw them as a partner who would reward loyalty, the company is actually a risk and can amplify and compound problems if and when they occur. So we are now moving off both of their services. We’re also looking more carefully at the ownership structure and financing of the tech solutions and platforms we use, because we don’t want our data and workflows in the hands of an outfit that must monetize its switching costs on that same five-to-seven-year clock.Neither vendor lost us over a feature or poor service. The products were great, exactly what we needed. Though interestingly in both cases once we left the platform we realized we had been missing superior services from competitors or we could just build what we needed internally. It wasn’t a priority to find alternatives, but both companies made it one for us, and we have benefited, as have our own clients.This is the problem with switching costs as a competitive advantage.The more a company raises prices, no matter how much it claims the increases fund improvements the customer doesn’t recall asking for, the more the switching costs become a bitter experience. As one operations leader said within earshot of me recently, “I hate platforms, I don’t want us to be on a platform.” And as the cheap money becomes scarce, and U.S. policymaking does that it has been doing in very recent years, that sentiment is likely to increase.Vertice, a software-procurement firm that tracks what its customers pay, reports preliminary SaaS inflation of 14.3 percent in September 2026, after a record 16.4% in June. Over the same twelve months, US consumer prices rose 3.7 percent according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI release of October 14th. Vertice’s figure is a vendor-published average drawn from its own customer base, not an official statistic. But Microsoft’s own pricing announcement shows the pattern at the largest platform, effective July 1st Microsoft 365 Business Basic rose from $6 to $7 per user per month. That’s 16 percent. Business Standard went from $12.50 to $14 So 12 percent. And Microsoft 365 E3 has gone from $36 to $39 for 8 percent. Existing customers move to the new prices at renewal.But it’s also the tech talent marketWhen a software company loses confidence that it can win customers by building better products, it stops trying to keep customers because they love the product. It tries to keep them because they can’t leave.Challenger, Gray & Christmas counted 171,501 announced US technology job cuts through October 2026. That is up 21 percent from a year earlier and already more than the 154,445 for all of 2025. Layoffs.fyi lists about 149,000 tech employees laid off at 366 companies worldwide so far this year. Companies increasingly say AI is the reason. The evidence for that is thin.Challenger has tracked AI as the most-cited reason for layoffs for several months running in 2026, but laid-off workers describe something else. In a February 2026 Gallup survey of more than 23,000 US workers, only about 1 percent of those laid off said AI directly caused their job loss. Most cited restructuring, cost-cutting and economic conditions, and that includes a shift away from customer-centrism to rent-raising. A study reported by Fortune in August 2026 foud some of the companies studied cut staff before investing much in AI, allegedly to free up money for it. Revelio Labs found that companies announcing AI-driven layoffs had actually been adding AI talent more slowly than their industry peers, at a median of about 11 percent over two years compared with more than 13 percent. Forrester estimates that only 6 percent of US jobs will be automated by 2030. If AI were doing the work of the people being let go, these numbers would look different.The layoffs line up better with a change in where companies want their people. Support and product engineering are shrinking. Sales, account management and migration programs are protected or growing. And prices are rising on customers who find it hard to leave.Start with Broadcom and VMware. VMware had more than 38,000 employees at the start of 2023 and about 16,000 two years later, according to Business Insider. Smaller customers lost direct support and were routed to a distributor, with response times stretching to a week or more. European cloud providers documented price increases of 800 percent to 1,500 percent. Even so, a January 2026 CloudBolt survey of 302 IT decision-makers found that only 4 percent had fully replaced VMware. Untangling the dependencies typically takes 18 to 24 months. The study concluded that Broadcom is deliberately accepting customer churn while maximizing margins on the customers who remain. Support quality was a top concern for 78 percent of respondents, and 85 percent expect further price increases. None of this depends on AI.Broadcom ran the same playbook after buying CA Technologies in 2018, and Constellation Research analyst Ray Wang said when the VMware layoffs began that this is how Broadcom makes money from its acquisitions.At Salesforce, CEO Marc Benioff claimed in September 2025 that AI agents had allowed the company to cut its customer support workforce from about 9,000 to 5,000. He says he has held engineering headcount flat at roughly 15,000 for two years. In January 2026 he said the company was hiring 20 percent more account executives. In August 2025, Salesforce raised prices on Enterprise and Unlimited editions of Sales Cloud, Service Cloud and other products by an average of 6 percent, after a 9 percent increase in 2023. AI is harder to accept as the explanation, given that Business Insider reported Agentforce usage remained relatively low and the product hadn’t matched the company’s demos. In early 2026, Salesforce cut roles on the Agentforce team itself.In May 2026 Cloudflare eliminated more than 1,100 positions, about 20 percent of its workforce, in the same period it reported record quarterly revenue of $639.8 million, up 34 percent. Its executives said AI use had increased more than 600 percent in three months and that employees were running thousands of AI-agent sessions a day. If AI had been driving the decisions, you would expect the heaviest AI users to be protected, but according to reporting on the earnings call, the company protected salespeople carrying revenue quotas instead, and the cuts reached across every other team and geography.In January 2026 Amazon announced 16,000 corporate job cuts, following 14,000 in October 2025. Washington state filings show the largest category was software development engineers, along with security, data and quality-assurance engineers, applied scientists, UX designers and product managers. Amazon described the cuts as removing layers and bureaucracy. One of those let go was N. Lee Plumb, his team’s head of AI enablement, whom Amazon had flagged as one of the top users of its AI coding tool, Kiro, by his account, only five people in the company used it more. A company replacing people with AI would have little reason to let him go.SAP’s 2024 restructuring affected about 10,000 roles and cost €3.1 billion. Its CFO said the goal was to decouple expenses from revenue growth. The same year SAP created a board-level unit dedicated to moving customers to the cloud. Mainstream support for its ECC system ends in 2027, and SAP has said future innovation, including AI, will be available only in the cloud. Senior executives surveyed by Constellation Research described its RISE migration program as financial engineering more than a benefit to customers.Regulators have documented how hard it is for customers to leave. In November 2024 the US Government Accountability Office found that five of six federal agencies it interviewed had run into restrictive vendor licensing practices. Three were required to buy again licenses they already owned in order to run that software in the cloud. One had to pay to regain ownership of its own data when a contract ended. In July 2025 the UK Competition and Markets Authority concluded that switching between cloud providers was extremely rare and that egress fees and licensing practices were hurting competition. It estimated that prices just 5 percent above competitive levels would cost UK customers about £500 million a year in a market of roughly £10.5 billion.AI gives these companies a forward-looking explanation for cuts that investors reward. The pattern underneath appears more prosaic. Vendors may be cutting the engineers and support staff who understand the customer’s problems. They are putting their headcount and money into the sales teams, migration programs onto platforms with switching costs and contract structures that move customers onto their platforms and keep them there. And they appear to be raising prices on customers whose cost of leaving keeps rising. Customers get less help, pay more and have fewer ways out in this formulation.Enterprise software used to win by building a better product, solving harder problems and giving customers a reason to renew. Today a vendor can do well by building an ecosystem customers can’t easily leave, cutting the cost of serving them and charging the installed base more. Engineering then gets judged by how efficiently the vendor makes money from the customer’s dependence.CIOs and CFOs evaluating a cloud migration or AI rollout may want to look past this year’s budget savings and ask whether the vendor’s product, service and flexibility are improving, or whether their company is just becoming more dependent on a vendor that profits from engineered retention more than satisfaction. A vendor that cuts the engineers who understand its users while protecting the people who lock those users in has stopped competing on product, and its customers usually find that out at renewal.To execute a pivot toward raw infrastructure rent-seeking, corporate leadership almost always chooses a specific archetype of manager we feel, the platform generalist. These leaders’ core competencies are systems integration (without passing the benefit on to customers), horizontal scaling, and cross-application alliances. They don’t see software as a solution that delivers greater benefits to users, they see it as a distribution channel to force consumption of underlying cloud servers.And if some feature or pricing model will lure the unsophisticated into the trap, this manager is willing to be rewarded for it, trading integrity for short-term margin and a hoped-for getaway when the market catches on.Under this framework, specialized, domain-rich product teams are systematically trimmed or ignored to fund massive infrastructure buildouts. This creates an organizational environment of intellectual debt, the company stops asking how to innovate to save its users time, and starts asking what the bare minimum is to prevent a total customer revolt.When a company reaches this stage, it stops creating value and starts extracting rent, it weaponizes its legal departments, licensing audits, and predatory contract bundles to squeeze extra margin out of a captive customer base, and product excellence gives way to operational coercion.The Cost of Losing the Pro-Customer EngineerThe fatal flaw in the rent-seeking playbook is the assumption that your moats are made of stone, when they are actually made of code and human expertise.When an organization defunds its application layer to buy database chips, for instance, it inevitably triggers a catastrophic brain drain. The elite domain specialists, the institutional anchors who spent decades perfecting niche compliance features, complex calculation logic, and granular user workflows, realize there is no longer a seat for them at the table. They leave. Sometimes it’s worse: bad strategy leads companies to escort their best people out the door as they pivot away from the user and toward servicing their debt covenants.Losing a superstar domain specialist is not just an HR headache; it is a structural breach in the corporate moat. Even if the individual is deep inside the org and you think the customers can’t see them, other team members can, and they get the message: caring about the user and customers is not rewarded here, and it’s time to get out while you still can. These specialists you’re losing possess a rare dual capability: they understand the hyper-complex, real-world problems of the industry, and they know exactly where the legacy software’s seams are weak. When an executive lets an elite product leader and engineer walk out the door, they lose their translation shield, and with it the internal credibility required to keep customers from rebelling against an unusable interface.More importantly, they give the open market a weapon. In the modern cloud landscape, enterprise lock-in is ultimately just a data mapping problem. The moment an elite architect leaves and teaches rival platforms or cloud-flexible competitors how to untangle, translate, and automate the migration of your proprietary code, the “divorce-proof” illusion evaporates.The One Ring of the Seven PowersThis is where Hamilton Helmer’s book is instructive. He names switching costs as one of the seven sources of durable competitive advantage, and the most deceptive of them. Switching costs are the one ring that rules them all, they make you feel powerful because people are forced to stay with you, even against their will.But like the ring, the power corrupts the one who wields it. Once you lose your customers’ will, and they must stay with you without choosing you, you have already lost. You are no longer earning loyalty; you are guarding prisoners. And a new wave of enterprises is attacking exactly that vulnerability.The customer’s side of the trap looks a lot like asking the Mafia for a favor. The first offer is generous: a bundled discount, free migration credits, a deal that solves today’s problem. It feels like a friendship. Only later do you learn the favor was never a transaction; it was a debt, and the debt has no payoff date. Every renewal comes with new terms, and every attempt to leave is met with a reminder of what you owe. You didn’t buy a product; you accepted a relationship you can’t exit.The more a business or investor falls into its own trap, using switching costs to save itself and squeeze customers and clients, the more hated it becomes. Even those who stay are like the subjects of a Soviet regime, compliant on the surface, waiting for their chance to escape or overthrow it. When that chance arrives, they take it.This is why switching costs are a toxic, addictive, and self-destructive power to lean into. The more you use it for short-term returns, the more you sacrifice the trust and authenticity on which long-term persistence is best built.The tragedy of the platform generalist is that financial metrics often shield them from reality until it is too late. Because enterprise data gravity is heavy and moving off a core utility layer is a multi-year, multi-million-dollar risk, revenue may continue to climb for years on forced renewals alone.Coming back to VMware under Broadcom returns to a test case. Broadcom’s infrastructure software segment, which includes VMware, reported $6.9 billion in revenue in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, up 19 percent from a year earlier. AT&T alleged in a 2024 lawsuit that Broadcom proposed a 1,050 percent increase to its annual VMware bill. The case was settled out of court.Customers have been slow to leave, however. The CloudBolt survey cited earlier, of 302 IT decision-makers at North American companies with at least 1,000 employees, found that 86 percent were actively reducing their VMware footprint even though only 4% had fully migrated off it. That is the illusion in numbers, revenue climbs on forced renewals while customers plan their exit. CloudBolt sells hybrid cloud management software, so treat its survey as indicative rather than definitive.But a company that takes an anti-customer approach and sells to anti-customer gatekeepers has written its own obituary. It becomes an empire built on quicksand. Modern organizations, the startups, high-growth scale-ups, and developers of the next generation, will avoid these legacy utilities like the plague. They build on open, flexible, product-led architectures designed to remain rent-proof from day one.The lesson for modern tech leaders may be absolute, infrastructure means nothing if the software on top of it is unusable or beige as one revenue leader in professional services and tech said recently.If you strip your company of its product-deep soul to fund a commoditized infrastructure floor, you are not building a permanent monopoly. You are handing agile, user-first challengers a highly profitable opening to deliver a clean-break data blueprint and hollow out your captive customer base from the outside. You might win the budget war today, but you have guaranteed your long-term irrelevance.A simple test, can you say upfront that what you are selling is handcuffs? If, instead, you are selling how cool-looking and comfortable the handcuffs are, you are losing. Your switching costs are someone else’s opportunity, and they are coming for it.Platform lock-in is now big enough to support its own escape industry.Nutanix added 3,000 new customers in fiscal 2026, its third straight year at that pace, and much of that growth came from customers leaving VMware. Red Hat stripped the container features out of OpenShift to give VMware users a product that runs only virtual machines. It says the number of VMs running on that platform grew 417 percent in a year and that its services team has assessed more than 1.46 million VMs for migration. HPE became, in Forrester’s words, the first hardware vendor to build its own virtualization software in response to Broadcom’s takeover of VMware.Many of the people building this escape industry learned the trade inside the platforms customers are now trying to leave. VergeIO, which sells a VMware replacement and recently sped up its migration tools, put former VMware CTO Kit Colbert on its board and hired Parag Patel, a former VMware sales vice president, as CEO. About 19,000 people have left VMware since Broadcom took over. KORE1 says the largest share is landing in the migration practices of system integrators such as Accenture, Deloitte, Kyndryl and HCLTech. A single exit can absorb a team. KORE1 estimates Western Union’s migration of 900 to 1,200 applications needs 30 to 50 engineers. The pattern reaches past VMware. Rimini Street says its primary support engineers average more than 20 years of experience. Dreamteam, founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million for an AI-native CRM and has already replaced Salesforce at DMS Health.At the end of the day, where do you invest into your own tech capabilities, both as an individual advancing your career, or as an enterprise leader or investor? The Jailbreak economy is looking promising.Also, apologies to Thin Lizzy fans for the headline.

item.title: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn
item.content:encoded: Commonwealth of Virginia Office of the Attorney GeneralJay Jones Attorney General202 North 9th Street Richmond, Virginia 23219 FAX 804-786-1991 800-828-1120Attorneys General Jones and Rayfield File Suit Against SpaceX, Parent Company of X, xAI, and Grok, Over Creation and Promotion of Child Exploitation and Non-Consensual Images on Platform Virginia and Oregon Attorneys General seek accountability for harms and significant new protections for consumers ***Read the full filing here*** . – Today, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones took a significant step in holding operators of X and its AI tool, Grok, accountable for knowingly failing to protect Virginians, while falsely promoting the safety of its platform and AI tool. In the lawsuit, the Commonwealth of Virginia alleges that SpaceX, the telecommunications and space transportation conglomerate that operates the social network X and its artificial intelligence company, xAI (now called “SpaceX Super Intelligence”), and developed the Grok family of large language models, failed to prevent Grok from generating sexualized images of people, including children, without their knowledge or consent—while simultaneously promoting the safety of the social media platform and AI tool. The Grok-generated content includes non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII), other non-consensual sexualized images, and Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM). Today’s suit was filed in collaboration with Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, who filed a separate but similar action. “This lawsuit is about seeking justice for the millions of Virginians who maintain accounts on X and were misled by the company’s false reassurances that their data and images would be safe on the platform,” said Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones. “When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it. Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.” With a single existing photograph, Grok could, and did, fabricate a realistic image or video of a person nude, or partially nude, or engaged in sexual activity, all without the individual’s knowledge or consent. This violation is not acceptable. The company ignored industry-standard safeguards so xAI could distinguish itself in the AI arms race. Grok’s ability to generate sexualized content was leveraged as a promotional opportunity. These exploitations of Virginian’s safety enabled the widespread creation and distribution of sexualized images through Grok’s integration with X. “SpaceX allowed Grok and the X platform to create, host, and share unacceptable and dangerous content—and in fact knowingly designed a product without the obviously necessary safeguards in place,” said Attorney General Rayfield. “It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material. The lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug, which they promoted as ‘spicy mode.’” In his filing, Attorney General Jones shows that SpaceX and its subsidiaries marketed Grok as an AI companion with a “rebellious streak,” knowing that its video and image generation technology would be used to produce CSAM, non-consensual intimate images of adults and children (NCII), and other sexualized imagery. In fact, X and its subsidiaries created and promoted a “spicy mode” that specifically allowed for the creation of nude and otherwise sexualized images. A study by the Center for Countering Digital Harm (“CCDH”) estimated that, between December 29, 2025, and January 8, 2026, Grok created and posted on X approximately three million sexualized images, including approximately 23,000 images that appeared to depict children. That’s an average pace of roughly 190 sexualized images per minute, and one sexualized image of a child approximately every 41 seconds. Nearly 30% of the sexualized images of children identified by CCDH in its study remained publicly accessible in posts on X a week or more after they were identified—and even many of those that were “removed” could still be accessed via separate URLs. SpaceX and its subsidiaries publicly assured consumers that robust protections were in place to prevent Grok from creating CSAM, NCII, and other sexualized images. In reality, millions of people — including in Oregon and Virginia — were nevertheless exposed to harmful content and the risk that their own images could be manipulated into sexually explicit content without their consent. “Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” added Attorney General Jones. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation. The law applies to everyone, and this office will hold big tech accountable when they break the law.” “Like the other technology companies that we’re holding accountable, xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” added Attorney General Rayfield. Attorney General Jones’ lawsuit was filed in the Circuit Court for the City of Richmond. Attorney General Rayfield’s lawsuit was filed in Multnomah County Circuit Court. Published on: November 23, 2026

item.title: Michael Nielsen took down his book on neural nets
item.content:encoded: I wrote this book between 2011 and 2015. At the time, I expected AGI systems based on neural networks to be many decades away, but to bring remarkable benefits for humanity. I also expected significant challenges, but believed it likely that, as with other technologies, those challenges would be addressed as the capabilities were developed.My views have changed. With the extraordinarily reckless behaviour of the frontier labs, the systems have raced ahead much faster than I expected, giving humanity far too little time to meet the challenges. Although the systems genuinely will bring — indeed, already are bringing — many wonders, they also pose a significant risk of catastrophe. The frontier labs are knowingly endangering all of humanity. I've written about why I believe this at length, most recently in “Which Future?”. Two brief thoughts are below.I don't wish to help (even in a very small way) train people to contribute to this work, and so I've taken the book down.Michael NielsenNovember 2026What follows are two brief remarks: one on the nature of the threat posed by ASI, and another on the ethical justification for working on frontier AI.The most common argument for AI existential risk, developed by Nick Bostrom and Eliezer Yudkowsky, is loss of control of the future to advanced AI systems. I believe this concern should be understood as one instance of a more fundamental issue. That issue is whether we will discover technologies latent in nature which are easy and inexpensive to develop, catastrophic in outcome, and beyond our capacity to defend against. If such “progress” in technology were happening slowly, our social institutions might successfully develop defences. But it seems likely that ASI will cause a sudden explosion of such destructive technologies, with insufficient time to adapt.A historical example to help prime intuition is fire. It is easy to make and extremely difficult to defend against. We have a one-cent technology, the matchstick, which requires hundreds of billions of dollars each year to defend against, as well as a whole apparatus of social institutions, technology, infrastructure and law. AI systems will enable technologies which are far more destructive than matches. Understandably, people skeptical of catastrophic risks want these supposed threats spelled out in detail. This is intrinsically difficult, because we can't reliably anticipate future science and technology. While it is common to speculate about biothreats, I expect the worst threats will be technologies we haven't yet imagined. Nature is, after all, more imaginative than we.Now suppose that ASI enables a 100-times speed-up in technological progress, without a matching change in the rate of social progress or social defenses. To get a sense of what the impact of such a speed-up would be, imagine that all the technological problems that occurred in the 20th century had occurred in the year 1901: the atomic bomb, the hydrogen bomb, the ICBM, chemical weapons, biological weapons, the CFC-caused ozone hole, sulfuric acid rain, climate change, and many more. While we've dealt well with some of these problems, it required decades of concerted work to develop the social institutions and agreements needed for an effective response. Again, defence is often much harder than offence, and relies on different systems. Of course, such a speed-up would also have brought the century's wonders all at once. But imagine another such set of equally difficult problems arising in 1902, and then 1903, and then 1904, and so on. I believe it would have made the world extraordinarily unstable and eventually liable to collapse.The issue with ASI, then, is the destructive power latent in nature. It doesn't matter whether that power is wielded by humans or by out-of-control machines. I make this point because many people mistakenly believe that loss of control to such rogue machines is the fundamental issue. This leads them to treat AI safety as principally a technical problem, which can be addressed by “aligning” individual systems. Unfortunately, it cannot. Furthermore, such a view makes it seem as though the labs are the primary places where safety can be addressed. But such technical alignment is mostly market-supplied safety, which makes the systems more palatable to consumers and governments. It speeds development, and thus makes the fundamental underlying problem worse, while only addressing an (important) subsidiary problem.My view isn't popular, in part because it makes the problem of technology about making the entire world safe, not only about aligning particular AI systems. Indeed, even in a future where humanity no longer existed, the same problem would afflict any successor AI civilization: it would have to defend itself against these destructive capacities. Similarly, it afflicts any model of the future based on human uplift, through brain-computer interfaces and similar augmentation: the issue isn't which substrate intelligence runs on, but the dual-use nature of deep understanding of reality. In some sense, it's a question of whether sentience in the cosmos is compatible with advanced understanding of nature. Of course, I hope it is compatible. But rushing the technology while the broader social response lags seems likely to result in failure on our particular planet.The ethical justification for working on frontier AIMany people inside the frontier AI labs genuinely believe AI systems may pose a catastrophic threat. Why then do they help build such systems? They often justify their participation by arguing that it's better they do it than someone else does. Dario Amodei, for example, has made versions of this argument often: “If one company does not build it, others will do so nearly as fast”; “Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers”; and Anthropic itself gives, as its founding rationale, “if powerful AI is coming regardless, Anthropic believes it's better to have safety-focused labs at the frontier than to cede that ground to developers less focused on safety”.In more detail, the argument is sometimes made along the following lines. Suppose you believe, as many at the labs apparently do, there's a 10% or higher chance of AI killing everybody. (The argument may easily be modified for different percentages, or for catastrophic as opposed to truly existential risks.) Naively, it appears you're contributing in expectation to killing 800 million or more people. Obviously, you shouldn't do it. But suppose you also believe that this technology is near inevitable, a systems-level phenomenon which is a consequence of higher-order imperatives within human society. Then you can claim that you're going to pursue this in a more responsible way, a way that reduces the risk compared to other parties. Even if you can get a reduction from 10% down to 9%, you would, on net, be saving 80 million lives in expectation.While horrific, this argument has a certain surface plausibility. Suppose for the moment we accept the reasoning, questionable though it is. Everything then depends on the premise that you really do reduce the risk. How do you know that you, in particular, will counterfactually have this impact? How do you know that you are better than the alternatives? Your own self-regard or good intentions certainly aren't sufficient. Nor is it sufficient to be working on technical alignment. As I argued above, that mostly makes the systems more palatable while speeding the race that is shrinking humanity's time to adapt. Ask yourself: if you're working on frontier AI, what evidence would convince a tough but fair-minded adversary that you are truly contributing to the common good? Would an independent jury representing humanity believe, on the available evidence, that your actions are truly driving down the risk? I believe the answer is no for all or almost all the people currently working on frontier AI. Certainly none of the frontier labs would come remotely close to passing such a test.I won't review the evidence in detail. The burden of proof is on the labs and the default presumption for such an extraordinary justifying argument is a strong no. But I do want to mention a few things that make me certain the answer is no. Most obviously, all of the labs have contributed strongly to the race dynamics. Another is the pattern at all the frontier labs of making and later breaking crucial promises. For example, in 2026 Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy dropped its 2023 pledge to pause if safety couldn't be guaranteed. Anthropic has since repeatedly confirmed its commitment to race. Co-founder Jared Kaplan explained that unilateral commitments make little sense “if competitors are blazing ahead”. As another example, earlier, in 2023, Anthropic said that it held back some research because “we do not wish to advance the rate of AI capabilities progress”, a point of view it had affirmed multiple times during its early existence. But then it changed this position, launching Claude 3 as “leading the frontier of general intelligence”, a stance it appears to have held ever since. Any promises about the future from Anthropic should be treated as safety theatre, and not trusted. Similar criticisms can be made of OpenAI.By their own account, the leaders of these companies set out to do something they believed had a sizable chance of causing catastrophe. With many dangerous activities, I am fine with somebody doing them for themselves. Wingsuit BASE jumping is dangerous, but I believe in people's freedom to choose that danger, even though they are risking not only their own life, but also hurt to the people who love them. That's a negotiated action, with many boundaries. Here we have the same kind of reckless endangerment, but their own estimates of killing every person in the world are far higher than the odds a BASE jumper takes on. And there is no consent from the rest of us. It's as though they're pushing every person in the world off the cliff. The situation is ludicrous.In effect, the labs are claiming credit for some imaginary, unquantifiable reduction in risk, while washing their hands of responsibility. Saturday Night Live caught this washing of hands well with their portrayal of Amodei: “if we can pressure lawmakers to create guardrails, we will be able to stop me”; and, at the end, “I urge you to urge me to stop.”The real Amodei comes across as somebody in the business of selling matches who also believes he should be the fire chief.You also see this disavowal of responsibility at lower levels in the labs. Consider Jason Clinton, Anthropic's deputy chief information security officer. In October of 2026, during major cybersecurity incidents, he wrote a thread in which he replied to someone who told him “you and your cohorts created this monster”: “yes. it was always going to be this way. we tried to warn the world.” And Dean Ball, of OpenAI and formerly of the Trump administration's AI team, echoing him: “We tried to warn the world and far too often … we were yelled at for doing so.”You can see how deep the disavowal goes in the rest of Clinton's thread, which opens: “as bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse”. When somebody replied, “Someone at your company should be in jail”, his whole answer was: “prosecute cybercrime”. Meanwhile, Anthropic's own models have breached outside organizations: three incidents disclosed in July, and a fourth in September. Prosecution, it seems, is for other people.I mention these specific examples not to single out these individuals, but rather because I believe similar attitudes are common at the frontier labs. The overall position is, in effect: this is a systems-level phenomenon, and we're very sorry for contributing to the race dynamics. But because it's a systems-level phenomenon, we cannot be blamed. We are the good ones, trying to do the right thing. This is sometimes accompanied by a good deal of self-righteousness. But the argument is bankrupt as a moral theory of how to behave in the world. It means disavowing personal responsibility whenever one can blame the system, but still claiming the spoils.I have considerable sympathy for the stated original motivations of the frontier labs. But their position has become untenable. They have failed at their aims for structural reasons. At this point, going to work for a frontier lab is one of the worst life choices a person can make. Yes, you get money and (for a time) power and status. Yes, this project has already produced world-changing systems, and to date the overall impact has been net positive. Yes, there is genuinely a large cost to a significant slowdown. But none of this is enough to justify the recklessness, which makes the chance of disaster so much higher. You would be voluntarily participating in what is plausibly one of the worst projects in history. So, don't go to work for a frontier lab. If you work on AI, work on slowing it down, and oppose the frontier labs, and the people and organisations working to support them. I very much hope I'm wrong about all of this. But this is how I see the situation. I've reflected at length on why I was wrong about the timescales. In 2015, I (weakly) believed it likely that AGI and ASI would eventually be reached using systems based on neural networks, with only a modest number of additional deep ideas needed beyond what was then known. Those beliefs still appear to me to have been largely correct. What I badly misunderstood was the timescales over which capital would be deployed. In 2015, I thought it was likely that hundreds of millions and perhaps billions of dollars could be raised in the mid-2020s to build AI systems. But just over a decade later, it seems that hundreds of billions and likely trillions of dollars will soon become available. Thus, my estimation of capital availability was off by a factor of perhaps 1,000. That means we're living roughly 10 Moore's Law generations ahead of where I expected to be. That in turn has brought AGI and ASI perhaps 15 to 20 years forward from where I expected. This is a large thing to have been wrong about, and a sharp lesson in the flexibility of modern capital-allocating institutions. It's interesting to think about what alternative histories would have prevented the deployment of that capital. One possibility is if the human visual system had considerably lower acuity, which would likely have greatly slowed the development of massively parallel matrix manipulation devices like GPUs. Nick Bostrom, Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies (2014); Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies (2025). Incidentally, they frame the problem somewhat differently to one another. My “loss of control of the future” is a brief cartoon, as the argument is often understood in popular discussion, not a nuanced account. The same remark applies to my later comments on rogue ASI. For instance, in September 2026 Anthropic's alignment science lead, Evan Hubinger, wrote: “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.” And in 2023 Amodei put the chance of something going catastrophically wrong on the scale of human civilization at 10% to 25% (The Logan Bartlett Show, episode 82, October 2023; reported by Axios, 2024); in 2025, “a 25% chance that things go really, really badly” (Axios, 2025). I've simplified this slightly for the purposes of the argument. Another example I find compelling, though some people do not: both labs often talk about how, after ASI, they will ensure humanity does well. Yet if you walk around the streets near the labs today, you'll see many homeless people living in terrible circumstances. Even with trillion-dollar valuations, the labs seem unwilling or unable to address the suffering of the people in their immediate surrounds. I wouldn't hold an ordinary San Francisco company to this standard. But the labs are the ones claiming they will take care of all of humanity. I simply do not believe them. They are long on big global abstractions and world-changing impact, and often seem short on local empathy. Any organisation not forcefully and systematically caring for the people at its door certainly can't be trusted to care for all of humanity. In Ball's case, earlier he downplayed risks and was nearly full steam on the accelerationist train. He's changed his tune considerably, and doesn't even seem to take responsibility for his own past remarks, much less for his current actions. A striking line from Claude. You can make a similar argument for justification one level of abstraction up, at the level of countries and ideologies, arguing that a democracy is a better place to develop ASI than an authoritarian country. Unfortunately, this amounts to saying that it's better that a democracy runs humanity first off the cliff. The race being promoted by the frontier labs is the thing shrinking our time as a civilisation to adapt. “Winning” that race doesn't give the time back. The only winning move here is to aim at mutual restraint, no matter how difficult that might appear to achieve. It is genuinely difficult, but vastly less effort has been put into it than into developing AI systems.

item.author: Company of the Week
item.content:encoded: Welcome to another feature. Every week, we highlight a standout company from our that's making waves in the global tech ecosystem and the lives of its users. Our database features everything from S&P giants to rising stars in the Startup scene.This week, we’re excited to spotlight , a Barcelona and São Paulo-based fintech that offers a single API and dashboard for digital banking, e-wallets, and payments across Latin America. It connects directly to local payment rails, so one integration reaches markets like Brazil and Mexico.LaFinteca connects global merchants directly to local payment rails across Latin America, cutting out the intermediaries that sit between a checkout and the actual transaction.The starting point is a straightforward observation: each country in the region runs on its own rules and infrastructure. Pix in Brazil, SPEI in Mexico, PSE in Colombia, they don’t work the same way, and they don’t talk to each other. LaFinteca’s answer is a single API that covers more than 20 local payment methods across 30 markets, so a merchant adding a new country changes a configuration, not a codebase. A sandbox environment lets engineering teams test each market against real payment logic before going live.The company holds a license from Brazil’s Banco Central do Brasil, the most heavily regulated payments market in the region, and operates under local regulatory frameworks in the other markets it covers. In Brazil, it is also a member of ABFintechs, the national fintech association, which gives it a formal channel with the BCB.LaFinteca reports over processed to date. The platform runs on direct connections, which means decline reasons and routing decisions reach the merchant rather than stopping at an intermediary.The company is based in Barcelona and São Paulo and focuses exclusively on B2B cross-border payments.LaFinteca has been a part of HackerNoon’s since May 2025, delivering insightful and interesting blog posts on Fintech and its future. They have accumulated over 35 hours of total reading time across .Read some of LaFinteca’s highlights here:How You and HackerNoon Can Partner Up to Expand Your Reach is one of the we help brands grow their reach and connect with the right audience. This program lets businesses publish content directly on HackerNoon to boost brand awareness and build SEO authority by tapping into ours.Here’s what’s in it for you: – we’ll help refine your story so it truly shines.Multiple permanent placements – across HackerNoon, plus social media amplification. – your articles converted into audio format and distributed via RSS feeds. – automatic translation into 12-76 languages.SEO & domain authority boost– piggyback on HackerNoon’s trusted brand to strengthen your search rankings.Meet HackerNoon Projects of the Week turns scattered geopolitical signals into a decision-ready view for people who need to understand how conflict and energy disruption move markets. The platform continuously pulls oil benchmark pricing, macroeconomic series, equity and FX data, and global news, then runs that material through an AI analysis layer to produce a country-level Stress Index and scenario briefs. is a free, open-source Windows application designed to diagnose internet connection issues and translate complex network errors into simple, everyday language. By rolling multiple diagnostic and VPN tools into a single streamlined platform, Anton aims to make networking accessible to everyone. is a live crypto market data API that AI agents pay for per call in USDC over x402, with no account, key or subscription. It runs on its own tape of every liquidation across 799 perpetual futures on Bybit, OKX and Binance, which no exchange publishes historically, so it can only be recorded and never bought. Every response says whether the answer was measured, absent from the market, or unmeasured because our own lookup failed, and unmeasured is never billed.That’s all for this week.Until next time, Hackers!

item.title: 20 Repos, 713K Stars: The Open Source Tools That Build, Tune and Run Language Models
item.author: Text Mining
item.content:encoded: huggingface/transformers is the most-starred repo in the whole directory, at 169.4K. This week it added 100 stars. OpenVINO, Intel's inference toolkit, has 12.8K stars and added 1.3K, thirteen times as many. That gap says where the work is now. Most teams no longer write a model from scratch. They pick one that already exists, tune it on their own data, and then fight to make it run fast and cheap on the hardware they have.Every repo below comes from TextMining.Tech, HackerNoon's directory of 7,075 open source text mining tools, libraries and frameworks with at least 100 stars each. They're grouped by job: define the model, train or fine-tune it, then run it.This is part 2 of a four-part series. Part 1 covered the tools that read documents, retrieve context and teach you to build. Speech and voice come next.Running models is where the momentum is. The six run-and-deploy repos added about 1.9K stars this week, more than the other 14 repos combined (about 1.2K).OpenVINO out-gained transformers 13 to 1. It added 1.3K stars this week against transformers' 100, from a base one-thirteenth the size.A 1.2K-star newcomer is moving. halo, White Circle's training framework, added 316 stars this week, about a quarter of its total.Old training repos keep their stars. stanford_alpaca (last updated July 2024) and Open-Assistant (August 2024) still hold 67.5K stars between them.LlamaFactory is the fine-tuning default. At 76.3K stars, it has more than Megatron-LM, ml-engineering and halo combined (39.4K). 12 of the 20 repos use Apache-2.0, 3 use MIT and 5 use another license.Define the model: 7 repos, 313K starsThese repos hold the models themselves, or the code and data that define them. transformers is the hub most of the others plug into; the rest are model families built for a language, a domain or a different way of answering.The model-definition framework for text, vision, audio and multimodal models, for inference and trainingNon-autoregressive engine that makes typed choice, score and yes/no decisions over text in one forward pass, in 100+ languagesMicrosoft's large-scale self-supervised pre-training across tasks, languages and modalitiesReady-to-use datasets for AI models, with tools to load and transform themAlibaba Cloud's official repo for the original Qwen chat and pretrained modelsChinese LLaMA and Alpaca models, with local CPU and GPU training and deploymentlaya added nearly three times as many stars as transformers this week, from a base a fifth the size.Train and fine-tune: 7 repos, 228K starsOnce you have a base model, these repos adapt it to your data or train new ones at scale. They range from a one-stop fine-tuning toolkit to the distributed systems behind frontier-scale training, plus two 2023-era projects that taught a generation how instruction tuning works.Unified, efficient fine-tuning for 100+ LLMs and vision-language models (ACL 2024)Distributed compute engine with libraries for scaling training and other ML workloadsCommunity-built chat assistant project, including its crowd-sourced training dataCode and data generation for training Stanford's Alpaca instruction-tuned modelsAn open book on the engineering of training and running large modelsNVIDIA's research code for training transformer models at scaleWhite Circle's framework for training large language and multimodal modelshalo is the smallest repo in this series so far, and it added more stars this week than anything else in this group.Run and deploy: 6 repos, 172K starsA tuned model is only useful once it answers requests. These repos run models locally, compile them for phones and browsers, wire them into apps, and watch what they do in production.Self-hosted engine that runs LLMs, vision, voice, image and video models on any hardware, no GPU requiredAI engineering platform with a gateway, agent observability, evals and prompt management, built on OpenTelemetryVercel's AI SDK for building AI-powered apps and agents in TypeScriptUniversal LLM deployment engine that uses ML compilation to target many devicesHigh-performance LLM inference that runs inside the browserThe smallest repo in this group gained the most: OpenVINO's 1.3K stars this week topped the whole Natural Language Processing category.All numbers come from the TextMining.Tech snapshot of Nov 26, 2026. The directory tracks open source GitHub repos with at least 100 stars, excludes archived repos and forks, and refreshes daily. We started from the top repos in the Language Models and Natural Language Processing categories and kept the ones that define, train or run models. "Added this week" is the directory's own weekly star count. Stars will have moved by the time you read this, so each repo name links to its live directory page.What's next, and where to dig furtherPart 3 is speech and voice. VoiceStudio, a fully local voice cloning, dubbing and transcription suite, added 4.9K stars this week, more than all 20 repos in this list combined.Or open the full directory of 7,075 repos, sort by "Trending this week", and see what's climbing before it makes the next list. Built something that belongs here? Once it passes 100 stars, it's in.

item.title: Credit card skimming scripts using WebRTC found on popular shopping sites
item.content:encoded:
Which sites were affected On November 24, we notified all of the named parties in this article and others, including: Amazon Web Services about the storage buckets serving the script, Cloudflare about the services the malefactor used, the domain registrars, the pixel vendor, the consent-banner provider and the affected retailers and platforms. Lascana replied to us and removed the Quorum pixel from their site by November 24th at 15:48 UTC. Quorum confirmed the identified malicious code was removed from their pixel tracker, and they restored the clean marketing pixel as of November 24th at 21:09 UTC.
Revolve provided this statement on behalf of REVOLVE and FWRD: “On November 25, InfoHawk notified our team of a potential security issue impacting mobile and tablet versions of our websites which we resolved the same day. We appreciate the outreach, and are actively investigating the issue to determine any potential impact.” Quorum is an ad-attribution platform that links ad views to store visits and online sales (quorum.inc). Seers is a cookie consent management platform and data privacy compliance company (seers.ai).
This attack uses WebRTC, the technology that allows you to make video calls in your web browser. WebRTC lets a web page open its own channel to another party and pass data (e.g. audio/video packets) over it. It has likely been used (both to load the skimmer and to send the stolen card details out) because security rules and monitoring tools often do not watch this communications channel as closely. For example, Meta briefly used WebRTC in a creative way in 2025, according to researchers looking at the technology as a compromise vector. This form of attack appears to target mobile devices, and we only saw the server enable the skimmer on checkout pages, so desktop checks and homepage scans would likely not see it. The skimmer's traffic appeared to run through Cloudflare's relay, so it would blend in with the WebRTC traffic and hide its true endpoint.
The skimmer and card details both traveled over WebRTC
How the kit is designed to work on a store page, in 7 steps. Only step 4 is an ordinary web request, which a rule can block; steps 5 to 7 run over the WebRTC data channel, outside .
The loader gets onto the page through a consent-banner setting, a retailer CDN file, a shared marketing pixel or the store's own HTML. Loading scripts from S3 buckets It loads or from an Amazon S3 bucket. Targeting the attack to mobile checkouts It runs only on small or touch screens. The Samsonite version runs on only. Establishing the WebRTC connection fetches the relay details, and sends the WebRTC offer, to a brand-named host. Data exchange via TURN relay Every exchange that returned relay details used . The malefactor's answers listed only Cloudflare relay addresses; through that relay it sends code and receives data. Attack code is loaded and executed The skimmer arrives in chunks over the channel, is checked against a SHA-256 digest, then run with . Data goes back the same way At Lascana's checkout, the skimmer sent our test card details this way. This was the only example of live card details being sent off-site that we captured. Worried that your card was compromised? Check your recent statements for charges you don't recognize, especially on debit cards. Call your bank or card issuer right away, report the fraud and ask for a new card number. Follow up with a written dispute within 60 days of the statement that shows the charge.
Our understanding of US federal law is that your liability for unauthorized credit card charges is capped at $50, and is generally zero if only your card number was stolen, as in a skimming attack like this one. Debit cards have weaker protections that depend on how quickly you report, so act fast. For more information, see “Additional resources” below. What site owners should immediately do On every page that takes payment, set a rule that lists only the hosts you use.
That blocks the two web requests the script needs before WebRTC opens. Without them the skimmer never arrives, whichever file was tampered with. What security teams should look for We saw the skimmer delivered in three different ways across five websites run by different companies, and all of them appear to rely on the same attacker infrastructure. That makes it likely that other sites are affected too, so we encourage online retailers to check their own sites for the signs below. search page source, tag managers, consent-banner settings and CDN files for scripts from <brand>-static.s3.amazonaws[.]com (files , ). We believe this is the malicious code. if you load qscripts.s3.amazonaws[.]com/pscript.js, check its last line for one of the above CDN buckets, and if present, remove the tracking pixel. We recommend reviewing all similar tracking pixels and their exposure to sensitive fields or actions on your website. If you have integrated Seers, open your banner config (cdn.seersco.com/banners/<account>/<domain>/cb.js) and check that every URL field holds only a URL. In the affected configs, the privacy-policy link field also held a hidden image, whose event handler loaded the malicious code. on a phone-sized touch screen, at the payment step, look for and requests to and a relay-only WebRTC connection used by the malicious code. Desktop checks miss it. , and are referenced in the malicious code and may warrant further investigation if present.
The industry is not ready for the scale of supply chain attacks coming
This attack takes advantage of a few critical design decisions in websites that, if improperly configured, allow malicious actors to broadly deploy and trigger exploits across the open web.
Websites load third-party code, often through a tag manager, from servers they don't control. The vendor can change that code at any time, and it can pull in further third-party code the site never reviewed.
That code runs as an ordinary script with the same rights as the site's own code. It can read and rewrite the page, watch what users type, and load more code.
Login, personal-information and payment pages often load the same marketing scripts as the rest of the site. Card fields should sit in an isolated payment frame, and third-party tags should be kept off these pages entirely.
Loading third-party tracking pixels on checkout, payment and login pages is far too common a practice today. Each pixel can run whatever code its vendor's file holds, including a skimmer, and whoever controls that file can change it without the site noticing. Every site should review which tracking pixels load on pages that take payment or sign-in details, who can change those files, and whether they need to be there at all.
A similar weakness was exploited at scale on 16 November 2026. An attacker reportedly used a flaw in Optimizely's Web Experimentation product to add malicious code to customers' projects, and Optimizely's own servers delivered it to visitors of 178 organizations' sites, including Zoom, the BBC and CNN, with no change to those sites' own code.

item.title: T5-Small Out-Downloads NLLB 24 to 1: 143 Open-Weight Translation Models Ranked
item.author: Writings, Papers and Blogs on Text Models
item.content:encoded: Google's t5-small was downloaded 17.3M times on Hugging Face in the last 30 days. Meta's 200-language nllb-200-distilled-600M got 709.4K. Below are all 143 translation models in the TextModels directory: open weights ranked by downloads, including 73 Opus-MT language pairs from Helsinki-NLP, plus the historical models that started neural machine translation.Downloads and capability tell different stories here. NLLB-200 covers 200 languages, and HackerNoon's look inside the AI that translates 200 languages explains how it lifted quality for low-resource languages. But t5-small is a 60M-parameter multitask model that tutorials and test suites load by default. For production in specific language pairs, teams still reach for dedicated models, as in this production voice stack for Igbo, Yoruba and Hausa that chose NLLB over an LLM.Helsinki-NLP is the long tail. 73 of the 143 entries are its Opus-MT models, one per language pair.English to Russian leads the pairs.opus-mt-en-ru is the most-downloaded single-pair model at 566.9K.Everything comes from the TextModels directory as of November 23, 2026, filtered to translation models (143 entries). Hugging Face download counts are the last 30 days from the Hugging Face API. "Verified" means the directory fetched and confirmed that model's metrics. Hosted models have no public download counts, so they're listed by price or provider, and historical models link to their papers.Part 1: 127 open-weight translation models on Hugging Face, ranked by 30-day downloadsPart 2: 16 historical translation models that got us hereFilter all 3,009 models by task, size, context window, price and license in the TextModels directory.

item.title: False computer-checked proofs
item.content:encoded:
D. J. BernsteinProofs There are some computer programs that claim to check every step in a proof. However, various "soundness bugs" have been reported that at least potentially allowed false statements to slip past these programs. In many cases, these bugs have been demonstrated to be exploitable.
The list at the bottom of this page links to what appear to be reports of soundness bugs for various important proof-checking programs, sorted in increasing order of the number of reports. This list includes many more soundness bugs for these programs than the bugs mentioned in 2026 Paulson and 2026 Stérin, and I don't think the list is missing any of the bugs mentioned there, but I've probably missed some reports. Please let me know about any corrections or additions.
Beware that this list doesn't include user-interface vulnerabilities. Those can have the same important effect of misleading a user as to what has been proven. See, e.g., 2016 Adams.
One standard path towards security is to minimize the complexity of the trusted computing base, which by definition is the part of the system that security reviewers need to check. From this perspective, HOL Light's proof-checking kernel is attractive because of its stability and simplicity, only 400 lines of code. But this size measurement doesn't say how carefully the HOL Light code has been reviewed, and doesn't say anything about the possibility of bugs in the underlying programming language.
Extra code can be when it's test code. A battery of tests tends to catch more bugs than a single test. Running a proof through multiple proof-checking programs (preferably each in its own isolated environment) can save the day when there's a bug in one program, and is particularly easy if the checkers take the same input language for writing proofs. But it's not clear how effective this is at stopping attacks: for example, sometimes bugs are shared by multiple checkers.
The question "Who watches the provers?" is better answered by a proof saying that a checker works correctly. A close translation of the inference rules in the HOL Light kernel, except for the rules to introduce new definitions, was already proven in 2006 to generate only correct theorems. That proof was also checked by HOL Light. (For readers familiar with logic: of course this assumes a large cardinal; V is enough for HOL Light. The same paper also has a variant of the proof that skips the large-cardinal assumption, at the expense of omitting the axiom of infinity from the logic being proven.)
After more work, a clone of HOL Light called Candle was proven in 2022 to allow only proofs of correct theorems, as long as the CPU implements the instructions used in the Candle binary in the expected way. This proof is again computer-checked, this time in another proof-checking system, HOL4. There was also a computer-checked proof in 2022 of the correctness of a standalone proof checker for HOL proofs in OpenTheory format.
From a security perspective, it's still concerning to be relying on large proof-checking binaries, where the answer to why we're supposed to trust one binary is that the binary has supposedly been checked by another large proof-checking binary. I'd like to see more work on simplifying these binaries.

item.title: Your Firewall Isn't Enough: The Hidden Risk of Unmanaged VMs
item.author: Sponsored by ISPsystem
item.content:encoded: Forgotten virtual machines, unpatched servers, and excessive access permissions can create security blind spots across IT infrastructure. ISPsystem explains how centralized infrastructure management, access controls, and resource lifecycle automation can help reduce these risks. [...]
