item.title: Rayshader 1.0: Exit the Matrix
item.content:encoded: Stay for the credits Be sure to read to the end for what I can guarantee is the most exciting and cinematric R package bibliography you’ve ever seen. Everything you see in the below blog post was rendered in R with the rayverse.Eight years ago, rayshader started as a small experiment in making beautiful maps in R. The first version was based on a simple question: what if we combined raytracing and cartography? I had always been interested in learning both about mapping and pathtracing, and what better way than to combine the two ideas into a single R package? The big “aha!” moment came when I applied that method with interactive 3D terrain for the first time and took it for a spin. Figure 1: Left: The original spinning 3D rayshader map made in 2018. Right: We’ve come a long way. The surface was no longer just a shaded map: it felt tangible and real, a 3D rectangle twirling like a Little Debbie cosmic brownie on a microwave turntable. The combination of cartographic hillshading and 3D raytraced terrain looked spectacular in a way that, at the time, mostly lived in bespoke Blender scenes or other advanced 3D modeling tools. And unlike Blender, you didn’t need to learn a whole new ecosystem to visualize your data in 3D: it lived in the same place your data did (R!), which allowed for a gentler learning curve.But as time went on and the package and userbase expanded, I had a nagging feeling: rayshader was still too hard.Not always, of course: plenty of people were using it, quite effectively. Simple use cases were fine: pass in a matrix, add a few layers, call , and suddenly you had a cool-looking 3D landscape. If that’s all you needed: great! But if the story you were trying to tell was about data within the landscape–well, that’s where the friction began to burn.I built rayshader for people who wanted to make data beautiful without leaving R. Beauty has a real purpose in the world: it draws people’s eyes. It doesn’t matter how accurate or well-constructed your map is if the reader swipes on by: in the market for human attention, beauty and form are table stakes.Journalists understood that quickly, and were some of rayshader’s earliest adopters.The Wall Street Journal’s The Future of Arctic Shipping used detailed shipping, bathymetric, and ice coverage data to explain the complexities of the Northern Sea Route. The piece was recognized by the Information is Beautiful Awards, which described it as a deeply researched story built from shipping, bathymetric, and ice coverage data. It appeared only a few months after I released rayshader: talk about an introduction! Bloomberg’s 2024 Gaza rebuilding story, Gaza Reduced to 42 Million Tonnes of Rubble. What Will It Take to Rebuild?, used R, rayshader, and rayrender as part of the visual system for communicating the scale of destruction and debris in Gaza. And in June 2022, a rayshader 3D flood visualization appeared on the front page of The Sydney Morning Herald, inset into coverage of the Lismore flooding.A June 30, 2022 front page of The Sydney Morning Herald showing a rayshader flood visualization inset into Lismore flooding coverage.That last one stuck with me (and not only because a rayshader map was featured “above the fold” in a major newspaper!). Rayshader had started as a way to make beautiful data visualizations in R, but here it was being used in deadline journalism to help explain a disaster to a general audience. The package had left the domain of “fun engaging social media posts” and entered the visual language of public-interest reporting.But getting a reader to stop scrolling is only half the problem. Working with journalists taught me how much friction stood between having the data and making the final product. A newsroom deadline is a very good detector of bad API design. If adding buildings takes half a day of coordinate fiddling, that feature might as well not exist. If a 3D path requires a hand-rolled coordinate transform pipeline, nobody is doing that 30 minutes before a deadline. If a pathtraced render looks great but takes too long to converge, it is not going to make it to print. Especially if the editor needs a slight tweak: “Oh, sure–just give me 8 hours to re-render the animation.” Ha. Nope.Working with journalists taught me how much friction stood between having the data and making the final product.The problem wasn’t so much with rayshader itself: it was how much spatial bookkeeping and manual fiddling you had to do to get data into rayshader before you could do all the fun stuff. And at the root of all that bookkeeping was the humble matrix, rayshader’s original choice for representing terrain.The problem with matricesRayshader used matrices to represent terrain because it simplified a lot of the work that went into turning a bunch of elevation values in a 3D object. But most real data does not arrive nicely packaged as a plain rectangular numeric array. It arrives as georeferenced rasters, polygons, lines, and points. It arrives cloaked in an unknown coordinate reference system. It arrives in meters, feet, yards, degrees, or German legal metres Choosing the matrix as the base input made it easy for me, the developer, by putting the spatial problem (mostly) on the user.Convert the raster to a matrix. Save the extent. Transform the vector data. Save the CRS. Crop the linework. Pass the heightmap again. Pass the extent again. Wait, is the extent format lat/long/lat/long or lat/lat/long/long? I never remember–whatever, try both. The first choice is (somehow!) always wrong. Pass again. Resize the overlay. Pass the CRS again. Check whether the map is oriented correctly. No? Surprise! Errant minus sign. Yuck.This was not just annoying for beginners. It annoyed me, and I wrote the damn thing: now that’s a usability red flag! The new version of rayshader includes a series of changes that gets rid of all of this overhead and allows you to focus on presentation instead of the data processing.rayshader has gained object permanenceThe big change in rayshader 1.0 is this: rayshader no longer has short-term amnesia. Rayshader now keeps track of all the spatial details from your underlying map so you don’t have to worry about it any more.This changes the user experience from:Transform and pass in your data into an aligned matrix coordinate system, and rayshader will render it in beautiful 3D.and rayshader will render it in beautiful 3D.The black diamond learning curve is now a gentle bunny slope. Terrain can stay a spatial raster. Road can stay a spatial line and will automatically be converted to the correct coordinate system when plotting. Buildings can be passed in as spatial polygons and will automatically be cropped to the underlying map’s extent.A rayshader scene now extracts and caches the important metadata from the input data: heightmap, extent, CRS, , vertical exaggeration, and rendered-object metadata. That cache lets downstream calls do the thing users always wanted them to do: simply drop data into the scene.Most of the functions can now add to the scene simply by passing the data, plus an optional argument that specifies altitude or height, either directly or through a column in an object. The rest of the arguments then focus on how you want to style the data.For example, let’s load in some road and elevation data and see what the new API looks like. The code below defines the helpers and loads the data into R. There’s no rayshader in it, so you have absolutely no obligation to read it :).Transform to a UTM CRS (so everything is in meters)Pass in our lat/long bounding boxPretty straightforward… just kidding, loading geospatial data is always a pain. Nothing I can do about that! But the real question is: how complex is visualizating all this data once it’s loaded?Not complex at all! You call the function named after the type of data… and it renders the data in the scene. Any additional arguments are just for styling the data to your liking.And the payoff is not just less typing: it lets us get to the fun part of 3D data visualization faster. The coolest part of rayshader has always been building strikingly beautiful 3D landscapes from your data. But the third dimension raises the cognitive cost of entry: before you can play director and cinematographer, you have to build the set. When every point, path, and polygon needs the user to track the CRS and extent info themselves and transform the data appropriately, many users never get to the stage where they can experiment with lighting and composition, styling the data (costume design!), or focus on editing the overall narrative.The third dimension raises the cognitive cost of entry: before you can play director and cinematographer, you have to build the set.This release automates almost all of the behind-the-scenes work. The boring parts–CRS juggling, extent passing, heightmap repetition, matrix conversion, and other bookkeeping–stay in the package internals. The user is then free to jump to the enjoyable creative roles: the executive producer of the analysis, the production designer of the world, or the sound designer of a multi-sensory data experience.Spatial data: free yourself from the matrix!Rayshader now accepts many more spatial inputs for the heightmap. The function can now accept a heightmap as a matrix, a , a object, or a raster filename. When the input is spatial, rayshader extracts and caches the extent and CRS. If is not supplied, rayshader derives it from raster cell resolution. If the raster is geographic longitude/latitude, rayshader estimates the meter-per-cell scale at the raster center. The data was always there; it just had to be piped around to the right place! Now I do the plumbing for you.Let’s look at an example. The same DEM and main-road data feed both versions below. The difference is who’s now doing the spatial bookkeeping (hint: it’s not you).Internally, rayshader still converts the raster to something it can render. Externally, the scene remembers enough to let the functions just work.There is now also a cleaner division between physical scale and visual exaggeration. now describes the relationship between horizontal and vertical units, while describes the stylistic exaggeration. For spatial rasters, rayshader can derive from the raster itself, placing the data at its physical scale. You can then adjust to emphasize the terrain without changing the underlying unit conversion.And this spatial data directionality can now be reversed. turns a rayshader image, matrix, RGB array, or RGBA array back into a georeferenced . It can inherit the cached extent and CRS from the active scene, convert rayshader’s linear color values to sRGB, and optionally append the source heightmap as an additional raster layer. So rayshader’s output can now feed back into other GIS software, rather than just assume rayshader is the final destination itself.This release lets rayshader fit into a real spatial workflow: spatial input, then rayshader styling, followed by spatial output. So you can generate beautiful hillshades and terrains in R, and then bring them into other spatial software like QGIS or ArcGIS. Work in the GIS interface you already know, render the terrain in R, and drop the result right back into your map.A watershed moment for rayshader waterRayshader’s water was always a bit of an afterthought: it was good for rendering an ocean with bathymetry data, but it didn’t really work if the water was localized to one portion of the map. A lake halfway up a mountain shouldn’t require flooding everything below it to see the water, but rayshader’s old water meshing method assumed one water level for the whole map. Which was perfect if all you needed was that one large body of water: set a level and fill the scene to that height. Separate lakes, reservoirs at different elevations, and imperfect shorelines called for something more flexible.Now water can arrive as a raster or a polygon, high in the mountains or below sea level. uses the terrain and coordinates already stored in the scene to properly place and render the water in a sane way. Water can follow grid cells with water_render_method = "raster" or preserve polygon boundaries with the default, water_render_method = "polygon". Both draw a watertight mesh at the footprint and elevation you supply, even when that means an exposed vertical water wall where the supplied shoreline doesn’t quite meet the terrain. Fast, flexible, and suitable for the rare case where you need to visualize Moses crossing the Red Sea. Figure 6: The optimized method (right) fits its shoreline to the terrain; the raster method (left) uses that exact fitted elevation. Raster edge expansion is disabled () to keep the grid-cell boundary visible–otherwise, the expansion would hide the edges in the ground. Another (much cooler, IMO) option is water_render_method = "optimized". It fits a closed shoreline to the actual 3D terrain mesh, adjusting the water elevation to match the supplied area. Using the elevations beneath your water footprint to seed candidate levels, the optimizer searches for a contour that comes as close as possible to the supplied water area without spilling out of the terrain. The animation below shows how candidate levels change the flooded area. Figure 7: Fitting the lake to its basin: candidate levels change the flooded area. The dark outline follows the actual triangle-clipped water polygon at each candidate level. If no closed water body is possible—for example, the supplied water would flood the entire map—rayshader falls back to raster water.A different problem arises when a DEM has no bathymetry: the lake bed and its surface occupy the same plane. is a new function that can lower the terrain beneath a lake polygon before you add water, making room for the lake instead of letting the surfaces overlap. It can also raise terrain SimCity 2000-style (no tornados or alien invasions… yet).Additionally, in , water can now use a rough dielectric material to spread reflections into the broad highlights you expect from a rippled lake. A perfectly smooth dielectric surface behaves like glass: reflected light stays coherent, so lakes and rivers can turn into polished sheets. Real water has small wind-driven ripples, each reflecting light in a slightly different direction. The microfacet material models this give a more realistic appearance to bodies of water, especially when viewed at a low angle. Figure 8: Glassy water on the left; microfacet water on the right. Rayshader: now streaming!Streams need to follow the terrain as they wind downhill. takes spatial line data, samples the elevation along each path, and builds ribbons of water that hug the surface. Widths can vary by feature, and connected streams can be merged to reduce visible seams in high-quality renders. Put those streams together with lakes and you have a hydrologic scene driven by data.Note that there’s no complex GIS concepts on the rayshader side: all the complexity is related to defining the visual style and appearance. As it should be–rayshader is a visualization package! The remaining complexity is just standard data complexity present in any analysis: get the data loaded, cleaned, and in a form that represents the thing you care about.The road to believable roads3D maps might seem like a fun little toy rather than a serious class of data visualization, but the third dimension is often surprisingly important for understanding geospatial data. This becomes less surprising when you realize that the most common mapping tool used by regular people–GPS apps–use 3D quite extensively. When you’re traveling through a city, buildings give you landmarks to match to your surroundings; on a walking or cycling route, the terrain shows where you’ll be climbing; and at a complex highway interchange, seeing which roads pass over one another helps you follow the right ramp and choose the right exit.I already had surface-hugging polygons working for streams. Swap the water for asphalt and there’s a road! Easy, peasy, right?No! What’s the issue? We’re spoiled with our GPS apps: we’re used to roads looking like roads. A strip of grey asphalt needs lane markings for someone to know it’s a road. With the help of some fun repeating UV coordinate tricks and our new spatial-first workflow, we can paint properly-sized lines on the road at the cost of a few small textures. And we can use the lane counts supplied in OpenStreetMap data to add the correct number of lanes to each road. Rayshader uses those counts to mesh and texture the road, while the scene’s spatial information keeps the markings correctly sized.In Figure 11, each dash is 10 feet long and each gap is 30 feet. Those familiar markings do double duty: they improve the picture and act as little scale bars scattered through the scene. Beautiful! Pack it up, put a bow on it, and move on to the next feature, right?No! Our roads are still smooshed together on one layer. At an interchange, that borders on uninterpretable.OpenStreetMap doesn’t provide a full 3D road model. But it does carry one tiny (but extremely useful!) nugget of vertical information needed to draw roads correctly in 2D: . Draw layer 0, then layer 1, then layer 2, and the right road appears on top. That tells us which road crosses over which; it doesn’t tell us their heights or how the ramps return to ground level. Is this enough information to fully reconstruct our 3D roads?The tempting shortcut is to turn each layer into a fixed height: find the crossings, lift each road by a standard overpass height, and ease it back toward the ground with some sort of ad hoc relaxation rule. What could go wrong?Everything. Everything can go wrong.Simple hacks? Don’t work here. Turns out the world is filled with little annoying complications like a bridge crossing a sunken highway (the highway is already below ground, so the bridge needs no change in elevation), or short segments in interchanges that are technically not stacked but fall between stacked layers, or places where the road is technically stacked over a traversable water body (which also counts as a layer!), or a thousand other pesky little details.What are we to do then? How can we implement realistic highways? It’s not like there’s a manual with explicit guidance and standards for how roads should be built in 3D—wait, what is that? There is an explicit manual?The American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO) has a design manual for Interstate highways. Two of the things it covers are exactly what our map is missing. How much room does a truck need under a bridge? How steep can the road get on its way up there? Now that rayshader knows the scale of the scene, I can give the solver a clearance in feet and a maximum grade in percent. Here are the default settings I gave the road solver (these are customizable):Keeping crossing road surfaces at least 14 feet apartLimiting the road grade to 7%Ensuring roads default to hugging the ground when not part of an intersection and do not rise unnecessarilyWe can turn these requirements into constraints on the road heights. While the rules aren’t guaranteed to generate roads that match the real-world roads exactly, it’s going to be pretty close: excursions from the bare minimum allowable ruleset will usually only increase cost, and we’re talking government contracts here. Around each interchange, we discretize the roads into short segments and solve for their elevations together: maintain the crossing order and clearance, limit the grades, and keep the roads close to the terrain wherever possible.It’s not like there’s a manual with explicit guidance and standards for how roads should be built in 3D—wait, what is that? There is an explicit manual?For example, a road can weave over and under several others. Lifting one crossing changes the grades leading into the next, so solving each crossing independently won’t work–we have to solve all the linked constraints at once. We build a graph of the road connections with {igraph}, locate crossings with {sf}, and follow the constraints along connected road segments. Each connected optimization region gets a sparse quadratic problem, assembled with {Matrix} and solved with {osqp}. It turns out, R has everything you need to build and optimize road profiles.It’s pretty cool how closely a set of road-design rules and OSM’s layer ordering can recreate a complex interchange. The layer tags tell us which road goes over which, and the rules guide how the ramps connect them. Here’s Houston, now modeled in a sane way:Beautiful. And since I went to Houston for this year’s Posit::conf, I was able to drive over specific intersections I rendered here and confirm that yes: the roads were accurately meshed. Minus the traffic.The novelty seeking half of my brain immediately followed this thought with: “You should put in cars now!” to which the logical, killjoy side of my brain responded “NO! STOP IT! YOU’VE IMPLEMENTED TOO MANY FEATURES ALREADY! You will never release this update if you keep indulging yourself! Stop it!”A human battery? No–a human measuring stick.Lane markings made the scale of a scene easier to read. Naturally, that led me to the ultimate human-scale feature: humans! But I couldn’t just throw the first set of free human models I found on the internet into the package. I did a fairly extensive search for a suitable pre-made model with both male and female variants, but to no avail. I had some requirements:Low-poly enough to fit in the package when compressed (an R package is limited to 5 MB).Proportioned like actual people, which rules out a surprising number of free models.I couldn’t find a model that met these requirements with a suitable redistribution license. So I decided this was a great opportunity to learning something new: mesh sculpting in VR! I pulled out my Quest 3 and downloaded Shapelabs, which after a bit of practice and futzing around got me exactly what I wanted. Low-poly, but still human enough that you can read the pose at a glance.From Shapelabs, the models went into Blender as GLB files for rigging and posing, then out as compact OBJ meshes for the package:Male models on a dark blue podium.Female models on a dark red podium. Figure 18: My inspiration for these poses were 1) many hours playing Human Fall Flat, 2) the guy who’s about to crack his head open on every “wet floor” caution sign, and 3) philadelphia Compressed, they’re roughly 18–21 KB each, checking the filesize box. Both model variants stand about 6 feet tall, with consistent proportions across their poses. Finally, a unit of measurement you can relate to!The original was based on a simple idea: take a ggplot2 object, turn a fill or color aesthetic into height, and map the original plot onto that extruded surface. This made it possible to create 3D ggplots without learning a separate 3D plotting API. Just drop in your existing plot and poof! A 3D version would appear.But this came with one limitation: the data had to be attached to the surface.Floating data needs something to ground it. I originally kept the data attached to the surface deliberately: actual 3D data is harder to understand on a 2D screen, since depth is ambiguous. Extruded 2D surfaces provide a continuous underlying substrate, which makes interpretation easier–the surface itself provides depth cues, by nature of surface continuity providing cues on depth ordering. It’s not hard to plop down some floating 3D data in a box and call it a day: before rayshader, that was what pretty much every 3D plotting library I encountered did. In my opinion, that lazy approach helped give 3D dataviz its terrible reputation. Adding 3D data disconnected from that substrate requires additional care and thought to keep the data interpretable.Which rayshader now provides!In rayshader 1.0, is much more tightly integrated with the family of functions that add real 3D data to the scene. Rayshader now extracts the data extent from the existing ggplot2 scene. Basically, we now track how ggplot2 transforms data into the image, so we can use the same transformation for our 3D data. Downstream render calls can use that extent to place real 3D geometry in the correct part of the plot. The ggplot is no longer just a surface extrusion: it’s now the base coordinate system for a complete 3D scene.And this can really help visually, as that surface extrusion wasn’t ideal for certain types of data. The original raster extrusion worked well for smooth surfaces, density plots, and continuous fields, but sharp polygon boundaries and abrupt vertical edges were harder.Take Figure 19: it shows a map of US states with height mapped to population. States share an boundary in the source polygons, but when rasterized to row of pixels, you can see the colors bleed down the step between states. This is an unavoidable problem when you try to force vector data into a raster format. So we avoid it by drawing the actual 3D data. On the right, each state’s own polygon makes a crisp vertical wall.Raster extrusion: transition regions get blurred between colors.Vector extrusion: each state has a continuous polygon edge. Figure 19: State population mapped to the z-axis. The same integration lets individual points float above a flat ggplot2 substrate (enabled with plot_gg(..., flat_substrate = TRUE)). The ggplot establishes the scales and coordinate system, and rayshader adds the observed values as actual 3D points, positioned correctly. gives those floating marks a scale you can read. It picks up the height scale from the ggplot, and you can put the axis inside a panel or along the outer edge of the plot. If you have facets, you can pick the panel. It works on regular terrain maps, too. Figure 20: Each point is one car in . Weight and fuel economy are on 2D ggplot2 axes, and its elevation gives the horsepower (noted in the z-axis). This removes a ton of visual compromises. Instead of forcing every feature to become part of the surface texture, we use the surface texture as the base and add the features as real 3D geometry. The plot layout and elements are still determined by ggplot2: we’re just adding data to the z-axis. Faceted plots can receive geometry one panel at a time. Spatial plots built with carry their geographic transform into the scene, too. Your base plot can use familiar geoms—, , , , or —while rayshader adds polygons, points, paths, and a labeled z-axis in those coordinates.3D ggplots were always a cool, sometimes useful novelty. Now they can be a foundation for complex 3D visualizations. How complex are we talking about? Watch me demo it below with a data visualization showing ADSB flight path data over Washington, DC. Come fly over the National Mall with me and I’ll walk you through how deep the 3D rabbit hole goes.Better buildings, paths, labels, and objectsThe functions have been rewritten around the same principle: spatial data already encodes where it is, so there is no reason to throw that information out. can accept spatial point objects. can accept spatial line objects. can accept points, multipoints, polygons, and multipolygons, converting polygon inputs to centroids when needed. and render_beveled_polygons() use cached heightmap and extent metadata. uses spatial footprints, roof materials, roof angles, height columns, and CRS-aware extent filtering. can place OBJ models using spatial point data. You can see most of these in action in Figure 22.There’s some new basic hillshading options as well. adds an RGBA haze overlay based on an exponential atmospheric model. It is useful for low-elevation haze, valley haze, and scenes where you want the atmosphere to participate in the map rather than sit behind it. It is a good way to subtly separate mountain tops from valleys. Figure 23: Haze fades in and out as the terrain rotates, softening low valleys while leaving higher ground clearer. renders a top-down radiance pass from a cached hillshade context, the active 3D scene, or a supplied heightmap. It gives 2D maps and 3D ggplot2 workflows access to more visually-striking physically based lighting without forcing the entire project into a final path-traced render. This is a nice way to get higher-quality shadows on a model you can still rotate and revise quickly. The result is still an RGBA overlay, so it can be composited back into the usual rayshader map pipeline or exported to other programs.For a small area, we can usually ignore Earth’s curvature. As a map grows to cover hundreds or thousands of kilometers, the bend of the Earth can become an important part of the story. For satellite orbits, long-distance flight paths, and regional coverage maps, curvature can help signal to the reader that we’re dealing with global-scale data without an explicit scale bar.Setting in adds that curvature to the scene. Mountains and valleys can look flatter beside the much larger bend of the Earth when no vertical exaggeration is applied, but the adjustment gives those other GIS layers a more useful spatial context. Figure 25: Alaska and its neighbors with a flat surface (left) and Earth curvature enabled (right). For example, Figure 25 shows three Starlink satellites cross Alaska along paths calculated from real orbital data. Their simulated beams track populated places below, switching targets as they move within reach. Both views show the same moment, but on the right, the surface and orbital altitudes are adjusted to match the global curvature. This helps give the viewer important context clues for the spatial scales we’re dealing with here that the flat projection does not provide.Even higher quality Want to realistically light a scene at a very specific time and date? Just give rayshader a date and time–it already knows the place. For a scene with cached spatial coordinates, render_highquality(datetime = ...) can infer the location and generate the corresponding sky and sunlight. You don’t need to look up the latitude, longitude, or sun angle again. Depending on the sky model, that can include stars, planets, and the moon’s phase and brightness.As an example, around the equinoxes, the low sun lines up with the National Mall’s east–west axis—a favorite alignment for photographers. On March 25, 2026, at 6:56:11 p.m. EDT, the modeled shadow of the Washington Monument runs parallel to the Mall’s main paths. A few days past the equinox, the sun is still high enough at that alignment to keep the shadow within this view.And separately, text and annotation lines were physical objects in the rendered scene. Their letters and lines cast shadows across the terrain and buildings, giving annotations the same simulated weight as the things they were annotating. A label should help you read the map without becoming another object in it. Figure 27: Mount Rainier, Mount St. Helens, and Mount Adams turn with the terrain, but their labels always face you. The leader lines stay anchored to the volcano locations. Terrain heights use 4× vertical exaggeration. The labels in Figure 27 are drawn in screen space: their positions stay attached to the map, while the text keeps its size and faces the camera throughout the orbit, without casting shadows over the volcanoes. The horsepower axis in Figure 20 uses the same approach. The lines and text are composited in real time when you’re looking at the high quality preview render in rayrender, so you can set up the shot exactly how you want to. Oh, and you can set now as well, which removes the sample timer so you can have all the time in the world to set up your render. This is especially important now, since rayrender is now fully GPU-accellerated on ARM macs, leading to 30-50x speedups in rendering performance, so your render can often end before you got a chance to click on the screen. This blog post, however, is about rayshader, so I won’t steal its thunder talking about the awesome improvements in rayrender :)It’s been a long, properly textured road–why 1.0 after eight years? I now feel that rayshader has firmly found its niche and purpose, and this overhaul feels like a graduation moment for the package. I’m no longer figuring out what a 3D GIS workflow in R should feel like–it’s now about making that workflow work for you. And thinking about all the people who used rayshader to produce everything from beautiful generative art and frameable cartographic works to scientific articles and award winning journalism made me decide to give rayshader the graduation it deserves, and make sure it knows: You’re number 1.0!The grand finale and most exciting part of any publication: the bibliography.Rayshader wouldn’t be possible without the work of all the packages and people that supported it and provided great user feedback during its development. In a normal blog post, this is where normally you’d have a list of citations and people to thank. But how often does R’s most cinematic package get a 1.0 release? I decided the people, packages, and data behind rayshader deserved the full cinematic treatment that rayshader has provided the R ecosystem. And that the cinematic treatment should be created entirely in R, using rayrender, of course. Please stick around and hit play for the credits below—and be sure to turn the sound on.

item.title: Monthly Churn Times 12 Is Not Annual Churn
item.author: Malek Damiri
item.content:encoded:
A company reports 2.2% monthly churn. Someone multiplies by 12 and writes "about 26% annual churn" in the board deck. It looks like basic arithmetic. It's wrong twice, and the two errors don't cancel out.The first error is the one people half remember from school: churn compounds. The second is bigger and less well known: the customers who churn in a typical month are not the customers you had at the start of the year. In a growing business, those two groups behave very differently.Here's both, with a simulation and the SQL to get the real number.If you lose 2% of customers in January, you lose 2% of a smaller base in February. Over 12 months, you keep 98% of 98% of 98%, twelve times. That's 0.98 to the 12th power, or 78.5%. Annual churn is 21.5%, not 24%."""Monthly churn to annual: multiplying by 12 vs compounding.""" print("monthly x12 compounded") for m in (0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.08): print(f"{m:>6.0%} {12 * m:>5.0%} {1 - (1 - m) ** 12:>9.1%}")
def monthly_from_annual(a): return 1 - (1 - a) ** (1 / 12)
print(f"\n20% annual churn = {monthly_from_annual(0.20):.2%} a month, not {0.20 / 12:.2%}") monthly x12 compounded 1% 12% 11.4% 2% 24% 21.5% 3% 36% 30.6% 5% 60% 46.0% 8% 96% 63.2%
20% annual churn = 1.84% a month, not 1.67% At low churn, the difference is small. At 5% a month, multiplying says 60% and compounding says 46%. At 8% a month, multiplying says you lose nearly every customer in a year, which isn't what happens.The same mistake runs in reverse. A contract business with 20% annual churn that divides by 12 to get a monthly figure for a lifetime value model will understate monthly churn and overstate lifetime value.So: compound, don't multiply. But that's the small error.Error two: the wrong customersI simulated three years of a growing subscription business. The key assumption, which matches almost every real subscription business I've looked at, is that churn falls with tenure. New customers leave at 6% a month for their first three months, 2.5% a month until they reach a year, and 1% a month after that.First, the usual monthly churn rate for 2025: customers who cancelled in a month, divided by customers active at the start of that month, averaged over the year.-- monthly logo churn for 2025 (months 24 to 35): cancelled in the month / active at the start of the month with months as (select range as m from range(24, 36)), monthly as ( select m, count(*) filter (where c.start_month < m and (c.end_month is null or c.end_month >= m)) as active_at_start, count(*) filter (where c.end_month = m and c.start_month < m) as cancelled from months cross join customers c group by m ) select round(avg(cancelled / active_at_start), 4) as avg_monthly_churn, round(12 * avg(cancelled / active_at_start), 3) as times_12, round(1 - power(1 - avg(cancelled / active_at_start), 12), 3) as compounded from monthly; avg_monthly_churn times_12 compounded 0.0221 0.266 0.236 2.2% a month. Times 12 is 26.6%. Compounded is 23.6%.Now the question the board actually means: of the customers we had on January 1, how many had left by December 31?-- what actually happened to the customers active on January 1, 2025 select count(*) as active_jan_1, count(*) filter (where end_month is not null) as gone_by_dec_31, round(count(*) filter (where end_month is not null) / count(*), 3) as annual_churn from customers where start_month < 24 and (end_month is null or end_month >= 24); active_jan_1 gone_by_dec_31 annual_churn 3308 571 0.173 17.3%. The compounded monthly rate overstates it by six points. The multiplied rate overstates it by nine.The reason is who's in the monthly numbers. Every month, the denominator includes customers who joined recently, and recent customers churn the most. In a growing business there are always lots of them. But the January 1 cohort doesn't get any new customers during the year. It only gets older, and older customers churn less.Split the January 1 customers by how long they'd been customers:-- the same, by tenure on January 1 select case when 24 - start_month <= 3 then 'a: 0-3 months' when 24 - start_month <= 12 then 'b: 4-12 months' else 'c: over a year' end as tenure_on_jan_1, count(*) as customers, round(count(*) filter (where end_month is not null) / count(*), 3) as annual_churn from customers where start_month < 24 and (end_month is null or end_month >= 24) group by 1 order by 1; tenure_on_jan_1 customers annual_churn a: 0-3 months 676 0.257 b: 4-12 months 1430 0.176 c: over a year 1202 0.121 Customers who'd been around for more than a year lost only 12% over the next 12 months. Customers who were brand new lost 26%. The monthly churn rate is a blend of both, weighted toward new customers because a growing business keeps adding them.They answer different questions, so each is right for something.Monthly churn on the whole base tells you how much work customer success has this month and how much revenue you need to replace. It's an operational number. Use it to run the business month to month.Annual churn of a starting cohort tells you how durable the customer base is. "Of the customers we had a year ago, 83% are still here" is what investors and boards are asking about. Use it for anything that sounds like a year. tells you where the problem is. If new-customer churn is high and mature-customer churn is low, the problem is onboarding or fit, not the product. That's a very different fix.What isn't right for anything is monthly churn times 12. It mixes a rate that's dominated by new customers with a time frame that implies the starting base. In a fast-growing business, it can overstate annual churn by half.Everything here applies to revenue churn too, with one more complication: customers who expand often churn less, and larger customers often churn less than small ones. So revenue churn by month and revenue retention of a starting cohort can diverge even more than logo churn. Compute both from the same cohort query, swapping a count for a sum of recurring revenue.One more trap. If customers sign annual contracts, they can only leave at renewal. A monthly churn rate on an annual-contract book measures which month the renewals happen to fall in, not how likely customers are to leave. For annual contracts, measure churn per renewal: of the contracts that came up for renewal, what share renewed. Then if you need an annual figure, that's already it.Compound, don't multiply. Measure annual churn on a starting cohort, not by converting a monthly rate. And split by tenure, because the average hides the only thing you need to know: whether customers leave early or late.

item.title: TikTok Shop Is Changing the Relationship Between Brands and Content Creators
item.author: Sanya Kapoor
item.content:encoded: Image:-By Aidan Castillo, VP of Client Success at MediaLabsThe traditional consensus around influencer marketing primarily treated it as a means of generating awareness. Pay creators to introduce products to their audiences, hoping that attention eventually translates into sales.Influencer marketing is now becoming a bottom-of-funnel channel, and TikTok Shop is substantially driving that evolution.By integrating commerce directly into the content experience, the platform has made it possible for creators to influence purchasing decisions and facilitate transactions without directing consumers to external websites.For brands, the implications extend well beyond another digital sales channel.In my role as VP of Client Success at MediaLabs, I work with consumer brands developing their TikTok Shop strategies and the creators responsible for executing them.One of the most significant changes I've observed is the growing importance of creators who aren't necessarily traditional influencers.Historically, a creator's commercial value was closely tied to the size of their audience. Brands paid premiums for reach, even when the relationship between impressions and actual purchases was difficult to measure.The idea of genuinely social commerce introduces a different set of considerations.A creator with a relatively modest following can produce a video that directly generates substantial sales. Conversely, an established influencer with millions of followers isn't necessarily as readily equipped to sell a singular product directly.The distinction matters because content performance and commercial performance are not interchangeable.This changes how brands approach creator partnerships.Rather than concentrating their budgets on a handful of expensive sponsorships, companies can work with larger networks of creators, test different approaches and identify which content consistently generates purchases.At MediaLabs, our network includes more than 3,000 creators producing content for consumer brands.During the first quarter of 2026, creators across our network generated approximately $19.35 million in gross merchandise value for participating brands. We also launched 29 creator retainer campaigns during that period.These figures illustrate the scale at which creator-led commerce can operate, but they also point to an important operational challenge.Managing a few influencer relationships is relatively straightforward. Coordinating hundreds of creators, maintaining content quality, evaluating performance and ensuring brands have consistent support requires considerably more infrastructure.Training, creator selection, campaign management and ongoing communication become as important as the content itself.There's also a meaningful change taking place on the creator side.TikTok Shop has created opportunities for individuals to generate income through product recommendations without first establishing themselves as recognizable internet personalities.That doesn't mean earning a sustainable income is easy. Competition is substantial, content performance varies, and creators must continually adapt to changing consumer preferences.But the commercial opportunity is no longer reserved exclusively for people with enormous audiences.As social commerce develops, I expect brands to place greater emphasis on measurable sales performance, repeatable creator partnerships and the systems required to manage them.The companies that understand this distinction will be better positioned to evaluate TikTok Shop as a serious component of their broader e-commerce operations, rather than simply another outlet for influencer marketing.

item.title: How Context Graphs Speed Up Incident Response and Root Cause Analysis
item.author: PlayerZero
item.content:encoded: A context graph links telemetry, deployments, code changes and support tickets into one connected model, so incident responders can trace what caused a production issue without jumping between tools.Modern engineering teams already have the data they need to resolve incidents faster, reduce downtime, and ship with more confidence. The problem is that this data's fragmented across too many systems, making it difficult to understand how production issues actually unfold. When something breaks in production, engineers still waste valuable time jumping between observability tools, deployment history, support tickets, analytics platforms, and pull requests just to answer a simple question: What actually caused this issue?That manual reconstruction slows incident response, pulls senior engineers away from roadmap work, and increases the operational cost of every release.Context graphs solve this by connecting production signals into a shared reasoning layer that goes beyond code as the sole debugging surface. They connect telemetry, user impact, infrastructure events, and code changes into a unified system for understanding not just what happened, but why.This guide explains why production understanding breaks down in modern systems and walks through three practical strategies for building a context graph that preserves operational context with every incident, instead of rebuilding it from scratch.Why production understanding breaks down in modern systemsModern engineering teams have invested heavily in specialized systems: observability platforms for infrastructure visibility, analytics tools for product insights, ticketing systems for customer operations, and CI/CD platforms for release orchestration.The problem is that these tools were never designed to preserve causality across the full production lifecycle. Each system captures a partial view of reality, but none preserves the relationships between them.Telemetry sees system behavior, not customer impactTelemetry platforms are excellent at exposing runtime behavior: latency spikes, infrastructure anomalies, failing traces, and degraded dependencies.But telemetry alone rarely explains:Which users were affectedWhether support is already seeing escalationsWhether the issue traces back to a recent deploymentA spike in API latency may appear in Datadog within seconds, but engineers still need to determine whether it’s breaking checkout or only affecting an internal admin tool, whether the issue is isolated to one customer segment or spreading across the platform, and whether it maps back to the latest release.As systems scale, a single runtime anomaly can propagate across dozens of services before teams understand the downstream customer impact.Analytics sees behavior, not system dynamicsAnalytics tools reveal what users are doing inside the product. Teams can quickly identify broken onboarding flows, declining engagement, and abnormal session behavior.But analytics platforms typically lack:Infrastructure dependenciesA product team may notice users abandoning a workflow after a deployment, but analytics alone cannot explain whether the issue came from backend latency, a failing dependency, a frontend rendering issue, or a configuration change introduced during release.That disconnect creates friction across engineering, support, and product teams because each group sees a different version of the problem, but no system preserves the shared context that connects them.Ticketing systems surface how issues appear to customers and stakeholders. Support and operations teams see failing workflows, frustrated users, and escalations tied to specific accounts and SLAs.But most ticketing platforms fail to preserve the reasoning behind resolution. Once an incident closes, critical investigation context often disappears:Which telemetry signals matteredWhich hypotheses engineers ruled outWhich runtime conditions shaped the issueWhich deployment triggered the regressionWhy a remediation path succeededThe result is a reconstruction tax across engineering organizations. Every major incident forces teams to manually reconnect dashboards, traces, session replay, deployment history, PRs, and institutional knowledge before they can begin fixing the problem itself.Context graphs create a shared reasoning layer across production systemsTelemetry already knows when services fail and where latency spikes. Analytics knows which workflows users abandon. Ticketing systems know which customers are affected and how severe the escalations become.The missing piece is how those signals relate across deployments, runtime conditions, user impact, and the decisions engineers made during resolution.Context graphs solve this by acting as a connective reasoning layer across production systems.Instead of treating telemetry, analytics, tickets, runtime behavior, and code as isolated datasets, a context graph connects them into a continuously evolving retrieval system that preserves how incidents, customer impact, and engineering decisions relate to one another over time.That changes how engineering teams investigate issues in practice. Instead of manually stitching together dashboards, traces, tickets, and deployment history, teams can:Trace anomalies back to the deployments that introduced themConnect customer escalations to affected workflows and sessionsIdentify which execution paths repeatedly appear across incidentsAt PlayerZero, this retrieval layer forms the foundation of an engineering world model—accumulated operational context that compounds with every incident, deployment, and investigation.Three strategies for building a context graph that scalesA context graph scales when it is built around the relationships engineers rely on most during debugging, release validation, and incident response.The three strategies below break down how to build that layer in practice, from connecting production signals to using accumulated operational context before changes reach production.Strategy 1: Build a retrieval layer anchored to stable execution pathsFrom an engineering perspective, building a context graph starts with a retrieval decision: what should be indexed ahead of time, what should be resolved dynamically at query time, and which systems are stable enough to serve as long-term reference points.A useful context graph does not attempt to index every production signal equally. Instead, it prioritizes the execution paths engineers repeatedly traverse during debugging, incident response, release validation, and root-cause analysis.In practice, that means connecting source code, PR history, telemetry traces, deployment metadata, support escalations, session replay data, and production events into a shared operational index. This also means precomputing indexes where schemas are stable and query volume is high—like code and PR history—and resolving more volatile, high‑cardinality signals, like telemetry parameters, at query time, rather than trying to index every possible relationship up front.For most organizations, code becomes the natural anchor layer because it changes more slowly than runtime infrastructure and remains structurally consistent across investigations. Telemetry behaves differently: schemas evolve rapidly, infrastructure states shift continuously, and relationships across services become too large and short-lived to fully precompute.That tradeoff is what makes code the most effective operational anchor. Instead of attempting to materialize every possible relationship across production systems, effective context graphs prioritize the operational pathways engineers revisit most often during real investigations.How to implement a stable retrieval layerIndex source code and PR history so runtime signals can be traced back to execution pathsMap telemetry traces to the services and functions generating themLink deployments to customer-facing regressions and support escalationsConnect user sessions to affected workflows and backend tracesConfigure bidirectional traversal between incidents and implicated code pathsPrioritize indexing high-frequency workflows that engineers repeatedly investigateReview recurring incident patterns quarterly to identify relationships worth preserving long-termKey Data experienced this challenge as its platform expanded across increasingly complex customer workflows. Telemetry, runtime behavior, and execution paths lived in separate systems, forcing engineers into lengthy debugging cycles when customer-reported issues appeared. After PlayerZero anchored runtime behavior directly to code paths, teams could move from symptom to likely root cause in minutes instead of manually correlating evidence across multiple tools.Strategy 2: Preserve operational trajectories as organizational memoryMost organizations preserve fixes but lose the investigation context behind them.An incident may end with a rollback, patched dependency, or merged PR, but the reasoning that led to that resolution often disappears across Slack threads, ticket comments, deployment reviews, and fragmented debugging workflows.A mature context graph solves this by preserving investigation trajectories instead of just final outcomes. It captures which telemetry engineers consulted, which execution paths were investigated, which runtime conditions mattered, and which remediation strategies succeeded.Over time, those pathways become reusable operational memory. Instead of relying solely on institutional knowledge or senior engineer experience, teams can retrieve how similar incidents behaved historically, which remediation paths succeeded under specific runtime conditions, and which execution paths repeatedly introduced fragility.The context graph learns which relationships matter most by observing how engineers actually traverse incidents, code paths, tickets, and telemetry during real investigations, and then prioritizing those pathways for deeper indexing.Importantly, this does not require perfect documentation. Even partial preservation of investigation pathways creates compounding operational clarity.How to preserve investigation trajectoriesAttach telemetry traces and deployment metadata directly to incident ticketsLink remediation PRs back to the runtime conditions that triggered the issuePreserve session replay data alongside escalation history during investigationsAdd short investigation summaries before closing major incidentsTag recurring failure pathways across services and releasesCreate shared conventions for documenting remediation reasoning during incident responseReview recurring incidents monthly to identify patterns worth preserving permanentlyCayuse used PlayerZero to unify repositories, observability systems, support workflows, and telemetry into a connected operational layer that preserved investigation context across teams. With investigation history accessible in a shared system, engineers and support staff could resolve issues faster without repeatedly escalating problems to senior engineers for manual reconstruction.Strategy 3: Use accumulated operational context to simulate failures before deploymentAs context graphs accumulate operational history, engineering teams can begin using that context to evaluate how proposed changes might behave before they reach production.Traditional testing validates expected functionality, predefined edge cases, and manually designed workflows. But many modern failures emerge from cross-service interactions, dependency behavior, infrastructure drift, deployment timing, and runtime conditions that engineers did not explicitly anticipate during development.Context graphs add a different validation layer: accumulated production history. Instead of testing changes only against what engineers expected to happen, teams can evaluate them against prior incidents, historical runtime conditions, dependency relationships, deployment patterns, and previously observed failure pathways.That changes release validation from static testing into historical reasoning. Every resolved incident becomes a reusable production scenario that informs future deployments.As operational history compounds, the context graph gradually evolves into an engineering world model that represents how systems behave, how failures spread, and how runtime conditions influence reliability outcomes over time.For engineering leaders, the long-term value is faster releases, fewer regressions, and more engineering capacity redirected from reactive debugging toward roadmap work.How to use operational history for pre-deployment validationEngineering teams should start simulation workflows in systems where incident history is already dense, regressions recur frequently, and release risk is consistently high.Reuse resolved incidents as regression scenarios during PR validationRun simulations against recent deployment patterns and runtime dependencies before merging changesValidate changes against historically fragile execution paths and workflowsCompare simulation outcomes against post-release defect escape ratesIncorporate session replay and runtime traces into release validation workflowsPrioritize simulations around services with recurring escalation patternsExpand simulation coverage incrementally as operational history accumulatesCyrano Video used PlayerZero’s accumulated production context to assign risk levels to upcoming releases and identify issues tied to customer-facing workflows earlier in the validation process. That operational visibility helped teams prioritize remediation faster, improve release readiness, and reduce engineering effort spent on debugging after deployment.The future of engineering velocity depends on persistent production understandingThe engineering teams that move fastest are not the ones with the most dashboards. They are the ones that preserve operational understanding across incidents, deployments, and production changes instead of reconstructing context from scratch every time something breaks.As software systems become more distributed, AI-generated, and release-heavy, persistent production understanding becomes critical. The first step is to unify your core production signals, anchor them to code, and capture what you learned from each resolved incident.PlayerZero builds and maintains that operational layer automatically, helping engineering organizations reduce repeated debugging work, improve release reliability, and ship more confidently at scale. Book a demo to see how to move from fragmented production signals to connected operational understanding.

item.title: Paolo Soleri built a utopian eco-city in the Arizona desert
item.content:encoded: ‘Arcosanti is traditionally about minimal living – a deliberate poverty of living simply for the sake of equity,’ says Ray Paskus, a resident of two years and an archivist for the Cosanti Foundation. Perhaps this is why so many co-living projects fail to last the journey. Arcosanti is the exception, not the rule – and it’s hardly thriving. Less than 10 per cent of Soleri’s masterplan has been realised and, despite a broader interest in communal living, Paskus says applications are at a standstill. ‘People project all sorts of things on to Arcosanti, but the lifestyle is harsh and isolating and full of hard work – it’s almost monastic. To grow the community you have to be able to sell that to people.’ There are few, he’s found, that are truly interested in the asceticism needed to make earth-conscious co-operative living work.It’s a shame, he says, because a philosophy of reuse and collaborative living could be one solution to the ills of our time. Soleri died in 2013 at the age of 93, still convinced that ‘we must reinvent the city to develop our civilisation’. Arcosanti endures as that living sketch – unfinished, alive and quietly radical.Edit: It is important to note that allegations of abuse have been made by Daniela Soleri about her father, the architect Paolo Soleri.For more information, visit arcosanti.org. A version of this story appears in the March 2026 issue of ‘The World of Interiors’. Learn about our

item.title: AI Tool Adoption for Engineering Teams Isn't Enough
item.author: PlayerZero
item.content:encoded: Adopting AI tools isn't an AI strategy: engineering teams see lasting gains only when their tools share context and AI activity ties back to business outcomes.AI adoption is moving faster than most organizations' ability to define what success actually looks like. The industry is pulling in multiple directions at once: some leaders see AI as a productivity breakthrough, others see it as a threat to jobs, and many organizations are struggling to explain how AI activity translates into measurable business outcomes.Inside engineering, that confusion is sharper. Most teams now have AI tools across the software delivery lifecycle: copilots for developers, QA automation, AI-assisted triage and support tools. But few organizations have defined what all of that AI activity is supposed to compound into.The result is an AI tool strategy, not an AI strategy for engineering teams.An AI strategy is not about maximizing usage across every function. It builds a shared picture of how software behaves in production, so engineering, QA, product, support, SRE, and leadership can reason from the same operational reality.The cultural signals behind the AI strategy gapThat gap between tool adoption and real strategy is visible across industries, not just engineering organizations.When former Google CEO Eric Schmidt was booed by graduates for mentioning AI during a commencement speech, the reaction revealed something more specific than job-displacement anxiety. It reflected growing skepticism toward productivity narratives that treat expertise as the thing AI is supposed to replace. That assumption is a design choice baked into how most engineering AI strategies are built.Uber offers a different version of the same tension. In December 2025, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi framed AI as making engineers “superhumans.” By May 2026, the company was slowing hiring to fund AI investments, even as its COO acknowledged that the link between AI usage and measurable product outcomes remained unclear.The issue was not simply that ROI measurement lagged adoption. The deeper problem was that the narrative about what AI would do arrived before organizations defined what it was supposed to improve. AI tools got deployed quickly, while the harder strategic questions about production outcomes and operational learning remained undefined.At the same time, researchers like David Autor are pointing toward a more important distinction. The real question is not whether AI replaces human work. It is whether organizations use AI to make expert judgment more widely available or push humans further to the edges of decision-making.That is the same strategic choice engineering organizations are now making, whether intentionally or not. Every AI workflow either helps distribute production judgment more broadly across the organization or concentrates operational expertise further inside the same small group of experienced engineers.China’s approach to automation offers another institutional signal. Its AI strategy reflects an explicit decision to use automation to expand industrial capability and workforce productivity rather than treat automation primarily as a headcount reduction mechanism. What makes that approach instructive is not simply the scale of automation itself, but the sequencing behind it. Strategic intent came first. China defined what automation was supposed to accomplish before deploying it broadly.Most engineering organizations are doing the reverse: adopting AI tools quickly and constructing the operational rationale afterward.These signals are not contradictions. They are evidence of the same underlying gap: adoption is not strategy. Organizations that get this wrong treat expertise as the cost AI should remove. Organizations that get it right decide up front how AI should preserve, distribute, and extend production judgment across the business. That is the strategic question engineering leaders are now being forced to answer.AI adoption is not the same as an AI strategyWhen the first wave of AI tools entered engineering workflows, productivity gains were easy to understand. Code generation tools accelerated implementation. QA automation reduced manual work. Support triage tools helped teams process customer issues faster. SRE and observability assistants surfaced signals from noisy production systems more quickly. Product teams gained faster visibility into how features behaved in production and which changes drove customer impact.For CTOs and engineering leaders, these tools appeared to solve an urgent business problem: improve software engineering productivity without scaling headcount at the same pace.But most of these engineering productivity tools focused on accelerating pre-production workflows such as coding, testing, PR review, and ticket routing. Few organizations defined how AI should participate once software reached production or how those workflows should improve the organization’s ability to learn from incidents, regressions, and operational failures over time.Developers optimized implementation. QA optimized test planning. Support optimized ticket intake. SRE optimized signal detection. But the operational knowledge generated by those workflows remained fragmented across teams and systems. As a result, every function became faster inside its own lane without improving how the organization understood production as a whole.That is the difference between tool adoption and strategy. Tool adoption answers which AI tools the organization is using. Strategy answers what new organizational capabilities those tools are building.Speed without shared context compounds operational complexityThe cost of an incomplete AI strategy becomes visible when every function accelerates in isolation, but the system remains just as hard to operate. For engineering teams, the real strategic test is whether every release, defect, escalation, and fix helps the organization better understand how its software behaves in production.PR velocity improves, but MTTR does not fall proportionally. Support teams process more customer-facing tickets, but escalations still reach senior engineers. QA teams generate more test coverage, but production edge cases still escape. SRE tools surface more signals, but teams still spend hours reconstructing what changed, who owned it, and why customers were affected.The problem is that local acceleration does not automatically reduce coordination cost. Teams end up adding more releases, alerts, AI-assisted changes, and operational signals into systems that are still just as difficult to understand when something breaks.The hard work remains bottlenecked around reconstructing context, tracing causality, and relying on the same experienced engineers to connect fragmented information across the stack. This is the same failure pattern: adoption first, operational model second.The metrics that define a durable AI strategyA production-focused AI strategy for engineering teams is defined by improvements in operational outcomes, not just activity metrics like tool adoption, prompt volume, token consumption, and PR generation.Mature teams treat tokens and agentic loops as units of work that represent specific outcomes rather than raw usage or increased code throughput. They are effectively buying work, not tries. AI ROI becomes legible when AI-assisted activity is tied to completed units of work and measurable improvements in MTTR, defect escape, incident volume, and senior engineering load.The signal that an AI strategy is improving system quality shows up in production metrics:Fewer customer-facing defects reaching productionFewer unnecessary support escalations to engineeringFaster resolution of internal engineering issuesLess senior engineering time spent reconstructing contextFewer repeated regressions from known failure modesThese outcomes reveal whether AI is reducing dependence on senior engineers or deepening it. Organizations that continue struggling with these outcomes often share the same underlying problem: their AI strategy stops at the point where code reaches production.Why code generation alone can’t be your AI strategyCode generation tools can accelerate implementation, but they do not address who carries production judgment once software reaches production.AI coding tools are strongest before code reaches production: generating boilerplate, summarizing unfamiliar files, accelerating pull requests, and helping developers move through routine implementation work faster. But once an issue reaches production, the work stops being primarily a coding problem and becomes a context problem.Production systems behave under conditions no isolated coding session can fully see, including customer-specific configurations, runtime dependencies, deployment timing, historical regressions, and operational signals spread across multiple systems.Teams have to understand what the customer experienced, which code path was involved, what changed recently, whether the issue has happened before, and whether a fix creates risk somewhere else in the system. That investigation usually spans multiple tools and multiple teams, which means the engineers who already carry production judgment become an even greater bottleneck as AI-assisted development accelerates.More AI-assisted changes flowing into production create more surface area for operational failures, but the judgment required to diagnose, contextualize, and resolve those failures still lives with the same small group of experienced engineers.That is the hidden cost of adoption without strategy: faster implementation without a corresponding system for making operational expertise more reusable across the organization.The missing piece is not another point solution. It is shared production intelligence.Shared production intelligence is the missing pieceShared production intelligence is a durable, shared picture of how software behaves in production, connecting code, tickets, telemetry, user sessions, deploys, dependencies, and resolution history into one operational layer that humans and AI agents can both reason from. Instead of every team working from its own incomplete slice of the system, engineering, QA, support, SRE, and leadership operate from that shared picture of production reality.Without this layer, every function accelerates independently while the same coordination bottlenecks remain in place. Support surfaces more customer issues, QA generates more test coverage, and engineering ships changes faster, but senior engineers still carry the burden of reconstructing context whenever something breaks.With shared production intelligence, those disconnected views begin to connect. A support ticket can be tied to a code path. A telemetry signal can be tied to a deploy. A regression can be tied to a prior fix. A customer-facing issue can be understood alongside affected users, historical incidents, and the system behavior behind it. MTTR and defect escape drop as operational knowledge from prior incidents, regressions, and fixes becomes broadly reusable across the organization.This is where the AI strategy shifts from individual productivity to organizational intelligence. It is also the shift from single-player AI to multiplayer AI: away from isolated tools that accelerate individual workflows and toward a shared production model every function can use. Shared production intelligence gives those teams a common operational map.How PlayerZero operationalizes shared production intelligenceShared production intelligence does not make expert judgment irrelevant. It makes that judgment more durable and accessible by preserving the operational context that usually lives in Slack threads, incident memories, and the heads of senior engineers.PlayerZero’s engineering world model is the architecture for this shared production intelligence. As investigations, fixes, escalations, and resolutions feed back into the model, production judgment becomes something the broader organization can reuse.An SRE investigating a latency spike can move from telemetry to affected user sessions, recent code changes, and known regressions in a single view, reducing the time to resolution without pulling in the same handful of engineers to reconstruct context manually.That is what enables AI-assisted work to compound into organizational intelligence instead of remaining isolated inside individual workflows.AI tools attached to isolated workflows can accelerate local productivity while leaving the same coordination burden in place whenever something breaks. When AI-assisted workflows feed a shared production model instead, every incident, escalation, and resolution helps make production judgment more durable, reusable, and accessible across the organization.That is where AI investment starts to compound: not through more tools attached to isolated functions, but through a shared understanding of how software behaves in production. The next phase of AI maturity is shared operational context across the full software lifecycle.Most engineering leaders running AI tools right now are seeing this pattern. The question is not whether they bet on the wrong tools—it is what comes after AI code generation tools.

item.title: Thanksgiving Security Guide: How MEXC's 300%+ BTC Reserves & Four Lines of Defense Protect Your Fund
item.author: MEXC Learn
item.content:encoded: ● Excess Reserves and Transparent Audits: The latest MEXC PoR report shows that the reserve ratio of core assets exceeds 100%(with BTC reaching 318% and USDT reaching 122%), and it undergoes monthly independent audits by Hacken.● Three layers of security fund protection: In addition to the PoR, there is a Guardian Fund (to cover losses from system hacks) and a Contract Insurance Fund (to cover losses from liquidation shortfalls), with respective sizes of 100 million U and 830 million U.● Comprehensive daily security protection: It builds a closed-loop protection for daily operations through hot and cold wallet isolation, intelligent risk control to block abnormal transactions, and assistance in retrieving mistakenly deposited assets.● Clear security boundaries: The Chengdu platform does not cover losses caused by user operational errors, private key leaks or phishing attacks, and reminds users to jointly build good security habits.Throughout our long journey in the crypto world, we have grown accustomed to chasing the ups and downs of the market. However, as the Thanksgiving holiday approaches and the market briefly returns to calm, there is one most fundamental question worth re-examining: Are the assets you entrust to a trading platform truly safe?In the traditional financial system, users can only passively accept the credit endorsement provided by banks. In the Web3 era, transparency and verifiability are the cornerstones of the industry. Today, we won’t talk about returns, but only about the most fundamental layer of trust — how MEXC builds a secure foundation for you through four core lines of defense and multiple daily security measures.Proof of Reserves (abbreviated as PoR) is a transparency mechanism born in the crypto industry to address trust crises. Its logic is very straightforward: platforms publicly disclose on-chain wallet addresses to prove that the assets they actually hold are at least equal to the total amount of user deposits. As long as the reserve ratio is ≥ 100%, the platform will have sufficient funds to meet withdrawal demands even if all users request withdrawals at the same time.According to the latest PoR data released by MEXC:● BTC Reserve Ratio: 318%(Total assets in platform wallets: 11,780.73 BTC, Total user assets: 3,709.11 BTC)● USDT Reserve Ratio: 122%(Total assets in platform wallets are approximately 1.525 billion USDT, and total user assets are approximately 1.246 billion USDT)● ETH Reserve Ratio: 112%● USDC Reserve Ratio: 110%A BTC reserve ratio exceeding 300% means that even in the face of extreme Black Swan events, MEXC still maintains nearly three times the Safety Redundancy. In addition, the platform submits its data monthly to Hacken, a globally renowned security firm, for independent audits. Users can also independently verify whether their balances are correctly included in the platform’s total reserves through Merkle Tree technology, achieving true “verifiable data, accessible verification for all. “ MEXC’s Proof of Reserves system adopts Merkle tree verification technology. Users can independently verify whether their asset balances are truly held in the platform’s asset pool through the Proof of Reserves page on MEXC’s official website, while preserving the privacy of their personal accounts. Audits are independently conducted monthly by Hacken, a leading blockchain security audit firm, with reports released publicly to ensure the objectivity and impartiality of the verification process.2. Second line of defense: A 100 million USDT protection fund provides sufficient buffer against extreme risksEven with sufficient reserves, unexpected events can still occur — cyberattacks, system failures, extreme market volatility. .. These unforeseen risks are challenges that every exchange must confront.MEXC’s approach is to prepare sufficient “ammunition” in advance, which is dedicated to protecting user asset security in extreme scenarios, and consists of two core funds:—this fund currently holds 100 million USDT and 2,000 BTC, with a goal of expanding to 500 million USD within two years. Its purpose is very clear: to compensate users for their losses in the event that the MEXC system is compromised or subjected to large-scale targeted attacks. The on-chain wallet address of the fund is fully public, and anyone can verify its balance and transaction records on the blockchain. In the event of any unexpected incident or abnormal situation, the Guardian Fund can be activated quickly to provide full compensation to users.The core features of this fund include strong defense capabilities (focused on responding to unexpected incidents), on-chain transparency (fund assets are verifiable on-chain and subject to public oversight), and 24/7 protection (100 million USDT in funds are on standby at all times), forming a solid and resilient protective layer for user assets.USDT Reserve Address (Ethereum):0x469AfE803C54A36674C55231489Cf4b61da8c1bCThe first BTC reserve address:1MDVjZdX8QD212pT8Z8EMP7DuFQHKqN3mxThe second BTC reserve address:19KYQDpyssRUtpfa4pfAWiNQLeysThd1us3. The Third Line of Defense: Contract Insurance Fund — Addressing Market Risks of “Position Loss Exceeding Margin”Contract trading involves a scenario uncommon in traditional finance: force closure loss. When there is extreme market volatility and insufficient liquidity, the execution price of a liquidation order may be worse than the bankruptcy price, resulting in losses exceeding the user’s margin.MEXC’s futures insurance fund is designed precisely for this purpose. As of November 5,2026, the total balance of the MEXC futures insurance fund has reached 830,411,315 USDT, representing a 4.89% increase from the September balance. When the actual loss from a user’s positioning after forced liquidation exceeds the margin, the insurance fund will cover the difference, ensuring the user does not owe the platform any additional funds. It also effectively reduces the frequency of Auto-Deleveraging (ADL) triggers, protecting the profits that winning traders are entitled to.4.
