The fourth line of defense: end-to-end assurance from pre-incident warning to post-incident responseIn addition to the “strong line of defense” for handling extreme scenarios, MEXC has built a rigorous protection network in its daily operations, and makes the platform’s security work transparent by regularly releasing bi-monthly security reports:● Bi-monthly Security Report: MEXC continuously discloses the latest data of the platform in areas including hacker prevention, fraud prevention, abnormal transaction interception, and misdeposited asset recovery. For instance, in the September-October 2026 bi-monthly report, the platform released specific data on blocking collusive fraud accounts and processing misdeposit recovery requests.● Cold and Hot Wallet Isolation: The vast majority of user assets are stored in cold wallets that are isolated from the internet, with multi-signature authorization, while hot wallets only hold funds for daily settlement.● Smart Risk Control Interception: MEXC has introduced an AI-powered real-time risk control system. This system monitors abnormal trading activities on the platform 24/7, with the accuracy of risk identification increased to 99.9%. It can automatically detect suspicious activities such as money laundering, fraud, and abnormal withdrawals, and block them in a timely manner before assets are transferred. According to the latest bi-monthly report, the system proactively identified and restricted abnormal transactions and malicious groups, successfully blocking a large number of accounts associated with coordinated fraud during the reporting period.● Wrong Deposit Recovery Assistance: The customer service team continues to manually process users’ wrong deposit refund requests, helping users recover losses caused by operational errors. According to the latest bi-monthly security report, the MEXC customer service team manually processed and completed 1,354 wrong deposit refund transactions from September to October, with the total refunded assets equivalent to 1,002,660 USDT. Compared with the July-August period, the number of processed transactions increased by 65.5%, and the refund amount increased by 66.5%.● Account Security Controls: Mandatory KYC identity verification and 2FA two-factor authentication are implemented to reduce the risk of account compromise.● Security Audit and Bug Bounty Program: MEXC regularly invites top security teams to conduct code audits, continuously identifying and fixing potential system vulnerabilities. At the same time, the platform has launched a bug bounty program to encourage white-hat hackers to help discover security issues. This proactive approach to security construction allows the platform’s security capabilities to remain consistently at the top of the industry.● 24/7/365 all-weather customer support, ready to respond and guard you throughout the journey: The cryptocurrency market features 24/7 non-stop trading, which means users may encounter trading issues, deposit delays, or account anomalies at any time. Meanwhile, the customer support system covers multiple languages and time zones. The platform has set up Localization customer support channels to ensure users can enjoy smooth, native-level communication and efficient responses.Whether you are a newcomer to cryptocurrency or an experienced professional trader, there is no need to feel anxious alone when you encounter issues. The MEXC customer support team is always a solid backer for users throughout their digital asset journey.5. Final Note: Safety is the prerequisite for returnsIt is not difficult for a trading platform to provide liquidity during a bull market; the real challenge lies in being able to firmly safeguard every bit of users’ principal through every stormy downturn in the market. The cryptocurrency market is never short of opportunities, but opportunities always come hand in hand with risks. In this industry, choosing a reliable exchange is just as important as picking high-quality investment targets. Founded in 2018, MEXC has so far served 40 million users across more than 170 countries and regions worldwide. Whether it is the acumen for new listing launches, the liquidity of trading depth, or its inclusive zero-fee policy, MEXC has always been at the forefront of the industry.And the very foundation of all this is security.This Thanksgiving, the core message MEXC wants to convey is: security is the prerequisite for all forms of giving back. From underlying reserves to daily risk control, and to boundary education, we are committed to building a complete and transparent security foundation.Thanksgiving Bonus Surprise:Against the backdrop of guaranteed fund security, MEXC’s annual “Blue Friday” event has officially kicked off. During Thanksgiving, you can participate in six exclusive campaigns to win iPhone Duo, interest rate boost coupons of up to 1,000%, and split a prize pool of 200,000 USDT!Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)Q1: What does it mean that MEXC’s reserve ratio exceeds 100%?A: This means that the total amount of assets the platform actually holds in its on-chain wallets is greater than the total sum of all user deposits. Taking the BTC reserve ratio of 318% as an example, even if all users apply to withdraw Bitcoin at the same time, MEXC has nearly three times the funds to make full redemptions, and is fully capable of withstanding extreme bank run risks.Q2: How can I confirm that my assets are indeed in MEXC’s reserve pool?A: You can use the Merkle Tree verification tool provided by MEXC. Enter your account information on the official Proof of Reserves page, and the system will use cryptographic algorithms to prove that your balance is accurately recorded in the platform’s total liability data, without revealing any of your privacy throughout the process.Q3: What is the “Guardian Fund” and how does it differ from the “Contract Insurance Fund”?A: The two funds are designed to address different types of risks. The Guardian Fund (100 million USDT + 2,000 BTC) primarily covers “systemic disasters”(e. g., platform hacks, critical vulnerabilities) and is used to fully compensate users. The Contract Insurance Fund (830 million USDT) primarily addresses “market-related position blow-ups”(e. g., when user losses exceed their principal under extreme market conditions) and is used to cover the deficit from such blow-ups, ensuring normal settlement for profitable parties.Q4: If I accidentally deposit to the wrong currency or network, can MEXC help me retrieve the funds?A: You can try applying for a recovery. The MEXC customer service team provides services for recovering incorrectly deposited assets. According to the latest bi-monthly security report, between September and October alone, the customer service team successfully processed 1,354 incorrect deposit refund requests, saving users over 1 million USDT in losses. If you encounter such a situation, please contact the 7×24 online customer service immediately.Q5: Is my capital 100% safe on a trading platform?A: No platform can offer an absolute “zero-risk” guarantee. MEXC minimizes platform-side risks through four lines of defense, but clear security boundaries are equally important: losses caused by users’ personal disclosure of passwords, API keys, phishing attacks, or their own operational errors are not covered by the platform’ s protection. Therefore, enabling 2FA (two-factor authentication) and keeping personal information secure are essential for every trader.

item.title: Medical AI Has a Trust Problem That Better Technology Alone Can't Fix
item.author: Sanford Diday
item.content:encoded: Approval is not proof: AI changed how fast claims arrive, not what it takes to know they are true.Three months ago, I argued that artificial intelligence had changed the volume, speed, and polish of information moving through the world without changing the standard that makes any individual claim reliable. The responsibility for separating one from the other, I argued, has never belonged to a piece of technology. It belongs to whoever decides what to believe, and to whoever approves what other people may use. Nothing in the three months since has required a correction. If anything, confirmation arrived from an unexpected direction: a government audit of the tools doctors use to write down what their patients tell them.The Case Nobody Was Watching ForOn May 12, 2026, Ontario’s Auditor General, Shelley Spence, released a special report on the government’s use of artificial intelligence. One section examined Ontario’s AI Scribe. Ontario promoted AI scribes to physicians in 2024, and the vendor-of-record approvals followed in April 2025 (“Ontario AG Finds Flaws in AI Scribes”; Hauen; Vescera and Giancola). The Auditor General’s own announcement described “limited use of security assessment reports, bias testing and live demonstrations of the AI Scribe systems for health care” among already-approved vendors (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario, “Ontario Auditor General Releases”). Evaluators tested twenty approved vendors against two simulated doctor-patient conversations each, then checked the notes against what was actually said. The results were not close. Nine of the twenty systems invented clinical details never discussed, including therapy referrals and blood tests no one had ordered. Twelve recorded a different medication than the one the doctor actually prescribed. Seventeen missed a key detail about the patient’s mental health in at least one of the two tests (“AI Transcriber for Use by Ontario Doctors ‘Hallucinated’”; Vigliarolo). Ontario approved five of the twenty vendors even though they had not submitted the risk and privacy assessments the process required (“Ontario AG Finds Flaws in AI Scribes”). Eleven of the twenty submitted no third-party audit reports at all (“Ontario AG Finds Flaws in AI Scribes”). The report put it bluntly: “Inaccuracies in medical notes generated by AI scribe systems could potentially result in inadequate or harmful treatment plans that may potentially impact patient health outcomes” (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario, Use of Artificial Intelligence, sec. 4.3).The scoring method helps explain why Ontario approved inaccurate vendors. Of 530 points in the bidding criteria, a vendor’s domestic presence in Ontario carried a maximum of 159, about thirty percent. The accuracy of a vendor’s medical notes carried a maximum of 20, about four percent (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario, Use of Artificial Intelligence, app. 2, pp. 46–47). Bidders could have scored zero on system security, bias controls, and note accuracy and still met the minimum score for approval (Hauen). A process weighting criteria this way risks more than approving an inaccurate vendor: it can let an inaccurate vendor outscore an accurate one on criteria unrelated to whether a transcript is true.Where the System Still Depended on a HumanNone of this is a story about careless technology. AI scribes exist to solve a real problem: physicians spending unpaid hours each week typing notes instead of treating patients. Spence called the tools problematic but said “AI is a tool that will improve efficiencies and delivering services [sic]” (D’Mello and Callan). Ontario’s Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement, Stephen Crawford, made a fair point in response: physicians oversee every aspect of the product. The errors, he said, surfaced during a testing phase meant to catch them before deployment, not during an actual patient visit (“AI Transcriber for Use by Ontario Doctors ‘Hallucinated’”). The point is incomplete, though: finding errors during testing is not itself evidence of failure, because testing exists to expose weaknesses before they reach patients. Still, a test protects patients only when its findings meaningfully affect approval, remediation, or deployment. According to the Auditor General’s office, all twenty approved systems showed at least one inaccuracy at the procurement testing phase, and there was no evidence of additional testing or evaluation at the time of the audit (D’Mello and Callan). Ontario approved them anyway. Physician oversight is also thinner than the minister’s framing suggests: none of the approved systems required doctors to sign off on notes (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario, Use of Artificial Intelligence, sec. 4.3). The test worked. The approval process did not adequately act on what the test revealed.A related weakness appeared elsewhere. The Investigative Journalism Foundation reported that ADGScribe, an approved vendor, had published testimonials from two physicians who appear to be nonexistent (Vescera and Giancola; Raza and Spithoff). That would be a fabricated source, one that reached physicians who had no reason to doubt it and could shape a purchasing decision through endorsements nobody made. In both cases, approval tells physicians that someone has already tested the source and found it truthful. The dangerous output was not only the inaccurate note or the invented endorsement. It was the institutional signal someone had already checked the system adequately. The physicians who choose one of these vendors trust a process strangers ran, on a product whose failure mode looks like a correctly written note, or a genuine endorsement, until someone checks what was actually said, or who actually said it.In my earlier piece, I proposed a three-part test for claims like this: Source, Method, and Motive. Each asks a different question when I apply it to a system instead of a sentence. Source asks where a claim originated, not merely that something which sounds official vouches for it: an approved vendor is not the same claim as an accurate transcript, and a doctor’s testimonial is not the same claim as a doctor. Method asks whether the output rests on the underlying evidence: a system capable of producing fluent clinical prose can generate a note that reads coherently even when the recorded conversation does not support parts of it. Motive asks who benefits if readers accept the claim: a vendor benefits from passing procurement and from an unchecked testimonial, and a government has reason to want a burnout-easing program to succeed. Neither interest has anything to do with whether a specific note or endorsement is accurate.Hearing Out the Other SideNot everyone who has studied this audit agrees it describes the tools doctors use today. Will Falk, a Toronto-based consulting executive who tracks AI adoption in Canadian health care, argued that the audit evaluated an earlier generation of the vendors’ products, and that today’s scribes have since improved (“Ontario AG Finds Flaws in AI Scribes”). Falk cited figures indicating 28 percent of Canadian physicians use AI scribes and three-quarters of those physicians use them daily, which raises the stakes of judging whether the audited products still match what doctors use now (“Ontario AG Finds Flaws in AI Scribes”). Dr. Paul Forman, a family physician in Markham, Ontario, added a related point: these tools reduce burnout because they work well most of the time, and the honest standard was never perfection. “No matter how advanced a system is, no system can ever claim 100% accuracy or efficiency,” he said (“Ontario AG Finds Flaws in AI Scribes”). The ministry has likewise said about 5,000 physicians use AI scribes, with no known reports of patient harm (“AI Transcriber for Use by Ontario Doctors ‘Hallucinated’”). These objections limit what the audit can tell us about the present accuracy of individual products. They do not answer the audit’s central procurement finding: Ontario approved vendors through a process placing little weight on accuracy and accepting critical assurances without consistent independent verification.The Part of the Story AI Did Not CreateNone of this is new, a point worth making to anyone tempted to treat AI Scribe as a uniquely artificial-intelligence failure. Procurement processes have always worked as vouching mechanisms officials run on behalf of people who were not in the room for the testing. A pharmaceutical label, a safety certification, and a credit rating all perform a similar institutional function: they allow people who cannot independently reproduce an evaluation to rely on someone else’s verification. Two family physicians who reviewed the audit for Healthy Debate argued the AI Scribe rollout amounted to a test run for a larger project: a province-wide electronic medical record system that will carry far more patient data than any single transcript (Raza and Spithoff). What AI adds to this older procurement problem is not a new category of risk. It adds scale and fluency to an old one. A fabricated blood-test referral reads exactly like a real one, with none of the tells, misspellings, or implausible claims that once flagged a human transcription error for a second look. The claim sounds no different whether it is true or not.What Three Months ConfirmedThe audit required no new theory of how artificial intelligence works. It required Ontario’s Auditor General to do a job older than any government software: checking whether an approval process does what it promised. Spence did not conclude Ontario should abandon AI Scribe. Her ten recommendations aimed mostly at tightening security, privacy, and testing requirements. Supply Ontario agreed to review best practices and to require yearly external audits, but it disagreed with raising the weight on security and privacy (Hauen). That is responsible verification at work: not a referendum on the technology, but an ordinary check on a process meant to catch the problem.The Ontario audit demonstrated an old rule of institutional trust: approval is not proof, fluency is not accuracy, and a process protects the public only when someone acts on what the process discovers. AI made unsupported claims easier to produce and harder to recognize. It did not change the questions we must ask to assess them. Those remained human questions:What is the source of this claim?Who benefits if I accept it without checking?

item.title: 5 Fun Computer Tricks for macOS, Windows, and Linux
item.author: Alexandra Belski
item.content:encoded:
Have you ever seen those hacker scenes in movies and thought, “I wish I could do the same”? Actually, you don’t need to hack into the Pentagon to look cool at a computer. Some tricks are surprisingly easy to pull off. A few commands, and your laptop starts looking like something out of a sci-fi movie.Here are five fun tricks you can try on macOS, Windows, or Linux. And don't worry, you don't need to be a programmer to follow along.1. Kill a Frozen App From TerminalThe next time a program freezes, there’s a much cooler solution than desperately clicking around and tearing your hair out. You can terminate the frozen app directly from the terminal—which, let’s be real, feels like you’re in charge.Let's say Google Chrome has frozen.First, open your terminal. Find its process using:You'll see a list of running processes, including their process IDs, or PIDs.Once you've found the PID of the frozen app, run:Replace with the actual PID.This asks the app to shut down.If the application refuses to close, there's a more aggressive option:The forces the operating system to terminate the process immediately.Use it only as a last resort because the application won't get a chance to save its work or clean up.Open PowerShell and find the application:Then terminate the specific process using its PID:If it refuses to close, you can force it:Stop-Process -Id 12345 -Force Be careful to select the correct process. Browsers often run multiple processes, and terminating the wrong one can close tabs or interrupt work.2. Use a Video as Your ScreensaverMost of us have boring screensavers.But imagine walking away from your computer and watching a spaceship dashboard, a cyberpunk city, or your own hacker screen appear.This trick swaps one of Apple’s downloaded screensaver videos for a video saved on your computer.First, open System Settings → Screen Saver, choose an animated aerial screensaver, and wait for it to download.Next, locate its downloaded video file in Finder. Save a backup of the original, then give your own compatible video the same filename—including the extension—and replace the downloaded file. You may be asked to authenticate as an administrator.Select that screensaver again in Settings. The option still looks like Apple’s original, but it now plays your video.One catch: this is an unofficial workaround from the Sonoma era. Later macOS updates may block it or change where the files are stored, and playback can be unreliable.Windows doesn't natively offer a general-purpose option for setting an MP4 file as a screensaver.One approach is to use a third-party video screensaver utility that supports Windows 10 or 11.After installing a trusted utility, configure your video file and open the Windows screensaver settings.control desk.cpl,,@screensaver Select the installed screensaver and set the idle timeout.You can also use animated wallpaper software for a similar effect, although an animated wallpaper isn't technically a screensaver.Linux offers more flexibility, although the setup depends on your desktop environment and whether you're using X11 or Wayland.On X11, a tool such as can be combined with a video player to create a looping video background.For example, after installing compatible versions of and , a command along these lines can display a looping video on the desktop:xwinwrap -fs -ni -b -nf -ov -- \ mpv --wid=WID --loop-file=inf \ --no-audio video.mp4 This is a video wallpaper rather than a true idle-triggered screensaver. You would need additional idle detection and lock-screen integration to reproduce the full screensaver behavior.Remember the green characters falling down the screen in The Matrix? Easy and no hacking skills required.There's a tiny program that does exactly this.If you have Homebrew installed, open Terminal and run:Once it's installed, type:Your terminal is now filled with falling green characters. If you haven’t installed Homebrew yet, then you’ll need to start from there.The easiest way to run the original is through Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL).If WSL isn't installed, open PowerShell as administrator and run:Follow the setup instructions and restart if prompted.Open your installed Ubuntu environment and run:sudo apt update sudo apt install cmatrix cmatrix Now you have the same Matrix effect running inside Windows Terminal.The original is designed for Unix-like systems, so WSL is a convenient way to use it on Windows.You can customize the effect.Want red characters instead of green?Want the animation to stop when you press a key?Press to exit normal mode.Does it actually do anything useful? Absolutely not.Does it look amazing? Yes!4. Turn Your Terminal Into a Control CenterOkay, this one is actually useful. With one command, you can turn your terminal into a dashboard showing your CPU usage, memory consumption, network traffic, and running processes—all in real time.Open Terminal and install it with Homebrew:Your terminal transforms into an interactive dashboard.The official project provides packages for several Linux distributions and macOS.The main application doesn't run natively on Windows, but you can run its Linux version through WSL.Open your Ubuntu terminal inside Windows and type:sudo apt update sudo apt install btop btop You'll get the same interface, but the statistics will primarily reflect your WSL environment rather than Windows as a whole.What are you actually looking at?Once launches, you'll see several panels.CPU: How hard your processor is working.Memory: How much RAM your computer is using.Network: How much data is being uploaded and downloaded.Processes: Which applications are consuming your computer's resources.You can navigate the interface using your keyboard or mouse, depending on your terminal.Open , then launch a few applications or play a high-resolution video. Watch how the graphs change in real time.This might be my favorite trick because it makes your computer personal.Imagine opening your terminal and typing:And suddenly your computer displays:================================ WELCOME BACK, AGENT ================================
SYSTEM STATUS: ONLINE MISSION STATUS: CLASSIFIED
Initializing control center... You can actually build this yourself.We'll create a custom command called .First, open your shell configuration file.On modern macOS, the default shell is usually Zsh:On many Linux distributions, the default shell is Bash:At the bottom of the file, add:mission() { clear echo "================================" echo " WELCOME BACK, AGENT" echo "================================" echo "" echo "SYSTEM STATUS: ONLINE" echo "MISSION STATUS: CLASSIFIED" echo "" echo "Initializing control center..." sleep 2 btop } Save the file using , press Enter, and exit with .Now reload your shell configuration.Your custom welcome message appears, waits two seconds, and launches .Of course, you'll need to have installed from the previous trick.You can create a similar command using PowerShell functions.First, open PowerShell and type:If PowerShell says the profile's directory doesn't exist, create it first:New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force ` -Path (Split-Path $PROFILE) Then open the profile file again. Create the file if Notepad asks.Add the following function:function mission { Clear-Host
Write-Host "================================" Write-Host " WELCOME BACK, AGENT" Write-Host "================================" Write-Host "" Write-Host "SYSTEM STATUS: ONLINE" Write-Host "MISSION STATUS: CLASSIFIED" Write-Host "" Write-Host "Initializing control center..."
Start-Sleep -Seconds 2
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 } Save the file and open a new PowerShell window.Your custom command will display the welcome message and list processes with the highest accumulated CPU time.You don't have to stop at .You can create commands for almost anything.For example, on macOS or Linux, you could create a function that launches the Matrix animation:hack() { clear cmatrix } Add it to your shell configuration and reload the file.Now all you need to type is:And your entire terminal transforms into the Matrix.

item.title: AI Could Become the Front Door to Digital Banking
item.author: Anastasiia_D
item.content:encoded: Over the last several years, we have witnessed a real boom in AI technologies. Companies have been experimenting with agents, launching AI assistants, and trying to integrate new capabilities into existing products.However, the initial enthusiasm is gradually colliding with reality. Building an impressive demo is much easier than launching a safe, secure, and reliable product for millions of users.This is particularly evident in the banking sector, where companies work with sensitive financial data, face strict regulatory requirements, and where the cost of any mistake can be much higher. These challenges hinder the adoption of new technologies and bold innovations.Over the last 10–15 years, banks have invested huge amounts of resources in developing the digital customer experience. They have introduced new functions, new services, and complex customer journeys.Several years ago, the whole industry, not just the banking sector, was actively discussing and developing super apps — applications that bring together multiple functions, including financial and non-financial services, in one place.Having worked on banking products, I remember how complex it was to fit so many functions into a single interface.We conducted a lot of research. We tried to assess the clarity of the text and navigation, and we tested different screen designs. We needed to find out whether customers could find the right function or service, interpret the information correctly, and complete the entire customer journey.The interface had to be intuitive, simple, and clear because its usability could directly affect conversion rates and other business metrics.An entire industry has developed around UX research, design, testing, and customer behavior analysis.But what we see today is that ChatGPT and other AI assistants, like Claude, are forming a new habit. Instead of searching for specific information or services, you can simply explain what you want to do, and the assistant helps you find the right one among a myriad of other capabilities.And it's not just about the convenience of interacting with AI. Customers' expectations of digital products are actually changing.A recent found that 23% of surveyed banking consumers already use generative AI for financial tasks. Among those, 74% use ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini to ask financial questions and get help with banking-related tasks.But a banking interface is not just a collection of screens and buttons. It reflects the underlying banking processes.When customers navigate between screens, fill out forms, select options, and confirm operations, they are following a process designed by the bank. The interface guides them through each step.Now imagine that customers no longer need to navigate through these steps themselves. They simply explain what they want to achieve, and an AI assistant helps them get there.This raises an interesting question. Are we just making existing interfaces easier to use, or are we moving towards a different way of delivering services?And this is where the difference between automation and transformation becomes important.Today, you can find many AI assistants on the market. They help answer customers' questions, find information, and automate individual customer service processes.But it's important to distinguish between three levels of AI adoption: assistance, automation, and transformation.At the first level, AI helps people understand an existing process and complete tasks faster.At the second level, AI takes over individual steps, making the whole process faster and cheaper. But we are still operating within the same process.At the third level, we change the process itself.Instead of asking customers to follow predefined banking processes, we start with what they actually want to achieve. AI could then determine how to deliver that outcome, combining different banking services and capabilities without requiring customers to understand how they work behind the scenes.This is not just about making an existing process faster. It changes how customers interact with banks.And we are already seeing early examples of this shift. In the US, eligible ChatGPT users can connect their bank accounts through for read-only financial guidance. Banco has taken a different approach, building an app inside ChatGPT where customers can explore its banking products without leaving the conversation.These are still early steps rather than full process transformation. But they show something interesting: ** **within AI platforms, allowing customers to interact with banking services without opening a traditional banking app.What Is Holding Back the Transition?If the potential benefits are so obvious, why are we not seeing a large-scale transition to this model?In my opinion, one of the main challenges is, of course, security.Recent years have demonstrated not only the capabilities of AI but also the rapid growth of security threats. In 2025 alone, AI-enabled fraud increased by 1,210% in data analyzed by .And recent months have also brought particularly concerning examples of the difficulties in controlling autonomous AI systems.In July 2026, during OpenAI's internal cybersecurity evaluations involving models with reduced safeguards, AI agents bypassed isolation controls and compromised parts of OpenAI's research infrastructure and . The agents took actions beyond their assigned tasks, exposing the risk of giving AI systems access to real infrastructure.Another example came in October 2026, when researchers using AI tools helped identify and analyze critical vulnerabilities in PHP. These vulnerabilities could allow attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable servers. This was not an AI-caused breach, but it demonstrated how AI can accelerate vulnerability research.For banks, these risks are particularly serious. It's one thing to allow AI to answer questions about banking products, but it's something entirely different to allow it to manage financial operations or execute transactions.Moving from an assistant that provides information to one that can take action requires a completely different level of security, control, and trust.And not every company has the resources and expertise necessary to build its own secure infrastructure for AI agents. For smaller players, this could mean relying on specialized technology providers rather than building everything themselves.I don't think traditional banking interfaces will disappear. I believe they will remain necessary for visualizing information, checking data, and confirming important operations.But their role could change significantly.So far, we have tried to make complex banking processes simple and clear for customers through interface design.But the next step may be the opposite: making sure customers no longer need to understand the complexity of these processes.And the real transformation will happen not when every bank launches its own AI assistant, but when AI assistants stop being just an additional feature and become a new way of interacting with banking services.

item.title: How to Investigate Suspected Bot Traffic in GA4
item.author: Shabnam Karbalaeihadi
item.content:encoded: A spike in Direct traffic is easy to notice. The harder one to question is a spike that looks like a win. The new visitors scroll through articles, trigger plenty of events and sometimes rack up multiple page views. In a monthly performance review, that can look like audience growth.Working in publishing SEO, I’ve learned to ask what else grew alongside those sessions. Did more readers come back? Did more people log in or subscribe? Or did most of the increase come from sessions that all looked unusually similar?That question matters in the age of AI search, when visits from people clicking links in AI tools and requests from automated systems can both be part of the picture. A GA4 spike can tell me where to investigate. It can’t tell me which tool generated the traffic, or whether an LLM was involved.Direct or Unassigned spike: find which channel, landing page and country the extra sessions came from, and rule out Discover first.Unusual screen resolution: a rare square resolution like 1366 × 1366 suddenly driving most of the increase is a strong clue. a high-volume segment with almost zero returning users deserves a closer look.Flat logins or subscriptions: thousands of extra sessions with no change in verified account activity don’t add up to audience growth.Traffic from outside your core market: geography narrows the search but is never enough to exclude traffic alone.Views per session below 1: check your tagging and instrumentation before blaming automation.High engagement next to other red flags: automation can scroll to 90% and stay in focus, so engagement alone doesn’t prove real readers.No single signal proves bot traffic. I look for the same sessions matching several of them, then compare reports with and without that segment.Signal 1. A sudden spike in Direct or Unassigned trafficIn GA4, I start in Reports → Acquisition → Traffic acquisition and compare the spike with a comparable period. I check which session default channel group changed, then break down the increase by and . I’m looking for where the sessions came from. A sitewide average can hide a surge concentrated on a single URL.For a publisher, one of my first checks is Search Console → Discover, if the report is available. If Discover clicks climb on the same articles on the same dates, that gives me a plausible explanation for at least part of the lift, especially if referral information is missing in GA4. I compare the timing and URLs because Discover clicks and GA4 sessions are different measurements. Search Console performance reportsWhat I check inside the spikeSignal 2. A surge from the same unusual screen resolutionI add as a breakdown in a GA4 Exploration or check the Tech details report. I pay attention when a square resolution such as or goes from rare to accounting for a large share of the increase. The interesting part is the concentration. How common was that resolution before the spike? Does it also dominate the same landing page, browser or country? GA4 Tech details reportSignal 3. Almost no returning users in a high-volume segmentIf the same cluster shows substantial volume and zero or almost zero returning users over a meaningful date range, I take a closer look. Automation can start with a fresh browser profile each time, and it can also reuse one. Real visitors can look new when GA4 can’t recognise a previous visit, and a successful acquisition campaign can bring in a genuinely new audience. I compare the suspicious group with similar traffic over the same period. GA4 user metricsSignal 4. More sessions without more verified logins or subscriptionsOn a subscription site, I check whether the extra sessions produce any verified logins or subscription activity. A SaaS team could make the same comparison with sign-ups or account activity. If a site uses a custom dimension, a wave of values tells me to check when the tag sends that value. It might be missing for genuine anonymous readers or because the implementation only sets it after login. I get more confidence from a mismatch between thousands of extra interactions and flat account activity, especially where comparable traffic normally produces some.Signal 5. A sudden traffic surge from outside your core marketIf a UK-focused publication suddenly gets a large share of its Direct sessions from Singapore or China, I check whether that lines up with distribution, coverage, or a campaign. Geography helps narrow the investigation. I’m more interested when the same sessions also share a rare resolution and repeatedly enter through one page. Country on its own is too broad a reason to exclude traffic.Signal 6. Views per session drop below 1 below 1 is another prompt to inspect the events. GA4 counts both web page views and app screen views in this metric. If I see a low ratio, I separate web from app traffic and check whether events are arriving without their corresponding or . Missing tags or an event-only implementation can explain the same pattern. I check the instrumentation before attributing it to automation. GA4 dimensions and metricsSignal 7. Strong engagement alongside other red flagsGA4 records engagement time while a page is in focus or an app is in the foreground. An engaged session can qualify by passing the engagement-time threshold, recording a key event, or reaching two page or screen views. The default enhanced-measurement scroll event fires when 90% of the page becomes visible. Browser automation can navigate to a second page, keep a page in focus and scroll deep enough to trigger the same event. These metrics describe what the browser reported. They can look healthy even when I still have questions about who generated the activity. GA4 user engagement · Sessions · Automatically collected eventsI also check unusually long engagement against the metric’s denominator. More than a day of engagement across a large group can be ordinary. More than a day of average engagement per session is a reason to inspect event timestamps and tracking. The GA4 default of 30 minutes, adjustable up to 7 hours and 55 minutes, is an . It measures how long a session can sit idle before expiring, so it doesn’t set a hard ceiling on the length of an active session. GA4 session timeoutGoogle Analytics already excludes traffic from known bots and spiders automatically. For traffic that still looks suspicious, I build a session segment around the combination I’ve observed, such as an unusual resolution and a specific landing page within the channel that spiked. I compare with traffic excluding that segment across sessions, engagement and meaningful outcomes. If a rule also captures traffic I can tie to a genuine Discover spike or verified subscribers, I narrow it. GA4 known bot exclusionHere’s how I set that up in a GA4 Exploration:Go to and start a exploration.Next to , click and choose .Add conditions that match the pattern, for example exactly matches and matches the URL that spiked. Name it .Create a second segment for the channel that spiked and use with the same conditions. This gives you the adjusted view.Apply both segments and compare sessions, returning users, engagement and key events side by side.Where I have access, I ask the web team to compare the same URLs and time windows against CDN or server logs. Repeated request sequences or an existing bot classification can strengthen the case. Until I have that corroboration, I label the segment . I keep the original totals visible alongside the adjusted view so stakeholders can see how much the rule changes the story.In an illustrative example, Direct sessions fell from to once the segment was excluded, while all verified logins and subscriptions remained in the adjusted view. The outcomes didn’t move, which told me the extra sessions weren’t new readers.Set up a custom insight to catch the next bot traffic spikeOnce you know which patterns deserve attention, you can use GA4 custom insights to get an email when traffic changes unexpectedly. An alert gives you a reason to investigate using the signals above. You need the role on the property to create, edit and share custom insights. Ask your GA4 administrator to confirm your permissions or create the insight for you.Open the Insights dashboard. Select your property, go to and scroll to the section. Click , then . Under , click . You can also select beside a suggested insight and adapt its conditions.Choose the evaluation frequency. Select Hourly, Daily, Weekly or Monthly. Hourly evaluation is available for web data only. Daily is a practical starting point for monitoring changes alongside your regular reporting.Define the segment and trigger. Under , click to narrow the traffic using the dimensions available, for example Direct traffic. Choose an available metric and condition. lets GA4 identify an unusual change without a numerical threshold. Alternatively, choose a percentage-increase condition and set a threshold, such as , after checking the comparison period shown in the setup. Treat that threshold as a starting example and adjust it to your site's normal variability.Give the insight a clear name. Include the brand, frequency and reason for the alert. For example, “Brand name | Daily Direct traffic spike | Possible automation” helps colleagues recognise which property and pattern need attention.Configure email notifications and save. In the notification settings, enter the email addresses of property users who should receive the alert. Click . Triggered insights also appear in the property's Insights dashboard.Set up alerts for each property you monitor. Custom insights belong to individual properties, so check the configuration in each one. GA4 supports up to 50 custom insights per property.When an alert arrives, compare the spike with campaigns and Discover performance, then examine screen resolution, returning users, geography and account outcomes. The same alert could also flag a successful article or a tracking issue. Google's guide to Analytics InsightsIn a publishing report, I’d rather explain why sessions rose while verified subscriptions and returning readership stayed flat than turn that spike into an audience-growth claim. The question I bring back to the dashboard is simple.If we take out the sessions that all behave the same way, would we still make the same decision?Does GA4 filter bot traffic automatically?Yes, for known bots. Google Analytics automatically excludes traffic from known bots and spiders, and you can’t turn this off or see how much was excluded. Automation that isn’t on a known list can still reach your reports, which is why the signals above are worth checking.Can I create a custom bot filter in GA4?Not directly. GA4’s built-in data filters are designed for internal and developer traffic, so there is no dedicated filter for suspected bots. Instead, I build a segment around the pattern I’ve observed and compare reports with and without it.Can I remove bot traffic from GA4 data retroactively?No. Data that GA4 has already processed stays in the property, and data filters only apply going forward. For past periods, I use segments or comparisons in Explorations to show the adjusted view next to the original totals.Is every spike in Direct traffic caused by bots?No. Google Discover, untagged email or app links, redirects that drop the referrer and links shared in private messages can all show up as Direct or Unassigned. I check those explanations before labelling any traffic as suspected automation.Can GA4 tell me whether traffic came from an AI agent or an LLM?Not reliably. GA4 can show referrals from AI tools when the referrer is passed, but it can’t tell you which tool generated automated visits. A spike shows you where to investigate. Server or CDN logs give you stronger evidence.

item.title: Recent Outages Have Economic Causes
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyberattack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyberattack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile.Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society.A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience.There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream from the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problems lie.Security, safety, resilience, redundancy and recoverability are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are costs that don’t generate near-term profits.Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, prioritizes near-term profits over everything else. This squeezes all apparent inefficiencies—and, additionally, all other positive intangibles—out of a company in pursuit of those profits.Market competition, essential for the forces that nudge companies to provide better services, is another perceived inefficiency. Monopolization removes it in pursuit of near-term profits.From the perspective of a quarterly budget, spending on reliability measures is an inefficiency. They’re expenses that don’t generate revenue. They feel wasteful until something bad happens.But, if you’re lucky, you can push the costs of failure on to society, further increasing profits. So, we get stranded in airports when planes don’t fly, or have to deal with the fallout when we can’t withdraw money from our bank accounts.The effects of those economic pressures are brittle systems, with single points of failure and cascading failure modes. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes.The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.Upgrading our computerized systems, increasing their reliability, removing single points of failure, and making them more resilient are all technical problems. But they won’t happen until we fix the political and economic ones.We need to change the economic incentives that make it profitable to operate these systems just at the edge of functionality, and to push the costs of failure on to all of us. Fixing that requires regulation—with enforcement and meaningful fines—and stringent antitrust enforcement.But while that’s all easy to say, it’s much harder to implement—especially in the US where monied interests have such a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until this changes, we should expect lots more of these sorts of failures in the future.

item.title: systemd 263-rc1 Ships Initial Rust Code, Experimental Pseudo TTY Broker & Manifest
item.author: Michael Larabel
item.content:encoded: Systemd 263-rc1 was just tagged in gearing up for this next major release. Systemd 263 brings initial support for using the Rust programming language for creating new Rust programs. Plus systemd 263 ships with a new pseudo TTY broker service, a manifest tool, a new keyring service and much more...

item.title: Intel's Vulkan Linux Driver Now Enables Efficient 64-bit Mode "e64" By Default
item.author: Michael Larabel
item.content:encoded: Debuting with the upcoming Intel Nova Lake P processors with their Xe3P integrated graphics is a new efficient 64-bit addressing mode "e64". This efficient 64-bit addressing mode for the future Intel GPUs provides native 64-bit shader memory addressing as a replacement to the 32-bit offset mode used by Intel GPU shaders up to now. As of the latest Mesa Git code, the Intel ANV Vulkan driver is enabling the e64 mode by default...

item.title: Formlabs Form Studio 1 Teardown
item.author: bunnie
item.content:encoded: Formlabs has recently launched the Form Studio 1. I’ve had fun tearing down every new generation of their printers. I am pleased to continue that tradition, and to share the joy of learning by taking apart someone else’s product.Financial interest disclosure: Formlabs provided me with the printer for this teardown, with no contingencies on the contents or views expressed in this post. I am also a shareholder of Formlabs.The Form Studio 1 picks up where the Form 4 SLA printer leaves off. For details, you can review the teardown of the Form 4. The key point is that the Form 4 represented a watershed moment in Formlabs’ evolution from a galvanometer based printer to an LCD shutter based printer. The basic architecture of the Form 4, and the Form Studio 1, is reviewed in the diagram below.While the architecture of the Form Studio 1 mirrors that of the Form 4, the Form Studio 1 retails at roughly a quarter the price of a Form 4. This addresses one of the biggest pain points about the Formlabs printer line-up: the high base price of the printer. Since a big theme of the Form Studio 1 is cost reduction, let’s first explore some of the cost drivers in building products like printers.Complex electromechanical systems are expensive to assemble. The main driver is the cost of labor: a screw costs a fraction of a cent; the labor to install the screw is far larger. Furthermore, there is a big difference in the skills required between a person who only puts one screw into a single hole all day long, and someone who has to keep track of a fifty-step build, routing cables from a diverse number of endpoints, while attaching screws with the correct amount of torque and possibly other bespoke requirements such as thread lockers. A good production-line setup can go a long way to fool-proof the build process – e.g. pre-kitting parts, kanban systems, etc. – but these systems also cost money to set up and run, and the overhead only becomes negligible at the highest volumes.For complex, high-BOM cost builds, the cost of rework is also an important consideration. The high cost of materials means it’s almost never acceptable to simply scrap defective assemblies. However, complex builds have a low net yield, especially in the early phase of the production ramp. The statistics are daunting: a 50-step build where each step is 99% reliable would only yield 60% good product; at 100 steps, you’re well under 40% yield. Worse yet, the problem is often going to be a single subtle issue in just one step out of many, so you’re left looking for a needle in a haystack. This type of task requires the expertise of a senior technician, who bills at a higher rate.Thus, the most effective way to reduce cost is to simply design it out. One metric I can use to compare the Form Studio 1 to the Form 4 is how long it took to do the teardown. The Form 4 took me almost two solid weeks, on and off, of trying to figure out how all the parts came together. When I do a teardown, I try to envision the production flow and reverse it. The Form 4 had several forks in the process that I had to experiment with before I figured out a clean reverse flow. Even then, there were a couple assemblies whose build order I could not figure out. Eventually I gave up, and just tore them apart with brute force.In contrast, the bulk of the Form Studio 1 took me about two afternoons to tear down. The inverse flow was intuitive. At a minimum, this is a strong indicator that rework costs were more manageable.Improved Design for ManufacturingThis design improvement was driven in part by the choice to use a cast aluminum plate as the reference point for everything in the build. It is a solid chunk of metal with many complicated features molded into it, followed up by two CNC machining passes (one for each side) where critical surfaces are leveled, high-precision holes are drilled out, and alignment bosses are refined. Below is an overview picture of the base plate.The image below more clearly shows the CNC machined surfaces and drilled holes.Note the machining marks on the slightly raised surfaces in the casting. A small amount of extra material is roughly placed during the casting process in these areas, and then a precision CNC pass refines it into an accurate, smooth surface.This is in contrast to the Form 4, which assembles a rigid box out of multiple sheet metal and polymer parts. The machining tolerance of each of these sub-assemblies has to be carefully controlled, and often jigs are required during the build process to ensure tolerances.The way for an electrical engineer to think about this is that a cast aluminum plate is to a sheet metal build-up as a solid copper ground plane on a circuit board is to multiple isolated circuit boards cabled together (cast aluminum : sheet metal build-up :: single ground plane : multiple circuit boards; do they even teach analogies anymore in grade school, or is this just me showing my age?).When designing a circuit board, using a solid sheet of copper on an inner layer for ground allows one great freedom to use single wires to connect chips. However, if you separate the grounds, or if you are routing between two separate circuit boards, differences in ground references reduce noise margins. One needs to pay attention to either lining up the grounds (e.g. with lots of explicit ground ties) or making misaligned grounds not a problem (e.g. using differential pairs, etc.). This comes at the cost of more expensive connectors, more wires, or both.In mechanical design, the same reference problem exists. While it is trivial to say that a given beam is X centimeters long, that’s not the parameter that matters – what you care about is often not the height of a single hole above the base plate, but the height of the hole relative to the shaft that feeds into it. If both the hole and shaft are mounted on the same base plate, then any error in the base plate thickness cancels out. If the hole and shaft are mounted on separate plates, then any error in the alignment of the respective base plates adds to the tolerance.Mechanical systems are disadvantaged compared to electrical systems in terms of tolerance margins because in electronics we have an exponential in the device equations to drive noise margins to the rail at every stage of logic. However, mechanical systems generally have linear transfer curves, so tolerances stack additively throughout the build. Thus it is even more important to be aware of where your reference geometry is and to make sure it is faithfully communicated or preserved throughout the assembly. A single cast metal base part largely solves this problem by collapsing it into a single dimensionally stable part.The trade-off of using a cast aluminum base plate is that the molds for casting are quite expensive, which makes design revisions and tweaks correspondingly more difficult. However, the Form Studio 1 re-uses much of the Form 4 light architecture, and so the engineering team could take a clear-eyed look at the design, curating features from a much smaller design space than if they were trying to simultaneously revise the light architecture and do a cost down in the same design generation.Improving Cost, Starting with the Unboxing ExperienceAnother cost driver in large systems is logistics. The sheer bulk and complexity of inventorying components, storing them, and moving them adds up. Anyone who has experienced Ikea furniture absorbs this lesson indirectly. Ikea can warehouse fifty shelves in the space of a single show floor demo shelf, reducing warehousing and retail costs. In general, more compact products are cheaper to produce and sell.It also turns out that there is an optimal density for shipping based on modality. For air freight, that density is in the range of 0.16-0.2 grams/cc. This is why all mobile phone boxes are about the same size – there’s a certain net density target for air shipments that the manufacturers are looking to hit, and tuning the box size is one way to achieve that.According to Formlabs’ product data, the box is 107,525 cubic centimeters and weighs about 18,500 grams. That’s 0.17 grams/cc – exactly at the sweet spot for air shipping. In contrast, the Form 4 was 0.11 grams/cc. This means that even though the box only weighed 23kg, they were paying a rate to ship a 34kg product, because the box contained too much dead air.That 11kg difference adds up – assuming they are paying around \$10/kg (costs vary, but the rate is in the range of \$3-12/kg depending on volume and broker), that’s a \$100 extra cost for shipping due to having the wrong product density. Given that the Form Studio 1 starts at \$699, adding \$100 for shipping dead air significantly erodes gross margins, and thus it would make sense to pay attention to this detail.In previous Form printers, the build platform and resin tank were shipped separately, leaving the printer’s build volume as dead air inside its box. In the case of the Form Studio 1, I can see the extra attention to detail in total supply chain cost. The build platform and resin tank are packaged the dead air volume of the product, thus improving density and helping them hit the magic density for optimal air shipping.A notable feature of every Formlabs product is the inclusion of 3D printed parts in mass production. In this case, the maintenance kit and a port cover are 3D printed.In the case of the plug, it’s explicitly advertised as a 3D printed part; for the maintenance kit, I am only assuming it is, based on the texture and material feel. The plug in this case looks like it was optimized for a zero-post-process build: one end is flatted to stick to the build platform, and angled in such a way that the build proceeds without any support material. This leads to a nice product finish with minimal extra cost, in contrast to the previous plug on the Form 4:Despite the focus on reducing costs, some features improved compared to previous generations. For example, the build platform got a nice redesign to include integrated supports.The build platform itself has an interesting new detail to it. The texture of the surface now has a micromachined texture, probably done with a laser.I’m not sure of all the reasons for the microtexturing, but there are three I can think of:Minimizing the impact of small scratches on the build platform surface. The platform inevitably accumulates a variety of small scratches from scraping models off, and these tend to become defect sites for future builds.Improving release of the model. It might just be me, or it might be the improved scraper, but the items seemed to come off more easily with this texturing.Removing the resin stirrer from the design.The last point is the most speculative, but the Form Studio 1 loses a key mechanism from the Form 4: the resin stirring bar. The resin stirrer was not cheap – it required a fast, precise motor with an optical shaft encoder capable of whipping the stirring bar across the tank at high speeds. I don’t recall where I heard this rumor from, but I seem to remember that mixing with air had some property relevant to the chemistry of the resin, which is part of the reason why the stirrer was necessary. The stir bar also kept the resin evenly mixed helped mix the resin during tank filling and heating, but this is handled by gently churning the build platform up and down within the resin pool instead.So, one possibility is that the microtexturing traps small amounts of air, which allows the stirrer to be costed out. I would emphasize that this is really just my speculation, but in the end, somehow Formlabs was able to cost-out the resin stirrer without loss of quality.Another notable but simple quality of life improvement is the highly improved scraper bundled in the product. Previous generations’ scrapers were probably just a random paint scraper bought at the lowest cost – they were dull, flexed under use, and eventually rusted. The scraper included with the Form Studio 1 is serious business.This seems to be a full custom product, with the Formlabs logo emblazoned on it. The scraper body is made of much thicker steel, and the edge is sharpened to a point. Its build quality makes it border on a martial apparatus, but it functions so well I’m tempted to get more just for other scraping applications around the home.Before taking the Form Studio 1 apart, I repeated a test that I did on the Form 4 for light uniformity, where I put a piece of paper over the LCD panel and had it print a cleaning sheet, while taking a photo of the paper. This time it was much easier to do: I didn’t have to defeat the case closed switch; there’s a convenient diagnostic option in the Form Studio 1 menu for enabling this!Here’s what it looks like on the new Form Studio 1:Here’s what it looked like on the Form 4:Despite the cost-down, the light uniformity looks great! Now, let’s have a look inside and see what’s changed.I decided that the back panel was probably the right place to start – either that or the tank cover was the last thing attached, so it’d be the first thing to take off.A few screws later, and the back side is revealed. The most notable feature is a pair of tubes going from the frame to the back panel.I originally guessed these were for air circulation of some type, but upon consultation with Formlabs they informed me that the tubes are for facilitating the drainage of spilled resin. Makes sense, now that I think about it – if the thin film that forms the bottom of the resin tank failed for any reason, it’d be a spill-pocalypse!A few more screws later, and the bottom plate and air filter are removed, revealing what is primarily the heat sink assembly for the actual light source.The bottom cover itself has something very curious about it.The bottom cover has a pattern of air holes in it that are decidedly not regular, and not random. I thought this was an Easter egg of some type. I pondered it manually, and then I tried image processing it and throwing it into my machine to suggest other ideas, but still came up with nothing.One reason I strongly suspected there was a message is that I did this once upon a time in one of my products. The NeTV2 hid a coded message in its cooling holes:To the best of my knowledge, nobody ever figured this one out. The message is actually pretty easy to decode – if you want to give it a try yourself, I’ve hidden the decode method and answer as a “spoilers” tag:Unfortunately, upon consultation with Formlabs, the pattern of holes was an Easter egg – it was just the pattern they came up with to adequately cool various systems in the printer. Still pretty interesting to think about from that perspective. I wonder how they picked where to put the holes? A simulation of airflow? Some empirical measurements with a smoke machine, mapping out airflow? It’s perhaps even more curious that the pattern was deliberate and optimized; I wonder how they did it!The light source on the Form Studio 1 is greatly simplified compared to the Form 4. The Form 4 had multiple individually controllable light zones; the Form Studio 1 looks to have just a single chain of LEDs driven by a much simplified controller, and an EEPROM to identify the assembly.Like the previous generation, this is a single-layer PCB built onto an aluminum core PCB, for better heat sinking. Despite the simplification, the light uniformity is excellent, so this seems to be a cost-down without compromises (or perhaps the original light source was over-engineered).Accessing the lens assembly is just four screws to pull off the light source:The lens assembly is also simplified in the Form Studio 1 compared to the Form 4. On the Form 4 there was an additional diffuser stage; here, the extra diffuser is gone and all the diffusion comes from a pattern integrated into the lens texture itself.The molding on the lens is exquisite; a side view gives you an idea of the clarity and uniformity of the optical-grade plastics used in the assembly:With the lens assembly removed (and a few more parts taken off, which I’ll return to later in the post), we arrive at the base plate with the LCD still mounted.From this perspective, we can see how the base plate forms a shared reference point for the whole system:The LCD is firmly attached to the base plateThe Z-motor is likewise attached to the same reference planeThe light box would extend back from the plane of the LCDAll this combines to create a clean, straightforward optics path with minimal degrees of freedom for offsets, with most critical dimensions set by two CNC operations on either side of the base plate plus the precision of the injection molds. This means the precision of the assembly relies less on the skill of the operators and more on repeatable machine operations.The top side of the LCD assembly shows the embedded PCB trace heaters for the resin, required to maintain optimal resin temperature for printing. The texturing of the layer between the resin tank and the LCD shows some additional tweaks compared to the Form 4.The back side of the LCD assembly, once removed from the aluminum base plate, shows both the LCD data connector and the heater power cable. Like its predecessor, the LCD cell itself is bonded into the frame, and incorporates a thick sheet of glass to maintain mechanical rigidity throughout all phases of the printing process.Many of the other details of the printer – the resin level sensing, RFIDs, resin dispensing and camera subsystem – are largely identical to the Form 4. However, one difference of note is how the build platform is mounted. Detecting the build platform is not as simple as you’d think, because sometimes users can space out and start a print with the platform absent, or perhaps worse yet, with a leftover print still hanging off the platform.The Form Studio 1 has a major upgrade in this regard:The build platform itself integrates a load cell!To review, a load cell is the heart of every digital weight scale. It senses minute distortions in a beam to infer the mass of an object placed on it. Both the Form 3 and the Form 4 integrated load cells underneath the resin cartridge to measure remaining resin level and usage.On the Form Studio 1, the load cell is under the resin cartridge – it got moved to the build platform. So there is still one load cell, but instead of being used to monitor resin consumption, it’s being used to improve user experience. That’s a bit surprising given the general trend of enshittification – you rarely see a tech company transform a resource with real potential for extracting more customer revenue into one that genuinely improves user experience.The load cell in the Form Studio 1 evidently measures the mass of the build platform. After the build platform is installed, there is a calibration step – that makes sense, as load cells need to be tared. Once tared, they can sense tiny mass changes. I don’t have visibility into the precision of this load cell, but they can generally sense sub-gram mass changes. This means if a print is left hanging on the build platform, the device should be able to detect it by comparing the calibrated mass of the build platform against the current mass. This is a pretty elegant solution to a hard problem, which also did not involve adding cost to the system because it’s repurposing an existing component for a new feature.I asked Formlabs for their fact check on this feature, and they pointed out that the Form 4 was also able to sense forces due to a different type of force sensor at the bottom of the Z-axis; I had missed that sensor in the previous teardown. That being said, apparently a key function of the stir bar (properly referred to as the “mixer”) on the Form 4 was to detect foreign objects on the resin tank; since this was costed out in the Form Studio 1, the load cell in the build platform mount also takes on the task of foreign object detection inside the tank, as well as detecting misconfigured build platforms.Remarkably, the electronics are perhaps the least interesting part of this teardown because you don’t even need to tear down the system to see most of the main board!However, with the case off, we can get a clearer snapshot of all the part numbers. Here’s the right hand side of the circuit board:The board is beautifully labeled: no notes on this one. This board was made to be looked at.On the left hand side, I removed the heatsink on the SoM to reveal the components underneath. Instead of a Raspberry Pi compute module used on prior editions of the printer, this uses a Rockchip RK3568-based SoM by Forlinx configured with 1GiB of LPDDR4X RAM and 32GiB of eMMC. Given rumors of spotty supply and rising prices from Raspberry Pi, a migration to a pure-play SoM provider makes sense. One nice thing about using a SoM is you’re not locked into a given vendor – so long as you keep your usage of the Linux distribution generic and portable, it’s a modest lift to port to a new vendor and qualify the product, restoring negotiating leverage to the buyer.The back side of the mainboard is completely clean – not a single component. This makes sense for a cost-down like this – keeping the design single-sided with no through-hole component removes several steps in the PCB assembly process. Automated optical inspection catches most of the assembly errors, and the plethora of cabling to driven peripherals means you don’t need too many additional test points to do a comprehensive functional test of the assembled board.Not-so-secretly, I have an obsession with power supplies. Many system integrators reduce costs by cutting corners on the power supplies, and so this is one of the places I look to check if standards are being held after a cost-down. The Form Studio 1 power supply is provided in a tidy module that snaps into the chassis.Taking off the cover reveals the internals:This power supply checks all the boxes – tidy construction, all-new components, plenty of adhesive to hold components in place for reflow assembly, adequate heat sinking and modern architecture. There’s an additional layer of components on the back side which I did not reveal, because I’d like to keep this power supply intact and re-use it for my own projects after the teardown!Another generation of Formlabs printer, another teardown! I’ve always enjoyed being able to take these machines apart and to learn from them. This one was especially interesting because it demonstrates growth along a new axis for Formlabs. Previous printers pushed the technical frontier; this one is a pivot into cost-down territory. This transition is often fraught with difficult choices, and I think they did a good job of picking their battles, simplifying the design, and taking a holistic approach to reducing cost while not degrading the user experience. The move of the load cell from detecting resin consumption to build platform presence is especially interesting, because despite going for a lower cost architecture, they removed a knob they could use to extract more revenue from customers and instead deployed it as a sensor that improves customer experience. The 3D printing space has become a hyper-competitive cost-sensitive race-to-the-bottom market, and the Form Studio 1 is a solid move towards addressing the realities of today’s rapidly shifting business landscape.

item.title: Citroën Hydraulic System
item.content:encoded: Another advantage of the variable ride height was the ability to dispense with a conventional jack. To jack the car up, all that was required was to place it in the highest suspension position, place a simple stand under the car and then select the lowest suspension position. The two wheels on the side of the car under which the stand is placed lift themselves off the ground. Other car manufacturers, notably Rolls-Royce and Mercedes-Benz licenced the system which was also used on Berliet trucks. Similar systems are also used on some military vehicles.At the heart of the system are the so-called 'spheres' one per wheel and one main accumulator as well as a dedicated brake accumulator on some models. The purpose of the main accumulator is to even out fluctuations in pressure.On later cars fitted with antisink or Activa suspension, there may be as many as nine spheres. Each sphere consists of a hollow metal ball, open to the bottom, with the top and bottom of the sphere being separated by a flexible desmopan rubber membrane. The top is filled with nitrogen at high pressure, up to 75 bar while the bottom connects to the car's hydraulic fluid circuit. The high pressure pump powered by the engine pressurizes the circuit and the accumulator sphere. This part of the circuit is at between 150 and 180 bars. It powers the front brakes first, prioritised via a security valve, and depending on type of vehicle, can power the steering, clutch, gearchange, etc.Pressure goes from this circuit to the wheel spheres, pressurizing the bottom part of the spheres and rods connected to the wheel suspension. Suspension works by means of a rod pushing LHM into the sphere, compressing the nitrogen in the upper part of the sphere. Damping is provided by a two-way 'leaf valve' in the opening of the sphere. LHM has to squeeze back and forth through this valve which causes resistance and controls the suspension movements. This damper is far simpler and more reliable than those fitted to conventional vehicles and is also more efficient. Height correction and levellingCar height correction works by height correctors connected to the front and rear anti-roll bars and permit more more fluid to travel under pressure to the spheres when it detects that the suspension is lower than the pre-determined ride height (e.g. the car is loaded). When the ride height is too high (e.g. after unloading) fluid is returned to the system reservoir via low-pressure return pipes. Height correctors act with some delay in order not to correct regular suspension movements. Rear brakes are powered from the rear suspension spheres. Because the pressure there is proportional to the load, so is the braking power. Furthermore, under heavy braking, hydraulic fluid is removed from the rear suspension causing the tail to drop providing inbuilt anti-dive.Spheres are not subject to mechanical wear, but do suffer pressure loss, mostly from nitrogen diffusing through the membrane. They typically last between 60,000 and 100,000 km. Spheres once had a threaded plug on top for recharging. Newer spheres do not have this plug, but it can be retrofitted. The symptom of pressure loss is a hard ride.

item.title: Decoding the role of cellular senescence in wounds
item.author: Saranya P. Wyles
item.content:encoded: Studies that involve the direct manipulation of senescent cells, either by addition or elimination, in wound models have yielded conflicting results. This inconsistency probably reflects the inherently dynamic nature of wound healing and the complexity of targeting cellular senescence. In this Comment, we systematically evaluate current studies with respect to timing, experimental design and interventional strategies to clarify the role of various senescent-cell subpopulations in the wound healing process.
