item.title: How WinHelp Files Work
item.content:encoded: I wanted Paperback to be able to open some old WinHelp files I had laying around, so I wrote libhlp, a pure-Rust reader for them. I had my wisdom teeth out on a Friday morning, spent the rest of that day completely out of it, and then woke up Saturday and did this instead of resting like a normal person. Recovering patients make great decisions.Microsoft never documented the format, but Manfred Winterhoff did, in helpfile.txt, which ships alongside his decompiler, helpdeco. Between those and poking at real files, I worked out the format, and Claude wrote a lot of the actual Rust.A file starts with the magic number , followed by the position of its internal directory. A help file is really an archive, and that directory lists the files inside it. Most of them have names starting with a pipe: holds the title and settings, holds the text, holds the fonts, holds the topic names, and pictures live in files like .The directory is a B+ tree, and so is every other index in the file, all with the same page layout.All the text lives in , which is cut into fixed-size blocks. Each block can be LZ77 compressed, and positions in the file count bytes of the decompressed text, not of the file itself. Every block also takes up the same amount of that address space whether it fills it or not. In a typical file, each block gets 16 KB of space and only decompresses to about 4 KB, so reading has to skip the gap to the next block.Inside the blocks, the text is a linked list of records. Some records start a new topic, and the rest hold its paragraphs, each with a formatting part and a text part. The text part can be compressed a second time, which is where it gets fun.Compression, part one: LZ77WinHelp's LZ77 is about as simple as compression gets. The data comes in groups: one flag byte, then up to eight items. Each bit of the flag byte, lowest first, says whether its item is a literal byte or a back-reference. A back-reference is two bytes, with 12 bits of distance and 4 bits of length:The length is stored minus 3, since anything shorter isn't worth a back-reference. A distance of 0 means "repeat the byte I just wrote", and since the copy can read bytes it's still writing, followed by a back-reference of length 5 becomes .One fun quirk: some real files have back-references that reach behind the start of the data, where there's nothing to copy yet. helpdeco keeps its 4 KB window in a buffer that starts out full of zeroes, so those references just copy zeroes, and the files come out right that way. libhlp starts its window out zeroed too, instead of treating it as an error or reading off the front of the buffer.Compression, part two: phrasesOn top of LZ77, a help file can swap its most common phrases for short codes, and there are two versions of this.WinHelp 3.1 keeps the table in . In the text, any byte from 1 to 15 starts a two-byte code, and every other byte is just itself:The lowest bit of the code says whether a space follows the phrase. Phrases usually end at a word, so that saves a byte most of the time.The Windows 95 help compiler added a fancier scheme, called Hall compression, with the phrases split across and . Here, the lowest bits of each byte say what kind of byte it is. If the lowest bit is clear, the rest of the byte picks one of the first 128 phrases, so the most common ones fit in a single byte. Ending in starts a two-byte code for the rest of the table, starts a run of literal bytes, means a run of spaces, and means a run of zero bytes. For the runs, the upper bits hold the length minus one, since a run of nothing would be a wasted byte. doesn't store where each phrase starts. It stores how long each one is, packed into as few bits as it can get away with. Each length is a unary count in steps of some power of two, followed by the remaining low bits to add on top. The step size is set once for the whole file.My first version always read at least one remainder bit. That works until a file uses a step of one, where there's no remainder to store. Then every length reads one bit too many, and everything after the first phrase is garbage. The fix was a single check.When a help author wrote a topic, they gave it a context string, a name like . You'd expect a link to store the position of the topic it points to, but it actually stores a hash of the target's name. To follow a link, you hash its target name the way WinHelp does and look the result up in , which maps hashes to positions.Each byte goes through a lookup table that gives uppercase and lowercase letters the same values, so links are case insensitive. The table's entries are signed, so anything at or above subtracts instead of adding. Get that wrong and almost every hash still comes out right, so it's really easy to miss. Oh, and an empty name hashes to 1, not 0, because that's what WinHelp does.Text doesn't store its own formatting. A paragraph says "switch to font 4", and says font 4 is the bold one. Links are drawn the same way. WinHelp underlines a link by switching to an underlined font, so libhlp has to tell that underline apart from underlining the author actually asked for.WinHelp is older than Unicode, so text is stored in whatever Windows code page the author used, which might be a double-byte one for East Asian languages. Sometimes the file's language ID says which one. When it doesn't and the text is mostly non-ASCII, libhlp guesses the code page from the text itself.Then there's WinHelp 3.0, the version from Windows 3.0, which is different enough to almost be its own format. Its topic blocks are 2 KB and never compressed, its records give the distance to the next record instead of its position, its topic headers are 12 bytes instead of 28, and its links point at topic numbers instead of hashes. libhlp reads it, but it took its own commit.And then there are the files that only share the extension. Borland's help compiler and MS-DOS QuickHelp both made files that have nothing else in common with WinHelp, so libhlp just turns those away.It reads the text, titles, tables, emphasis, links and pictures of every WinHelp version I know of, from 3.0 to the Windows 95 compiler, and it bounds checks everything. Paperback uses it to open files, so if you've got an old one sitting around, now you can read it.

item.title: Name that Ware, November 2026
item.author: bunnie
item.content:encoded: The Ware for November 2026 is shown below.I felt a little nostalgic, as I always do around this time of year. I picked an easy-to-guess ware, but one from that era when I anticipated the holiday season the way a child would. This one was plucked from a trove I found recently – a board I distinctly remember being quite curious about, but which had been kept safely out of reach because back then it was expensive and my father didn’t want me pulling the chips off and breaking it (and apparently it has remained hidden there ever since!).I find it interesting that even back then, some chips had their part numbers ground off to discourage cloning. Also, note the Foxconn-branded connectors, reflecting the company’s origin story as a manufacturer of discount connector clones. I think this board dates from a vintage when Foxconn was still mostly making connectors and only just starting to diversify into other lines of business.

item.title: Winner, Name that Ware October 2026
item.author: bunnie
item.content:encoded: The ware for October 2026 is the control board from a SodaStream drinking water carbonation machine. It was really interesting to see people puzzle over the nature of the board – I would say I’d have a similarly difficult time guessing this. On the flip side, I also never would have suspected that the operating principle of a carbonation controller would be sensing the vibration signature of the gas moving through various valves and releases.In retrospect, it does make sense – the sound the machine makes is unique and repeatable – so it would have a signature one could discriminate and trigger on. Accelerometers have several hundred hertz (if not more) sensing bandwidth – adequate for the task – and they are a low-cost, mass-produced commodity, thanks in part to smart phones anchoring their demand. Meanwhile, a microphone would pick up too much ambient noise and could miss signatures if operated in a noisy room. All in all, it’s a pretty clever solution to the problem, and the sort of trick learned by taking things apart. One more for the pile of tricks in my head!Above is a photo that gives some more context to the overall solution inside the SodaStream. Thanks again to FETguy and Renew Computers for sharing this ware! There were many great attempts at guessing this one, but none were quite spot-on, so there is no prize awarded this month.

item.title: sqlite3_rsync: Database Remote-Copy Tool For SQLite
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: This additional SQLite tool has been around for a while now - it was added as "experimental" in SQLite 3.47.0 in October 2024 and enhanced in SQLite 3.50.0 in May 2025. It was only today that I understood one of its most attractive characteristics.Normally, if you want to grab a snapshot copy of a SQLite database, you need to use either the backup API or VACUUM INTO. In both cases you need enough disk space to create a duplicate copy of your database, so if you're on a small instance and you already use more than half of the available disk you are plain out of luck. can copy a snapshot of your database over an SSH connection to another machine, without first needing to create a full local copy!It's also good for synchronizing an existing copy of a database without re-transmitting the entire thing over the network. It works in a similar way to regular rsync:The core idea behind the protocol is that the replica sends cryptographic hashes for pages or groups of pages over to the origin side. The origin sends back page content that differs, or requests finer-grain hashes if a multi-page hash does not match. If the origin and replica start out being vastly different, the total network bandwidth can exceed the size of the entire database, due to the overhead of exchanging hashes, but the excess bandwidth is not great - a few percent at most.

item.title: Sydney Fire Ant Infestation
item.content:encoded: Authorities are ramping up efforts to manage a fire ant nest in Sydney after investigations revealed a larger and more complex infestation than first identified.A nest detected in Auburn was successfully treated at the weekend, but further surveillance has revealed a more extensive presence of fire ants requiring intensive treatment and a broader biosecurity response.It comes after Commonwealth authorities detected the insects, known for their painful sting, at the Enfield Intermodal Logistics Centre, in Sydney's inner west, on September 23.Imported goods are suspected to be the source of both incursions, which are not otherwise believed to be connected.NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty said a task force was being established to determine the ants' origins.Ms Moriarty says the infestation is more complex than first thought."The experts believe that they came in through containers that have come in likely from China," she said."At this stage, they are still only on this particular site in Auburn, but we will undertake further surveillance … to see if they have spread."I was able to check [the Auburn site] out myself yesterday, and even though the area is not geographically big, the types of ants that we have here do spread in a different way than what we've seen ants do in New South Wales."Ms Moriarty said the Auburn infestation was located in an industrial area and included businesses that imported goods from Asia and elsewhere.Management efforts underwayA biosecurity order is expected to be issued by Friday to regulate the movement of high-risk materials through Auburn, including soils, turf, mulch and building materials.Additional biosecurity officers and detection dogs will also be deployed as part of the response.Detection dogs were deployed in Auburn on Monday.()Ms Moriarty said there had been more than 900 reports of suspicious nests from the public recent days, and asked locals to remain on the lookout for infestations."Biosecurity is everybody's responsibility,"The ants are up to 6 millimetres long, dark reddish-brown with brown-black abdomens and are known to be aggressive.Bites that have a burning sensation can cause itchy blisters or pustules and lead to the hospitalisation of children and death in severe cases.If spotted, the nests must not be destroyed and members of the public are urged not to try to capture the ants, which are classified as prohibited matter in NSW.Suspected fire ants can be reported to the Biosecurity Helpline on 1800 680 244.

item.title: Quoting Scott Aaronson
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog. Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the stars. That might give you idea of how our resolution into the complexity-theoretic universe, and the whole universe of mathematical truth beyond it, has now improved.

item.title: What Is the Metabolism-First Theory for the Origin of Life?
item.content:encoded: or well over 4 billion years, the fire of metabolism has powered the engines of life. The ability of cells to gather, transform, and harness chemical energy from their surroundings is the central force driving the dizzyingly complex network of chemical reactions that sustains living things.Metabolism is so crucial to life that some researchers believe that these reactions could have helped spark life itself. They argue that life’s first glimmers were found in self-sustaining cycles of simple molecules, before genes or cells existed. Only later did more complex molecules like RNA and DNA develop and begin storing information for the purposes of heredity.The core argument behind metabolism’s primacy is that without a self-sustaining reaction to provide energy, it’s impossible to explain how the larger and more complex molecules necessary for cellular life could have been produced at all. Energy going through the system is what life is in its many manifestations, said William Martin, an evolutionary biologist at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf in Germany. “It synthesizes genes that contain the information to produce the catalysts that keep this reaction going, and those catalysts have changed over time.”The concept that reactions driven by nonliving geochemistry could have eventually triggered living biochemistry has been decades in the making. In 1968, the American biophysicist Harold Morowitz proposed that energy that flows through a system organizes that system, and he applied this to the concept of a proto-metabolism. Essentially, Morowitz suggested that energy from external environmental sources, such as the sun or geologic processes, could nudge chemical networks into self-sustaining reactions because they were thermodynamically favored. In time, those could become biological reactions.A very simple version of early self-sustaining reactions might be something like the acetyl-CoA pathway, a process that some modern microbes use to build complex organic molecules and generate chemical energy from hydrogen and carbon dioxide. But what conditions could have sparked these types of lifelike reactions?Deep-sea submersibles first encountered hydrothermal vents in the late 1970s. These are wounds in the seafloor where geothermally heated water rich in dissolved metals pours out into the surrounding seawater. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, Günter Wächtershäuser, a patent lawyer with a doctorate in chemistry, proposed the concept of an “iron-sulfur world.” In this possible early Earth environment, self-sustaining reactions like the acetyl-CoA pathway could have been chemically catalyzed by the iron-sulfide minerals collecting around these vents.Here’s how that could have led to life. At first, a very simple pathway might have converted carbon dioxide and hydrogen into more complex carbon-containing compounds such as acetate and pyruvate, and released energy back into the environment. Hydrogen would have provided the energy; metallic catalysts kept this running in a loop. Once a primitive cycle was established, it could begin to produce increasingly complex compounds in layers, with more and more enzymatic loops, all gathering and releasing energy, building out from this original cycle. It’s possible that they could continue increasing in complexity well before any of life’s genetic mechanisms of inheritance had developed.“You start out with a simple inorganic catalyst, and then organic catalysts, and then enzymes, and the metabolic process becomes more complex,” Martin said. “But the nature of the reactions that start without enzymes has been up in the air and hotly debated.”To explore possible mechanisms, Martin and his colleagues mimicked temperature and pressure conditions around hydrothermal vents in the laboratory. In 2020, the team showed that chemicals found in these vents, such as carbon dioxide and hydrogen, along with nickel and iron minerals common at these sites, could combine to create formate, acetate, and pyruvate. These compounds are essentially the “spine” of the acetyl-CoA pathway, said Martina Preiner, a biochemist at the Max Planck Institute for Terrestrial Microbiology in Germany and lead author of the study. The findings “show that it’s possible to start these reactions before you have anything else,” including RNA or proteins, Preiner said.However, some scientists argue that the heated and pressurized conditions around hydrothermal vents may not have been required to form these reactions. Also in 2020, Ramanarayanan Krishnamurthy, an organic chemist at Scripps Research in California, and his colleagues demonstrated that two small molecules that may have been present in an early Earth environment, pyruvate and glyoxylate, could react to form almost all the components of the reverse citric acid cycle — which is analogous to the acetyl-CoA cycle — and could do so not only at temperatures and in water conditions far removed from the more extreme environment of a vent, but also without any metal catalysts. This suggests that metabolism could have kicked off in a tepid pool rather than a deep-sea crucible.Whatever environment provided the trigger, there is no well-formed understanding of how initial metabolic reactions could have become stable enough to develop complexity. Genetic material that can store and replicate information may have been necessary to transmit improvements to rudimentary metabolic reactions across generations.Researchers also need to establish a connection between metabolism and genetic information, as well as determine how these proto-metabolic reactions might have coexisted without sabotaging each other once they were placed within the confines of cell membranes.“How best can we mix them together so that we don’t get a complete mess that we can’t analyze?” Krishnamurthy said. “That is the challenge.”Editor’s Note: Ramanarayanan Krishnamurthy has received funding from the Simons Foundation, which also funds this . Simons Foundation funding decisions have no influence on our coverage.

item.title: The Quantum Omelette Problem
item.content:encoded: “Sunday or Monday, eat eggs every day.”My mum took this advice rather seriously. On weekdays, we ate boiled eggs for breakfast. Sundays, however, were omelette days.Our ritual was always the same. Each of us siblings announced how many eggs we wanted as we streamed into the kitchen. My mum cracked the eggs into a shiny steel bowl, added our chosen mix-ins, and whisked them together. The yolks, whites, salt, and chili powder quickly disappeared into one speckled mixture. She poured it into a hot, oiled pan, where it hissed and sizzled before sliding onto our plates.The omelettes were soft, spicy, and gone within minutes.My diet is now plant-based, but the nostalgia of those Sunday-morning breakfasts remains strong—the steel bowl, the sizzling pan, and all of us gathered around the table, waiting eagerly for the omelettes to arrive.Our weekday boiled eggs and Sunday omelettes offer a useful contrast. In a boiled egg, the yolk and white remain distinguishable. In an omelette, they are mixed and transformed. Some properties—texture, flavor, and structure—belong to the finished mixture rather than to either component separately.When two parts interact strongly, which properties still belong to the parts, and which belong only to the whole?This question appears across science whenever interacting parts become difficult to describe independently. In quantum thermodynamics, it becomes a question of energy. Picture a small quantum system, an atom, say, surrounded by a much larger environment. The total energy of the setup comes from three sources: the atom, the environment, and their interaction.When the atom barely interacts with its surroundings, separating the energy contributions is easy. The interaction energy is small enough to ignore, and we can speak cleanly of the atom’s energy and the environment’s. When the interaction is strong, however, that shared energy can no longer be brushed aside, making it difficult to decide how much belongs to the atom and how much to its surroundings.For a large object, interactions with the environment typically occur at the surface, while most of its energy is associated with the much larger bulk. As an object grows, the surface becomes less important compared to its volume, so the interaction energy can often be ignored. But this reasoning breaks down for very small objects, where surface effects remain significant, or for systems whose interactions extend through the bulk, allowing interaction energy to scale with volume.Such strong interactions are not limited to tiny systems; they also appear across condensed matter, nuclear, and high-energy physics. Lattice gauge theories provide one important example: their particles and fields are tied together by interactions and local constraints, making it especially difficult to draw a clean boundary around one part and declare, “This energy belongs here.”In all these cases, the energy of the whole may be perfectly clear. The challenge, however, is deciding how to divide that energy among pieces that are no longer truly separate.That brings us to a deceptively simple question: How should we define the internal energy of a strongly interacting system?Definitions in physics do more than attach names to things. They tell us what counts as a system, which quantities can be measured, and how mathematical ideas connect to experiments. A useful definition must do more than sound reasonable: it should recover familiar results in familiar situations and remain consistent with the laws of physics. When two plausible definitions lead to different conclusions, the choice between them cannot be settled by language alone.Consider the internal energy of a system. When a system is strongly coupled to its surroundings, some of the total energy is stored in the interaction, and several reasonable ways of assigning that shared energy become possible. But which definition of internal energy is consistent with thermodynamics? This is the question I explored with my collaborators Zohreh Davoudi, Christopher Jarzynski, Niklas Mueller, Connor Powers, and Nicole Yunger Halpern.Physicists describe a system’s energy using a mathematical object called a . In our recent paper, we consider three ways of defining the internal energy of a strongly coupled system.Definition 1: Subtract the environmentStart with the total energy of the system-environment composite, then subtract the energy the environment would have on its own at the same temperature. Whatever remains, including the interaction energy, is assigned to the system.Definition 2: Include the environment’s influenceRather than separating the interaction energy by hand, describe the system’s energy using a that captures how the interaction energy affects the system’s energy at equilibrium. Physicists call this the Hamiltonian of mean force.Definition 3: Account for temperature as wellThe Hamiltonian of mean force depends on temperature. The third definition takes this dependence into account when calculating the system’s internal energy.All three definitions have appeared in the literature on strong-coupling thermodynamics, each offering a seemingly reasonable way to account for the environment’s influence on the system. We wanted to find out whether choosing one definition over another would change how we describe the same physical process.To test the three definitions, my collaborators and I considered a —the physicist’s term for changing something in the setup almost instantaneously. Imagine rapidly turning a knob that controls the system, perhaps by suddenly switching on a magnetic field. We can also suddenly change how strongly the system interacts with its surroundings, effectively turning the interaction between them on or off. Either change happens so quickly that the system and its environment have no time to respond: their states remain constant during that instant. Yet the system’s internal energy can change because the rules governing it have changed. Since this energy change results from deliberate external control, we call it .After the quench, the knob is left alone. The system then evolves under the new, fixed conditions and exchanges energy with its environment. This later change in the system’s internal energy is called .Separating the process into two stages makes it easier to tell work and heat apart: work enters during the sudden, controlled change, while heat flows during the evolution that follows. It is a little like whisking an egg first and then placing it on a hot pan, rather than trying to whisk and cook it at the same time.Once we have chosen a definition of a system’s internal energy, we can ask how that energy changes during any thermodynamic process. The first law of thermodynamics tells us that the change in internal energy must be accounted for by work and heat ,The first law is essentially a statement of energy conservation. It tells us that any change in the system’s internal energy must be accounted for: the energy must have entered as work, as heat, or as some combination of the two.But here is the catch. Each of the three definitions of internal energy comes with its own corresponding definitions of work and heat. If we change what we mean by , we also change how we split that energy change into and . For each of the three choices, however, the definitions are constructed so that work and heat add up to the total change in internal energy. All three therefore satisfy the first law.At first, this seems reassuring. Perhaps any of the three definitions will do.To decide whether all three internal energy definitions are truly acceptable, we need a stricter test: the second law. The first law tells us that energy must be conserved, but it does not tell us which direction a process will naturally take. The second law supplies that direction. An egg can be whisked and cooked into an omelette, but an omelette left on the plate will not spontaneously uncook itself, separate into a yolk and a white, and return to its shell. Energy conservation alone would not rule out such a reversal, yet nature overwhelmingly favors one direction. Cooking an omelette is therefore an irreversible process. A perfectly reversible process, by contrast, could be undone without leaving any lasting changes to the system or its surroundings.For the sudden changes studied in the paper, we can quantify irreversibility by comparing the work actually performed with the minimum work required in an ideal, perfectly reversible process. Thermodynamics captures this minimum through a quantity called the free-energy change, ​. The difference between the actual work and this ideal minimum,is called . It measures the extra work associated with carrying out the process irreversibly, and the second law says that it cannot be negative.This is where the three definitions part ways. All three satisfy the first law, but only two satisfy the second law for the processes considered in the paper. The third definition, which accounts for the temperature dependence of the Hamiltonian of mean force, can predict negative dissipated work.Does this mean that our quantum system has somehow broken the second law? Not at all. Rather, the third definition assigns internal energy, work, and heat in a way that makes a valid process look thermodynamically inconsistent.The next question is why the three definitions agree in classical physics but separate in the quantum case. The answer lies in one of quantum mechanics’ defining features: observables do not always commute. Roughly speaking, when noncommuting observables describe two quantum properties, they cannot both be measured simultaneously. This has no direct counterpart in classical physics, where two observables describing different properties can be measured simultaneously. When the system’s energy and interaction energy cannot be simultaneously measured, the three definitions of work can give three different values.To explore this connection, we considered what happens when the system’s Hamiltonian commutes with the interaction Hamiltonian, both before and after the sudden quench. In this classical-like limit, all three expressions for work give the same value, which also obeys the second law. In hindsight, the result may seem obvious. Still, there is something oddly satisfying about pinpointing precisely when the three definitions agree: strong coupling alone does not force them to give different answers. Quantum noncommutativity is what allows them to part ways.Over the years, our family’s egg repertoire expanded. MasterChef episodes, new cookbooks, and travel brought poached eggs, Scotch eggs, shakshuka, eggs-in-purgatory, Tamagoyaki, and plenty of experiments in between. In some dishes, the yolk and white remain almost perfectly distinct; in others, the boundary between them nearly disappears. A whole spectrum exists between separation and complete mixing.The same is true of a system and its environment: their interaction can range from barely noticeable to overwhelmingly strong. Our results identify two definitions that remain consistent with the laws of thermodynamics for the processes we studied, even when those interactions become strong.

item.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months.Here's the video of the talk. In this post I'm going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply.Coding agents in November 2025Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5. With hindsight, this was a consequential model.In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said:Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach.Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn't been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn't feel reliable enough - I had to correct it often enough that it didn't feel like a clear accelerant.The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself.Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks.The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work.Fable class models in June/JulyWe got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was to release, due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them.In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5 - a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work.After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn't get it back until July 1st.For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as . My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive, after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug.A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm.Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook.I'd currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as "cheap Fable"). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well.These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model.3D modeling and game development in September/OctoberSomething interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they'll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for.I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here's Gemini 4 Neon's attempt at "Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data", for example.3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don't know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa.I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play!Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 "This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun." And it worked. My Battledrones Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay.Opus 5.5 was the first model I'd used that appeared to understand fun. I've since worked on several little game projects where prompts like "Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful" produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time.It's good at 3D modeling, too. Here's the "Goliath" mech from my Battledrones game, as seen in the model viewer debug tool:Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I've been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they'd been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games.It feels like another inflection point to me.Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too?I'm still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement.I'm getting done with that model right now!It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I've been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42, 1.0a43, and 1.0a44 - plus LLM 0.37, 0.37.1, 0.37.2, 0.37.3, and 0.38 - all in the last three weeks, represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it. That's a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks.Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don't think I'll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand.

item.title: Build your own amp modeler: $78 DIY pedal kit from TONE3000
item.content:encoded: TONE3000 has sought to bring the biggest disruptor of today’s amp modeling game to the masses in a novel way by partnering with Daisy Audio for a DIY pedal kit.This isn’t your standard build-it-yourself overdrive or fuzz pedal. Instead, this is a fully fledged capture and IR player that can be completely assembled at home, and tap into the ever-growing network of Neural Amp Modeler (NAM) tones.It’s an enticing prospect. TONE3000 and the free-to-use NAM A2 have taken the gear world by storm this year, rewriting the rules of amp modeling in the process.NAM A2 is widely believed to be one of the best modeling technologies of today, outperforming the industry’s big guns in a blind listening test. What’s more, it’s an open-source platform that lets players create, download and use captures of amps and effects for free.Blackstar, Fractal, HeadRush, Positive Grid, Line 6 and Fender are all cottoning on to the game-changing tech – TONE3000 even launched a free plugin to play captures – but now NAM A2 hype has reached fever pitch with this new partnership.According to TONE3000, every part of the pedal is open source, from the firmware and companion app to the schematic, circuit board, and drill template. In other words, anyone can build the pedal.And it looks like a neat pedal, too. Once assembled, it has room for four presets, with a rotary switch to go between them. There’s a three-band EQ, as well as controls for Input, Output, and Noise Gate.Once together, it can host any NAM A2 capture, of which there are quite literally hundreds of thousands. It can also stack captures, too, or run primary models into an Impulse Response.Of course, this is way more advanced than wiring up an overdrive pedal, so the build is not for the faint of heart. TONE3000 goes as far as to suggest you should have at least two home builds under your belt before even thinking about this one.It has about 150 solder joints, plus 14 wires to jacks, footswitch, and the rotary control. It has a through-hole construction, with no surface-mount parts. It’s all built on the Daisy Audio Seed3 module, which costs just $34.99.The rest of the hardware comes separately courtesy of Tayda Electronics. That set is priced at $42.99, and comes with the circuit board, aluminum enclosure, and all the remaining bells and whistles. In all, that amounts to $77.98 for the entire pedal kit.For those who aren’t afraid, the chassis has been made plenty big enough to inject a few modifications of your own.“Daisy was built so anyone could turn an idea into a real piece of audio hardware,” says Daisy co-founder, Andrew Ikenberry.“TONE3000 has taken state-of-the-art neural modeling and open-sourced every piece of the pedal around it, which is exactly the kind of project we hoped Daisy would make possible. We can't wait to see what builders do with it.”

item.title: GPT 6.2 Astra Solves a Historical Mystery
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Here's an interesting case-study in using GPT-6.2 Astra for historical research, from history professor Mark Humphries:With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians.Astra found a diary reference reference to a visit by the vicomte de Chabot dated five days before a date mentioned in the sketchbook at a nearby river, and suggested that Chabot's journal of his travels (only available by order from Cleveland State University) might confirm that the sketchbook was his work.Are historians due for a round of Deep Blue? Mark thinks it will be mild:But if the experience of mathematics is any guide, we can also anticipate that sometime next spring or summer we’ll face a sort of crisis of confidence as we struggle to understand how to respond to agentic systems that can do things human historians cannot. To be fair, that crisis will almost certainly be less profound for us than it is for math. The problem in mathematics, of course, is that solving hard math problems was the whole game. Historians, on the other hand, constantly reinterpret the past in light of an evolving present; we don’t chase a single universal truth. We also (in the ideal at least) write books and articles that are closer to works of philosophy and literature than they are to scientific tracts. Humanity is thus something of a requirement for the production of historical literature.

item.title: What happens if you accidentally eat moldy food? - Josephine Wee
item.author: TED-Ed
item.content:encoded:
Explore how mold spores form and grow, the difference between harmful and helpful molds, and which are dangerous to eat.
--
You open your fridge to grab a snack and recoil at the scene before you. Strawberries coated in fuzz, green islands floating in your yogurt, and bread growing a patchy, white beard. But as your stomach growls, a question pops into your head: surely you could eat around these masses of mold, right? Josephine Wee explores how these common spores form and what happens if you eat moldy food.

item.title: Enabling zero trust: ALLEN’s move to Chrome Enterprise Premium
item.author: Rishabh ChhajerVice President – IT & CybersecurityALLEN Career Institute Pvt. Ltd.
item.content:encoded: With a workforce that lives in the browser across a SaaS and multi-cloud estate, securing our digital environment is paramount. Our 5,000+ users include faculty, operations, engineering, contractors, and a large Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) population.Operating at this scale, our top priority is protecting student personally identifiable information (PII) flowing through web applications. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA), protecting this data is critical to regulatory compliance and maintaining brand trust. We needed security within the browser.The challenge of a fragmented browser estateWe previously operated a mixed-browser environment, but managing multiple browsers made consistent policy enforcement and visibility challenging. We explored several options to standardize; however, our team didn’t want users to have to learn a new tool, and many of the options had high overhead costs.Testing and rolling out Chrome Enterprise PremiumWe implemented a phased Chrome Enterprise Premium pilot over a few weeks. Our team first validated the management capabilities in the Google Admin console by testing policy, deployment, extension controls, and reporting. Once we felt confident that Chrome Enterprise Premium provided our desired level of visibility, we rolled it out to several hundred users across various environments, including BYOD, Windows, and macOS. We deployed Safe Browsing and URL filtering for immediate threat protection, DLP rules to restrict copy/paste, downloads, and uploads on sensitive SaaS apps, and context-aware access to restrict application entry based on device posture.The proof of concept succeeded across all criteria including consistent policy enforcement, measurable reduction in risky-site and risky-download events, minimal user friction, and a centralized dashboard to give our teams visibility into managed user activity.The real decision moment came when we realized we could achieve a true Zero Trust posture. With Chrome Enterprise Premium as our backbone, access decisions now happen dynamically based on identity, device posture, and context. A teacher on a school-managed laptop enjoys seamless, full access. On a personal phone, that same educator can review materials without compromising security—downloads and clipboard sharing remain locked down. It delivers airtight data protection without disrupting daily instruction.A simpler, stronger foundationWith Chrome Enterprise Premium, we replaced virtual desktops (VDIs) and fragmented security tools with built-in browser protection. Securing the browser itself means we no longer need to install heavy security software on every computer. This makes it easy to apply security policies to personal devices used by contractors and employees. Whether our team uses Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, iOS, or Android, we manage updates, policies, and audit reports from a single Google Admin console.Chrome Enterprise Premium ensures we only grant access when it is safe. Every time someone tries to log in, we verify three things:Identity: Is the user signed into their corporate account?Device: Is the laptop or phone managed and secure?Context: Where are they logging in from, and on what network?We use Chrome Enterprise’s built-in features, such as Safe Browsing sandboxing and site isolation, and auto-updates to keep end users secure while they work on the web. These benefits plus Chrome Enterprise Premium prove that security does not have to slow down business. Employees work without security interruptions, and our IT team gets a single, clear audit trail across all devices. This helps us maintain high efficiency and supports our regulatory compliance efforts.Read more customer stories including how Mercari drove a 50% plus cost reduction with Chrome Enterprise Premium.

item.title: Amazon says hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server.The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system.“These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said.

item.title: We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: This essay originally appeared as part of a round table in entitled “Is America’s Infrastructure Under Attack?”Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, the NSA—it’s been a really bad week in cyberspace. But, amazing as it might seem, these are not related. As far as we know, they’re not the result of cyberattacks. They’re not even related to AI. (Well, that’s mostly true. The NSA will probably never tell us what went wrong.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.Our computerized infrastructure is vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old, and has been incrementally patched and upgraded. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. And more and more of it is centralized: the same systems affecting many different aspects of our lives and society. In many cases, it just barely works. And when it fails, it tends to fail badly.There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream of the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problem lies.Security, safety, resilience, redundancy, recoverability—these are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs.More importantly, they are inefficient: costs that feel wasteful until something bad happens. Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, squeeze all inefficiencies out of a company in pursuit of near-term profits. Competition, with multiple companies competing to do the same thing, is another inefficiency. Monopolization removes that in pursuit of near-term profits.The result is brittle systems, single points of failure. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes. The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.Fixing this is technical, but it’s political first. It requires changing incentives, and that involves regulation and control. “What to do” is easy; finding the political will to stand up to moneyed interests and do it is hard.

item.title: Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code with webserver privileges.The following versions of Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series are affected:AK-SM8xxA <=5.4.0 (CVE-2026-129713)Stack-based Buffer OverflowCritical Infrastructure Sectors: Commercial FacilitiesCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: DenmarkA stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated CGI handler of the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controller allows remote attackers to send specially crafted HTTP/S POST requests, leading to memory corruption, webserver restart and hypothetically potential arbitrary code execution with webserver privileges. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.Danfoss AK-SM8xxA <=5.4.0Product Status: known_affectedThis vulnerability will be addressed in an upcoming Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series software release (version 5.5.x). In addition, Danfoss will remove the ability for users to disable Strict Mode in future software releases.Until a software update is available, Danfoss recommends the following mitigations: * Follow the guidance provided in the product documentation and do not expose devices directly to the Internet or assign them public IP addresses. * Restrict remote access to affected devices by using a secure VPN or other protected network architecture. * Configure all affected devices to operate in Strict Mode, which provides enhanced security protections. * Use strong, unique passwords for all user accounts and administrative access. * For additional security recommendations and best practices see the Danfoss AK-SM 800 security guidance page: https://www.danfoss.com/en/service-and-support/downloads/dcs/adap-kool-software/ak-sm-800a/#tab-overviewCarlo Meijer of Midnight Blue reported CVE-2026-129713 to CISA.CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.2026-11-24Legal Notice and Terms of Use

item.title: AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: If you cannot update to the latest software or firmware version right away, apply the following compensating controls to reduce risk until the update can be performed. These measures are temporary and do not replace the update, which remains the primary and recommended remediation. Apply these controls as appropriate based on the vulnerability, assessed risk, operational requirements, and characteristics of your environment. Implement changes under your established management-of-change process. Before implementing isolation, access-control, or network-configuration changes, evaluate potential impacts to safety, availability, and essential operational functions. • Isolate affected engineering workstations and OT systems from external and nonessential networks, including the internet and corporate IT networks, where operationally feasible. • Disable or tightly restrict vendor, contractor, and other remote access to the affected OT environment until the vulnerability can be remediated. Where remote access is operationally required, use a hardened jump host, enforce multi-factor authentication, apply least-privilege access, and limit access to authorized, time-bound sessions. • Use trusted, dedicated OT networks for device communication. Where practicable and appropriate to the assessed risk, use dedicated or physically separated infrastructure for higher-criticality systems. Where logical segmentation is used, ensure segmentation controls are appropriately configured, secured, and monitored. • Restrict both physical and logical access to affected systems to authorized personnel only. Apply least-privilege principles to administrative, engineering, maintenance, and service access. • Configure application allowlisting, where supported, so that only trusted and pre-approved applications are permitted to execute. Block unauthorized software. • Use appropriate antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools where supported and compatible with the affected system. Configure host-based and network firewalls to permit only required communications. • Disable unnecessary services, ports, protocols, and communication pathways associated with the affected systems. Where a service or protocol cannot be disabled for operational reasons, restrict access to trusted systems and authorized users wherever possible. • Enable and regularly review available system, security, and network logs to identify suspicious or unauthorized activity. Where appropriate, monitor communications to and from affected systems for unexpected connections or changes in network behavior. • Maintain secure, tested, and preferably offline backups of PLC programs, device configurations, engineering workstation configurations, and other information necessary to restore operations. Periodically verify that backups can be successfully restored. • Verify that critical OT functions can continue operating without unnecessary dependencies on external networks, cloud services, remote-access services, corporate IT services, or other nonessential systems. • If removable media is required to transfer files into an isolated or restricted environment, use controlled and trusted media and scan it for malicious content before use. • Continuously evaluate the risks associated with operating vulnerable or outdated firmware or software. Adjust compensating controls as the threat environment, operational requirements, or available vulnerability information changes. These compensating controls are intended to reduce exposure while remediation is pending. Organizations should prioritize applying the vendor-provided update as soon as it can be safely tested and deployed within the operational environment.

item.title: Путешествия во времени ВОЗМОЖНЫ? Профессор MIT и Сабина Хоссенфельдер
item.content:encoded: Можно ли отправить сообщение в прошлое? Теория относительности Эйнштейна допускает существование временных петель, через которые информация теоретически могла бы попасть в прошлое. Но если путешествия во времени не противоречат некоторым уравнениям физики, почему мы до сих пор не создали машину времени? И можно ли изменить события, которые уже произошли?В новом выпуске - разговор с Сабиной Хоссенфельдер, физиком-теоретиком и исследователем квантовой гравитации, и Сетом Ллойдом, профессором MIT и одним из пионеров квантовых вычислений. Поговорили о том, допускают ли законы физики путешествия в прошлое, как черные дыры могут искривлять время и почему учёные всерьёз исследуют возможность передачи информации назад во времени.Обсудили, что такое кротовые норы, возможна ли связь быстрее скорости света и почему путешествия во времени порождают парадоксы. Сет рассказал об эксперименте, моделирующем путешествие во времени, а Сабина объяснила, почему даже теоретическая возможность вернуться в прошлое ещё не означает, что мы сможем его изменить. Также разобрали гипотезу параллельных вселенных, природу времени и вопрос о том, может ли будущее влиять на настоящее.▶︎ Телеграм-канал Глеба Соломина - https://t.me/gleb_solomin▶︎ Мой закрытый телеграм-канал - https://t.me/gleb_solomin/4107▶︎ По вопросам сотрудничества - https://t.me/solomin_pr▶︎ По вопросам сотрудничества (почта) - adv@glebsolomin.com

item.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this:In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count.This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said:Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality.GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights:We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening.I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API.It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model.I built a llm-glm plugin, then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up.I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4.It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look.I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark.

item.title: Ladybird's first alpha release
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Ladybird is an astonishingly ambitious project: a new browser, in 2026, with its own implementation of most of the key components - HTML parsing, CSS engine, layout, JavaScript, even WebAssembly. It still uses a few external components - things like HarfBuzz for text shaping, Skia for 2D graphics, ffmpeg for video, and SQLite for the things you do with SQLite. Everything else is part of Ladybird, or code brought in from Ladybird's even more ambitious predecessor project SerenityOS.I've been trying it out today, and it's very impressive. It feels fast, the UI is lightweight and intuitive, and most of the websites I've tried to load in it have worked as they should. It looks like this (showing my video-compressor tool):Here's the process tree after I opened six tabs in one window and another tab in a second window (generated by this script, thanks Claude):Ladybird (72925) [240 MB] └── Hub (72926) [61 MB] ├── RequestServer (72927) [29 MB] ├── ProcessReaper (72928) [1 MB] ├── Compositor (72930) [123 MB] ├── RequestServer (72953) [36 MB] ├── WebContent (72984) [819 MB] ├── MediaServer (73006) [118 MB] ├── VideoDecoderServer (73007) [20 MB] ├── WebContent (73052) [144 MB] ├── WebContent (73057) [73 MB] ├── WebContent (73073) [166 MB] ├── WebContent (73094) [70 MB] ├── WebContent (73112) [116 MB] ├── RequestServer (73113) [27 MB] └── WebContent (73185) [60 MB]Ladybird runs different tabs in different processes, an isolation mechanism used by most browsers (well, technically Chrome uses a process-per-site).I tried Ladybird against several of my more advanced tool examples - like the video-compressor shown above, which runs ffmpeg compiled to WebAssembly. I had it resize its own screenshot using my image-resize tool. It happily runs my Pyodide REPL (Python compiled to WebAssembly) too.The one thing I tried that didn't work was Datasette Lite, which runs Pyodide in a complicated arrangement of service workers and web workers. Attempting to start Datasette Lite displays this error:undefined is not a function (evaluated from 'navigator.serviceWorker.startMessages')The project has been leaning heavily into coding agents this year. On February 23, 2026 Andreas Kling published Ladybird adopts Rust, with help from AI, describing how they ported parts of their LibJS JavaScript engine from C++ to 25,000 lines of Rust in two weeks using Claude Code and Codex.That uptick in October corresponds to the landing of a wealth of big improvements.How did they do that? Coding agents:Most of that gain came in five days, from about 2.12 million on October 22 to about 2.18 million on October 27. We pointed AI coding agents at WPT and asked them to fill in missing functionality. They made lots of small fixes, and those added up. Our biggest gains for the month were about 30,000 in and 10,000 in .I'm interested in what models they are using here - I know Andreas uses Codex and Claude Code, but I haven't seen him talk about specific model versions. Claude Opus 5.5 came out on September 22, 2026 and Claude Fable 5.2 on November 9, 2026 (after that window). I'd love to know what they were using for that huge leap in the last week of October.Here's what Andreas says about Ladybird's suitability for use as a daily browser:This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!Given how hard it is to secure a web browser, and the hostility of the environment they operate in, I won't be using Ladybird to sign into GitHub or Gmail or any of my other sensitive accounts.I'm going to keep it around for anonymous browsing though, partly to participate in the testing efforts but mainly because it gives me a glimmer of optimism to see a promising new entrant in the stagnant browser engine market start to grow its wings.

item.title: Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it. In May 2025, Judge Anne Conway accepted neither.Character.AI’s maneuver is part of a larger pattern. When the parents of a sixteen-year-old sued OpenAI over his suicide, the company’s answer also pleaded the First Amendment: the claims would restrain protected speech. The very same document argues ChatGPT is offered “as is,” with no promise of accuracy, and that the boy had circumvented its guardrails. Elon Musk’s xAI (since renamed SpaceXAI) told a federal court in Colorado this spring that every choice in building Grok is an expressive act, and that Grok’s outputs are protected speech. When Grok praised Hitler last summer, xAI said the posts came from a code update independent of the model, and the apology appeared under Grok’s own name. Google, which spent two decades telling American courts that its search results are its own opinion, answered a Minnesota defamation suit over an AI Overview by saying the system merely summarized the web. It also told a Munich court in May that no one should trust an AI overview without checking it. Back in 2024, Air Canada told a Canadian tribunal that its customer-service chatbot was a separate legal entity, responsible for its own actions.When the output causes harm, the companies deny responsibility. It is the machine’s doing, or a product no sensible person would rely on, or the user’s misuse. When a state or a plaintiff would hold the words to account, the same output becomes speech, and the First Amendment applies.Social media companies deployed an earlier incarnation of this strategy. They called themselves publishers when editorial discretion was profitable, and neutral carriers when faced with liability for what they published. The result was a privatized public square in which tech platforms were unaccountable. AI companies have taken this even further. A social media platform could at least point to a human author somewhere in the chain. A chatbot’s prose differs; no person at the company wrote it, read it, or chose it before it reached the user. Yet the companies ask that it be protected as though a human had written it.The question grows more urgent as these systems stop talking and start acting. In July, a poorly controlled experiment at OpenAI resulted in its AI model hacking the network of HuggingFace. Since then both Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed numerous instances of AI agents hacking outside networks in pursuit of their prompted goals. These are examples of AIs exhibiting genie-like behavior: behaving in ways its controllers neither expected nor wanted. Nothing in the actions count as speech. Breaking into a server is an act that no person at OpenAI explicitly chose. Jill Lepore, surveying this record in , puts the blame on Congress, which has passed no federal statute governing AI agents.The First Amendment protects expressive choice. It presumes a speaker who can be persuaded, shamed, jailed, or moved to change their mind. Its remedy for bad speech is more speech, which assumes that speech is costly and attention plentiful. A system that can produce millions of individually tailored political messages an hour reverses both assumptions. Verbiage that no person chose is a product, and the company that built the model should answer for it.The industry wants a self-serving third category that bridges AI speech and action: AI output is human speech when expressive rights are at issue, and the machine’s own doing when blame is. The result is agency without accountability, something no human speaker has ever possessed. That’s why Massachusetts convicted a young woman of manslaughter in 2017 for urging her boyfriend, by text and by phone, to kill himself.The Court has already glimpsed the problem. Upholding the TikTok divestiture law in January 2025 without dissent, the justices warned that “new technologies with transformative capabilities” counseled caution, then decided the case on national-security grounds and left the larger question for another day.

item.title: datasette-charts 0.1a0
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin.The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3, Observable Plot, and topojson-client), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows.Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch.As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others.The most important feature is that the charts take . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows.The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set.I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible.

item.title: Muru
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since.Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production.As he did with wrapture, he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process.Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks:The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too.
