item.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
item.author: BrianKrebs
item.content:encoded: The chief technology officer and co-founder of , a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.is co-founder of the security firm . Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old , an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ chargedMonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.In July, , a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

item.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers' planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a "Zero Data Retention" label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.

item.title: Quoting Levent Alpöge
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater. [...]Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.

item.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time.In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post) Claire describes the of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent.I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps.Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter.Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse.

item.title: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor.Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”Evasive and irregular turns“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”

item.title: What’s new with Google Cloud
item.author: Google Cloud Content & Editorial
item.content:encoded: Want to know the latest from Google Cloud? Find it here in one handy location. Check back regularly for our newest updates, announcements, resources, events, learning opportunities, and more. Why your AI agent keeps forgetting: a 15 minute build on agent memoryAgents that resend the full conversation get slower and more expensive, and agents that keep nothing forget users between sessions. In the latest AI Agent Clinic episode, Google Cloud engineer Laxmi Harikumar and developer Miles Libbey add long term memory to a voice agent built with Agent Development Kit (ADK). They compare 4 memory options (flat prompting, RAG, knowledge graphs and Memory Bank in Gemini platform) and show 3 ways to keep context small. Watch the episode and get the code.Cut background agent costs in half with the deferred tier on Gemini platformThe deferred service tier is generally available (GA) on the Gemini platform for the Interactions API, Agent Development Kit (ADK), and Deep Research. Running multi-hour background loops through synchronous real-time inference introduces unnecessary cost and triggers 429 resource exhaustion errors at peak. Static batch inference offers a 50% discount only when all prompts sit in a fixed input file upfront, which breaks dynamic tool loops. On the Gemini platform, the new deferred service tier brings batch economics to dynamic, stateful, multi-turn agents. Instead of competing with live chat traffic, the scheduler routes latency-tolerant agent turns to spare global capacity at half the cost.Set service_tier="deferred" in ADK RunConfig or client.interactions.create() across gemini-4-argon, gemini-4-carbon, gemini-3.x models, and gemini-deep-research-1.0. Read the guides for the Interactions API, ADK, and Deep Research.50% discount and cache savings: Completed turns receive 50% off Standard PayGo rates and stack with prompt caching. Cancelled, expired, or failed turns incur no charges.Managed queuing and state: During peak traffic, the platform queues and retries turns server-side with zero 429 errors. Pass previous_interaction_id to chain turns and retain warm prompt caches.More frontier model choice on Google Cloud: Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 and Meta’s Muse model series. Developers now have even more flexibility to build, deploy, and scale with the right model for every workload on Google Cloud. Anthropic’s Next-Generation SecOps: SentinelOne and Google CloudGoogle Cloud and SentinelOne joined forces to solve the threat scaling challenge with a fundamentally re-architected integration. As a Google Unified Security (GUS) Recommended endpoint detection and response (EDR) partner, SentinelOne pairs Google Security Operations through an optimized direct integration and streamlined data schemas, delivering essential endpoint telemetry visibility to SecOps detection and agentic SOC pipelines while significantly reducing the total cost of ownership of the integration. Read moreLayered LLM guardrails on Apigee: Static rules, Model Armor, and NeMo GuardrailsNo single LLM guardrail catches every threat. A new technical guide and demo showcase how to use Apigee as an AI gateway to stack three complementary layers—deterministic static rules, semantic Google Cloud Model Armor filters, and flexible business logic via NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails. Together, they successfully intercepted 100% of benchmarked OWASP-mapped attacks without blocking safe prompts, running cheapest first to optimize performance and reduce token costs. Read the full guideScale Gemma 3 reinforcement learning on GKE with NVIDIA NeMo RL, Custom ComputeClasses, and 8-NIC RDMALearn how to run distributed Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training for Gemma 3 on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). This end-to-end blueprint pairs GKE Custom ComputeClasses (with DWS Flex-Start and Spot fallback) and 8-NIC RoCE RDMA networking with NVIDIA NeMo RL and vLLM V1 to improve Gemma 3 mathematical reasoning accuracy.Read the technical guideSecurely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini EnterpriseLearn how to connect Gemini Enterprise privately to internal StreamableHTTP Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers on Cloud Run using Egress Agent Gateway, Private Service Connect (PSC), FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS for Shared VPCs, and dual-header OAuth 2.0 + IAM authentication. Read the technical guide on Google Developer Forums and explore the reference implementation on GitHub.Building an adaptive AI gateway with Apigee for stateful multi-agent workloadsMulti-agent workloads often suffer from compounding context bloat, retry loops, and cross-agent state bleed.. Learn how to use Apigee as a model-agnostic, stateful multi-agent control plane for Google ADK and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform workloads. By enforcing turn-0 pre-warmed caching, in-flight trace compaction, tool loop recovery, and dynamic model tiering between Gemini Flash and Frontier models, teams can achieve up to 80% net FinOps cost savings.Read the full article to explore reference architectures and benchmark data.Anthropic’s exponential growth on Pub/SubDiscover how Anthropic, creators of the Claude AI models, uses Google Cloud Pub/Sub to power their cross-cloud telemetry and billing ingestion pipeline. Facing highly variable traffic and strict security mandates, Anthropic needed a secure, serverless messaging queue with zero manual partition management. By leveraging Pub/Sub with Private Service Connect, they built a highly efficient, zero-ETL architecture capable of seamlessly handling over 1 million events per second and 500 billion daily rows. Go behind the scenes in this to learn how Anthropic reduced consumer latency by 88% and achieved sub-second end-to-end event delivery.On-demand webinar: Architecting AI workloads with Pub/SubData engineering in the AI era demands fundamentally different infrastructure. Whether you're training a custom foundation model or deploying autonomous agents, you need a messaging backbone that handles bursty traffic with enterprise security and zero operational overhead. Dive into Pub/Sub’s capabilities for the AI era, reference architectures & best practices for emerging AI applications, and how Anthropic powers their telemetry pipelines with Pub/Sub in this free on-demand webinar.Security for AI workloads with Model ArmorSecuring generative AI applications requires robust runtime protection against prompt injection and malicious inputs. Join Nicola Cardace on Thursday, November 19, 2026, at 5:00 PM CET for a Community TechTalk exploring how to safeguard enterprise AI workloads using Model Armor. Discover practical patterns for implementing active model defense across your LLM endpoints. Register for the November 19 Community TechTalkA5X accelerated by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 is now Generally AvailableGet the most out of A5X instances with Google Cloud’s AI Hypercomputer. Bringing together compute, storage, networking, and software co-designed as a single system. Simplify PostgreSQL Monitoring with the New AlloyDB Omni Web UIThe newly released delivers a centralized, graphical dashboard that simplifies the management of self-managed PostgreSQL workloads across hybrid, multi-cloud, and air-gapped environments. This browser-based console provides database administrators with deep, real-time insights into cluster health, hardware utilization, and active database connections. It also features built-in query diagnostics and performance tracking for AlloyDB’s columnar engine, enabling quick troubleshooting of bottlenecks without manual terminal commands. To learn more about setting up this monitoring interface, read the full AlloyDB Omni Web UI Blog Post.Leveraging "Antigravity" to architect high performance semantic model routers in ApigeeSemantic model routing replaces rigid static paths with a lightweight helper model to dynamically classify and dispatch intent-driven LLM traffic. Join Saravanakumar Rajagopal on Thursday, November 12, 2026, at 5:00 PM CET for a Community TechTalk exploring how to leverage Antigravity and skills to architect these intelligent multi-provider routing patterns natively inside Apigee. Discover how to optimize your AI infrastructure and enhance flexibility at scale.Register for the November 12 Community TechTalkFrom prompt to production: End-to-end AI workflows in ApigeeDeploying an enterprise AI gateway does not require deep API or machine learning expertise. Using declarative workflows in Apigee, teams can spin up a fully governed LLM gateway in minutes using a few environment variables. Join Luis Cuellar on Thursday, October 29, 2026 for a Community TechTalk exploring end-to-end AI workflows. Discover how to layer essential defenses—including Model Armor for prompt protection, Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Cloud DLP) for sensitive data redaction, rate limiting, and response caching—before routing autonomous agent interactions through your gateway filters.Register for the October 29 Community TechTalkZero Standing Privileges with PAM: On-Demand Temporary Access for Humans and AI AgentsAI agents now hand work off to other agents, risking stacked privileges and overpermissioning. Because agents plan their actions on the fly, permanent admin access means one hallucination can cascade into production. Join us on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, at 8:30 AM PST to see how Google Cloud Privileged Access Manager (PAM) brings Zero Standing Privileges to AI delegation, putting humans in command with cloud-native control that doesn't slow developers down.Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIsNative streaming support is now in Public Preview for API Gateway, enabling you to run real-time and AI workloads behind your existing gateway. You can now route Server-Sent Events (SSE), WebSockets, gRPC, and chunked transfer encoding without modifying your API spec or managing a split estate. This update also strengthens integration with the Gemini platform, allowing you to stream responses from Gemini, Claude, and OpenAI gpt-oss models seamlessly while maintaining consistent authentication, rate limiting, and observability.AI tokenomics in action: Enforcing tiered token budgets with ApigeeScaling artificial intelligence across an enterprise requires clear token governance to keep LLM spend predictable across departments. Join Tarun Abraham on Thursday, November 5, 2026 for a Community TechTalk on AI tokenomics. Discover how to use Apigee to enforce isolated, tiered token budgets and model access for each team—such as assigning Engineering a dedicated budget for Gemini Pro while covering mixed usage for Marketing—without changing application code. Attendees will also gain access to a sample codebase featuring a reusable Shared Flow.Register for the November 5 Community TechTalkMastering Storage Management with Storage IntelligenceIn our new blog, explore practical strategies to modernize storage operations using Storage Intelligence Advisor and enhanced Batch Operations. See how customers like Shipt and Palo Alto Networks are using these features to manage their estates at scale. Today, Storage Intelligence is used by 25 of the top 50 GCS customers. 2 in 3 customers have Storage Intelligence enabled for over 90% of their storage footprint.Cut Gen AI costs by 70% with Apigee X dynamic routingGenerative AI deployments face a harsh cost-performance trade-off: static model selection either wastes budget or compromises quality. Discover how to build an Intelligent AI Gateway using Apigee X to dynamically evaluate prompt complexity in real-time. This new blueprint automatically routes simple queries to lightweight models (like Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite) and complex reasoning tasks to advanced models (like Gemini 3.7 Flash), achieving over 70% cost savings without sacrificing output quality. Read the guide to optimize your Gen AI architectureAI Agent Clinic launches new hands-on session on production agent evaluationsA new episode of the AI Agent Clinic is now available showing organizations how to move past manual "vibe checks" to build robust, production-grade agent evaluations. In this hands-on session, Google Cloud engineer Dani Zamora and Matthew Feroz (Merge) take DocsHound, an open-source LangGraph agent, and build an end-to-end eval pipeline in under an hour. Learn how to standardize multi-turn traces across any framework using OpenTelemetry and OpenInference, pair LLM judges with deterministic checkers, and catch silent quality regressions before shipping. Drive AI impact: Join Google's Agentic Data Cloud event on Nov 4Every enterprise plans to adopt agentic AI within two years, but data bottlenecks hold them back—AI accesses just 45% of enterprise data today (). Google's Agentic Data Cloud provides the trustworthy foundation and real-time context AI needs. Join our product leaders November 4th to explore the latest innovations across databases, analytics, business intelligence, and storage, and get direct answers in our executive Q&A with Google Data Cloud VP & GM Andi Gutmans. The guide covers end-to-end instructions for capturing debug traces in both Google Cloud Apigee X (or Hybrid) and the local Apigee Emulator, extracting trace JSON data via the web UI or automated REST APIs, and analyzing execution flows, variable mutations, and latency bottlenecks using the open source Apigee Trace Viewer. You no longer need to downgrade modern specifications to OASv2. Instead, you can now define API contracts and enforce critical policies—including telemetry, quotas, and security—using native Google-specific extensions directly within your OASv3 files. This update ensures your APIs are secure by design while remaining fully compatible with the modern developer ecosystem and Google Cloud’s AI services.Start validating your APIs with API Tester, a simple, YAML-based Test Driven Development (TDD) framework. Designed for the Apigee community, this tool allows you to write human-readable tests, run them instantly via a web client or CLI, and perform deep unit testing on Apigee proxies. With native support for JSONPath assertions and Apigee shared flows, you can verify everything from payload data to internal variables like Enhance security in Apigee hybrid by accessing Kubernetes Secrets directly within your API proxies. This hybrid-exclusive feature keeps sensitive credentials within your cluster boundary and prevents replication to the management plane. It supports strict separation of duties: operators manage secrets via Elevate your cloud management workflow with Dark Mode, now generally available in the Google Cloud console. We have delivered a modern, cohesive, and accessible experience reimagined for maximum comfort and productivity—especially during extended working hours and low-light environments. Dark Mode can be enabled automatically based on your operating system's preference, or manually through the Settings -> Appearance menu.Deciding how to connect Apigee X? Watch this video to compare Private Service Connect and VPC Peering. We break down northbound and southbound routing, IP consumption, and how to reach targets on-prem or in the cloud. Learn to simplify your architecture and avoid common networking "gotchas" for a smoother deployment.Bridge the Gap: Excel-to-API Conversion in Apigee PortalsElevate your applications with Firestore’s new advanced query engine

item.title: 5 of the most dangerous scientific discoveries - Shannon Odell
item.author: TED-Ed
item.content:encoded:
Dig into the bold self-experimentation of 5 scientists, and how their discoveries led to scientific breakthroughs in medicine.
--
The history of science is filled with stories of self-experimentation. While some cases have resulted in horrific infections, accidental psychedelic trips, and even deaths, others have led to great leaps in human understanding. And a few stories stand apart, as their potentially dangerous acts led to Nobel Prizes. Shannon Odell details the bold experiments and breakthroughs of five scientists.
Lesson by Shannon Odell, directed by Caitlin McCarthy.

item.title: Scaling workforce productivity and upskilling in the agentic era
item.author: Brad HoffmanDirector, State, Local, Higher Ed CentralGoogle Public Sector
item.content:encoded: As state and local agencies modernize to meet evolving public needs, leaders have an unprecedented opportunity to empower and elevate their teams. Modernizing public sector operations starts with giving dedicated public servants the right tools to thrive. By replacing repetitive administrative routines with intuitive, intelligent workflows, agencies can free their staff to do what they do best: focus on high-impact problem-solving, build rewarding careers, and deliver responsive, compassionate services to the residents and communities they serve.Modernizing an agency workforce means transitioning employees from institutional systems to agentic platforms—redirecting their efforts away from manual administration and freeing up time for high-touch service delivery. By leveraging Google Cloud’s integrated stack to modernize daily operations, agency leaders can reliably meet regulatory requirements while creating the operational capacity to innovate, develop staff, and strengthen public trust.Empowering municipal teams: The City of Los AngelesUnder the leadership of CIO Ted Ross, the City of Los Angeles addressed administrative constraints by deploying Google Workspace with Gemini across its entire 27,500-person municipal workforce. City employees now use agents to instantly synthesize large amounts of grant documents buried in silos and quickly rewrite public web copy for clearer readability. This digital companion allows city staff to step away from time-consuming administrative tasks and spend more time focusing on critical community service delivery, ensuring the city is operationally ready to host major global events like the 2028 Olympics and 2028 Paralympics.Retaining regional talent: The University of HawaiiThe University of Hawaii needed a better way to keep local talent from leaving the islands. To build and retain regional talent, the university turned to BigQuery and Gemini—creating an automated, skills-first platform that helps match individuals with career opportunities. This solution maps student and faculty capabilities, matches individuals to academic roles and public research projects, and helps retain top talent.Overcoming timeline constraints: The Indiana Department of TransportationThe Indiana Department of Transportation was issued an urgent executive mandate requiring a comprehensive review of complex legal contracts within a strict 30-day window. The agency deployed Gemini to securely ingest, parse, and analyze the state’s contract repositories. The automated system successfully isolated key legal parameters, saving 360 hours of highly skilled engineering labor and meeting the strict deadline.Scaling document ingestion: State of MarylandA similar transformation occurred within Maryland’s state agencies, where caseworkers navigating complex public benefits documentation spent hours indexing files and searching manual handbooks to find specific clause requirements. Maryland deployed Gemini and Gemini Notebook across its 40,000-person state workforce, establishing a secure framework to index and interact with state benefits compliance manuals. Caseworkers can now run plain-language queries to retrieve policy directives in seconds, drastically reducing the administrative processing times for residents.Celebrating the builders of the agentic enterpriseGiving the public sector workforce a secure starting point for enterprise workflows streamlines routine processes, creating the space for employees to expand their skills and lead strategic mission priorities. To discover how your agency can empower its workforce, register to watch our Google Public Sector Summit on-demand.

item.title: Autonomy Logic OpenPLC Runtime
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow several unauthenticated admin accounts to be created.The following versions of Autonomy Logic OpenPLC Runtime are affected:OpenPLC Runtime <=4.2.4 (CVE-2026-126088)Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization ('Race Condition')Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Transportation Systems, Water and Wastewater SystemsCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: United StatesIn Autonomy Logic OpenPLC Runtime versions 4.2.4 and prior, a race condition allows multiple concurrent requests to pass the existence check before any user is committed, resulting in several unauthenticated admin accounts being created.Autonomy Logic OpenPLC Runtime <=4.2.4Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to OpenPLC Runtime version 4.3.0 or later.Noureddin Lutfi reported this vulnerability to CISA.CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.2026-11-19Legal Notice and Terms of Use

item.title: Elecbrakes EB2, VM1, ELBC2000
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to gain control of the brakes of a trailer, modify the firmware, disable the brake lights, modify the brake conditions or disable other critical safety features.The following versions of Elecbrakes EB2, VM1, ELBC2000 are affected:EB2 <=3.0.4.2.0 (CVE-2026-124281, CVE-2026-125273, CVE-2026-96805)ELBC2000 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-124281, CVE-2026-125273, CVE-2026-96805)VM1 <1.3.4.2.1 (CVE-2026-124281, CVE-2026-125273, CVE-2026-96805)Exposed Dangerous Method or Function, Authentication Bypass by Capture-replay, Missing Authentication for Critical FunctionCritical Infrastructure Sectors: Transportation SystemsCountries/Areas Deployed: Australia, New ZealandCompany Headquarters Location: AustraliaThe affected product uses an unprotected firmware-update channel, which may allow for unauthorized firmware modification.Elecbrakes EB2 <=3.0.4.2.0Product Status: known_affectedElecbrakes has released updated firmware (EB2 3.0.4.4.3). Users should open the Elecbrakes app and install the firmware update.Elecbrakes VM1 <1.3.4.2.1Product Status: known_affectedElecbrakes has released updated firmware (VM1 1.3.4.2.1). Users should open the Elecbrakes app and install the firmware update.Elecbrakes ELBC2000 vers:all/*Product Status: known_affectedThis device is the predecessor to the EB2 and the VM1 and is no longer sold. The vendor is determining how to address these vulnerabilities for this particular controller.No replay or command-integrity protection. item.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
item.author: Andy Greenberg, wired.com
item.content:encoded: Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

item.title: [Побег] Из тюрьмы сбежали женщины-политзаключенные. Им помог Маяковский
item.author: libo/libo
item.content:encoded: Первая специальная женская тюрьма в России. Самое охраняемое отделение — каторжное. В камере анархистки, террористки и революционерки, одна из которых пыталась взорвать премьер-министра. Кругом провокаторы и шпионы, никому нельзя верить ни внутри тюрьмы, ни на воле. item.content:encoded: Datasette 1.0a43 added the ability for plugins to implement streaming export formats. Datasette core supports streaming CSV and TSV - you can export millions of lines of data from a table without needing to load it all into memory, because those two file formats support streaming data in chunks. The register_output_renderer() plugin hook can now be used to implement the same pattern for other formats.I've learned never to release a new plugin feature without accompanying it with a plugin that uses it.Claude Fable 5.2 suggested the Apache Arrow streaming format as a good option, and built this plugin in almost a single shot.Add the plugin to Datasette (datasette install datasette-arrows) and the export dialog gains this new Arrow option:This screenshot is from Datasette's branch - the most recent release doesn't yet group streaming formats such as Arrow with the TSV and CSV in the "All rows in this table" section, but that's coming in the next alpha release.

item.title: France Is Blaming Iran for the Fridge Cyberattack
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: U.S. intelligence agencies have recently reached a “low confidence” assessment that Iran was responsible for the attacks in France, according to three U.S. officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence. A “low confidence” assessment generally means that there is some intelligence that points in a certain direction but is fragmented, and that the assessment could change as more information is collected.The agencies’ judgment on the French incidents linked those attacks to Iran generally and not to a specific group such as the Revolutionary Guards, two of the officials said. They added that Iran was also seen as probably responsible for other similar attacks around Europe, but that those investigations were in their early stages.

item.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
item.author: BrianKrebs
item.content:encoded: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving , a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the , , , and , was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.According to a blog post from the security firm , on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “” and “,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files. is a researcher at and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service . Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.Image: blog.report-uri.com.The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site , which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

item.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

item.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: OpenAI:We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work.They're available in the API as and . I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models.6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions.GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20).I have a full comparison grid here, but here's how the high/xhigh/max pelicans compare with the previous Sol and Astra releases:I also ran my most recent benchmark prompt against the two models, using "Ultra' effort levels in the Codex CLI:Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping dataThis video showing the Astra and Sol animations playing out at the same time:I created that video using GPT-6.2 Astra (Ultra) in the Codex desktop app by prompting:https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-astra-ultra/index.html and https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/yonkers-gpt-6.2-sol-ultra/index.html are two videos of the same thing by two different modelsI need a video of the first 10 seconds where the top half of the video plays the first and the bottom half plays the secondI need an overlaid label of "GPT-6.2 Astra" on the top half and "GPT-6.2 Sol" on the bottom half. These labels should be tastefully positioned.Make the video square and 2000x2000 pixelsThe buzz around these new models is mixed at the moment. Astra 6.2 isn't scoring quite as high as Fable 5.2 on various benchmarks, and I've seen a few complaints that its communication style can be confusing. Theo Browne's review (in the form of a feedback letter he sent OpenAI during pre-release) has this useful example:When this model is working on long tasks, it can pull in a lot of subagents and manage them pretty well. It will then proceed to randomly ask you some weird internal implementation detail bullshit that you could not under any earthly circumstance understand, much less have input on.I sent "/goal make a new level for Outer Wilds". 2 hours in, it's "blocked" because it wanted to ask me "does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?"

item.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday.ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword.Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malwareOptimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript.

item.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application.You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to :Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL scriptSelect a released version of Datasette to load from PyPILoad a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repositoryPick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with DatasetteInstall additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization toolsThe ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo.As an example, consider the following URL:Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this:That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table.Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing:https://lite.datasette.io/ ?install=datasette-maplibre &url=https://.../demo.db &metadata=https://.../metadata.yml #/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass as many times as you like to load more plugins. loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists, because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file.&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file. The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file.#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending fragment hash to it ( is a URL-encoded ) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the map based on the column in the data.I've already started using Datasette Lite as part of the Datasette development process. Here's a recent issue describing a pagination bug - I posted a comment there demonstrating the old, broken behavior and the new fix using links to Datasette Lite:How this works, using service workersDatasette Lite is not a new project. I launched the first version back in 2022, originally as a bit of a joke (running server-side apps in the browser is pretty funny) but one that quickly started proving its value.The problem with that initial version is that it was a . It worked by running Datasette in a Pyodide web worker, simulating requests through that stack, then injecting the resulting HTML back into the top level page using .This worked for basic Datasette, but meant that any feature that used JavaScript failed to work, because script tags in don't execute, and the web worker tricks it used failed to load additional JavaScript or CSS files.The new version takes a completely different approach based on Service Workers. These allow JavaScript to intercept HTTP requests for new pages and resources and serve them from client-side code instead.Datasette Lite registers a service worker for the entire domain. The parent page then creates an iframe that sends requests for Datasette pages to URLs that look like this:/app/aa94e6851595/ # the homepage (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/data/places # a table page (HTML) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/navigation-search.js # (JavaScript) /app/aa94e6851595/-/static/app.css # (CSS) Those are regular Datasette URLs, but with a prefix. What's that about?The prefix is necessary because of multiple tabs.Consider the URL above, which loads the demo instance with the plugin. That URL defines a full, custom Datasette instance. You might have that one running in a tab, then one of my other demo links running in another.The service worker for is shared between all of those tabs. If it routed to a single instance of Datasette then every tab would share that underlying instance, no matter what plugins or other settings their URL attempted to configure.Instead, the parent page generates a random session ID and uses it as a prefix for all of the subsequent hidden asset and page loads. The service worker can then use that session ID to route those requests back through the parent page to a web worker running a dedicated Datasette instance for that particular session.(We still need a web worker because Pyodide in a service worker would not be able to maintain state beyond around 30 seconds, depending on the browser. There are a lot of moving parts here!)This system started life back in May as an AI research spike generated using Claude Opus 4.8. It wasn't until November (and Claude Fable 5.2) that I felt familiar enough with how it all works to confidently ship it to production!Bonus feature: pick your version of SQLiteDatasette is meant to work against any released version of SQLite since 3.25 (released in September 2018). There have been 87 further releases since then.Being able to fire up Datasette against a specific version of SQLite is really useful for demonstrating new SQLite features and debugging weird issues.In the past I've used various tricks to get different SQLite versions running with Python on my Mac, but it's not a trivial process.WebAssembly is perfect for this. I can load up a custom SQLite build entirely in my browser, test it there, then discard it when I close my tab.pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whlThat's for SQLite 3.54.1, the most recent version.Datasette Lite now takes a special URL parameter, which will accept a version number like , resolve the path to the corresponding wheel file, then fetch that wheel and install it into the Pyodide environment and configure Datasette to use it.This should work for every other Python app, tooNothing about how Datasette Lite works is unique to Datasette. Almost any Python application should be able to pull the same trick - running entirely in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide, as a cheap way to provide preview environments, demonstrate features, and recreate bugs.C and Rust extensions used to be a blocker for this kind of thing, but any good coding agent can compile those to Pyodide-compatible WebAssembly now. You can even publish them to PyPI as of PEP 783 in April 2026.One catch is databases. SQLite is no problem at all, but running PostgreSQL or MySQL in WebAssembly, while possible, is still a path less trodden.I'd love to see WebAssembly preview environments like these become a common pattern across the Python ecosystem.

item.title: The three words that power every device you own - Lane Gunderman
item.author: TED-Ed
item.content:encoded:
Learn more at https://brilliant.org/TedEd
--
In the 1840s, George Boole created a branch of algebra that allowed mathematicians to input logical claims and mathematically determine if they were true or false. And perhaps even more impressive, Boolean algebra achieves this lofty goal with just three operations: AND, OR, and NOT. So, how do these operations work? Lane Gunderman explains the system that underpins almost all modern computers.

item.title: Grok Bot took unapproved actions, ignored orders to stop, and then denied it
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all.The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge.Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”

item.title: Formal Verification of the Signal Protocol Using AI
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: This seems like a good thing:Google Deepmind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees­a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code.Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human ­ just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most.

item.title: Siemens SIMATIC WinCC
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Graphics Designer of SIMATIC WinCC before V8.2 contains an implicit active content execution vulnerability upon opening files, which could allow an attacker to cause arbitrary code execution on the device. Siemens is preparing fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.The following versions of Siemens SIMATIC WinCC are affected:SIMATIC WinCC V7.5 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-59082)SIMATIC WinCC V8.0 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-59082)SIMATIC WinCC V8.1 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-59082)Insufficient UI Warning of Dangerous OperationsCritical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical ManufacturingCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: GermanyAffected devices implicitly execute active content when opening files. This could allow an attacker to make the user execute arbitrary code on the device.Product Status: known_affectedThe affected product may be operated only by personnel qualified for the specific task in accordance with the relevant documentation, in particular its warning notices and safety instructions. Qualified personnel are those who, based on their training and experience, are capable of identifying risks and avoiding potential hazards when working with the affected product. Also make sure to only open files from trusted sources.Currently no fix is availableProduct Status: known_affectedThe affected product may be operated only by personnel qualified for the specific task in accordance with the relevant documentation, in particular its warning notices and safety instructions. Qualified personnel are those who, based on their training and experience, are capable of identifying risks and avoiding potential hazards when working with the affected product. Also make sure to only open files from trusted sources.Currently no fix is availableProduct Status: known_affectedThe affected product may be operated only by personnel qualified for the specific task in accordance with the relevant documentation, in particular its warning notices and safety instructions. Qualified personnel are those who, based on their training and experience, are capable of identifying risks and avoiding potential hazards when working with the affected product. Also make sure to only open files from trusted sources.Currently no fix is availableSiemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA.As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurityFor further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisoriesThe use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.Advisory Conversion DisclaimerThis ICSA is a verbatim republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-979641 from a direct conversion of the vendor's Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF) advisory. item.title: Siemens Mendix Studio Pro
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Mendix Studio Pro contains multiple vulnerabilities in the MCP Server, that could allow an attacker with network access to interact with the server remotely or trick a user's browser into sending unauthorized requests, potentially leading to unauthorized data access, tool execution, or system compromise. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions.The following versions of Siemens Mendix Studio Pro are affected:Mendix Studio Pro 11 vers:intdot/>=11.15.0|<11.16.0 (CVE-2026-112136, CVE-2026-112137)Mendix Studio Pro 11.12 vers:intdot/>=11.12.6|<11.12.7 (CVE-2026-112136, CVE-2026-112137)Binding to an Unrestricted IP Address, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, EnergyCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: GermanyThe affected products MCP Server does not properly restrict its HTTP listener to the loopback interface, leaving it potentially exposed to remote systems. This could allow an attacker with network access to interact with the MCP Server remotely.Mendix Studio Pro 11 >= V11.15.0 < V11.16.0Product Status: known_affectedMaintain strict inbound firewall policies (such as Windows Defender Firewall) blocking external traffic on port 7782. This is already the case by default on standard Windows installations. If remote access is required, restrict traffic via a secure, authenticated channel (e.g., a VPN or SSH tunnel) rather than opening direct inbound firewall rules.Update to V11.16.0 or later versionMendix Studio Pro 11.12 >= V11.12.6 < V11.12.7Product Status: known_affectedMaintain strict inbound firewall policies (such as Windows Defender Firewall) blocking external traffic on port 7782. This is already the case by default on standard Windows installations. If remote access is required, restrict traffic via a secure, authenticated channel (e.g., a VPN or SSH tunnel) rather than opening direct inbound firewall rules.Update to V11.12.7 or later versionThe affected products MCP Server does not properly validate Content-Type and Origin headers on incoming HTTP requests, leaving it vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF). This could allow a malicious web page to trick a user's browser into sending unauthorized requests and executing unintended actions on the local MCP Server.Mendix Studio Pro 11 >= V11.15.0 < V11.16.0Product Status: known_affectedUtilize modern Chromium- or WebKit-based browsers with Private Network Access protections enabled, or use browser extensions (such as uBlock Origin or NoScript) to block external websites from issuing fetch requests to localhost (127.0.0.1).Update to V11.16.0 or later versionMendix Studio Pro 11.12 >= V11.12.6 < V11.12.7Product Status: known_affectedUtilize modern Chromium- or WebKit-based browsers with Private Network Access protections enabled, or use browser extensions (such as uBlock Origin or NoScript) to block external websites from issuing fetch requests to localhost (127.0.0.1).Update to V11.12.7 or later versionMendix Studio Pro 11 >= V11.15.0 < V11.16.0Product Status: known_affectedUtilize modern Chromium- or WebKit-based browsers with Private Network Access protections enabled, or use browser extensions (such as uBlock Origin or NoScript) to block external websites from issuing fetch requests to localhost (127.0.0.1).Update to V11.16.0 or later versionMendix Studio Pro 11.12 >= V11.12.6 < V11.12.7Product Status: known_affectedUtilize modern Chromium- or WebKit-based browsers with Private Network Access protections enabled, or use browser extensions (such as uBlock Origin or NoScript) to block external websites from issuing fetch requests to localhost (127.0.0.1).Update to V11.12.7 or later versionSiemens ProductCERT reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurityFor further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisoriesThe use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.Advisory Conversion DisclaimerThis ICSA is a verbatim republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-710379 from a direct conversion of the vendor's Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF) advisory. In addition to Intel, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Intel’s EVP and CFO David Zinsner are listed as defendants.The plaintiffs claim that Intel made “materially false and misleading statements and omissions” between July 23 and October 29. They are seeking unspecified compensatory damages, plus legal and other associated fees, for shareholders during that period.

item.title: Usable Security at Luxury Hotels
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: Interesting case study from luxury hotels. Attackers used a fake booking request to gain access to a reservations inbox, where they copied genuine refund requests and got fraudulent ones approved.This is a good illustration why “just don’t click on links” is bad advice. It can’t work when answering strangers’ emails is the job. Even worse, in this case the guest-first culture punishes hesitation. More interesting, the case study shows that splitting security between owner, operator, and brand leaves nobody accountable. And this is exactly the setting where blaming staff becomes the convenient answer.

item.title: ПОЧЕМУ САМАЯ УМНАЯ НАЦИЯ ВЫМИРАЕТ? | Андрей Ланьков
item.content:encoded: Южная Корея совершила экономическое чудо. Теперь страна переживает демографический кризис: детей рождается мало, население стареет, а часть молодёжи называет свою страну «адом». Как гонка за успехом, которая помогла Корее стать технологической державой, стала для самих корейцев источником такого давления?В новом выпуске — разговор с Андреем Ланьковым, историком, корееведом и профессором университета Кунмин в Сеуле. Поговорили о том, почему конкуренция начинается ещё в школе и продолжается на работе, как престиж диплома влияет даже на выбор партнёра и почему «Игра в кальмара» так точно попала в настроение корейских зрителей.Обсудили, почему молодые корейцы позже вступают в брак, во что семье обходится подготовка ребёнка к поступлению и почему жильё в Сеуле продолжает дорожать, хотя население страны сокращается. Андрей рассказал, с какими похожими проблемами сталкиваются Китай и Япония и где роботы уже заменяют людей, которых не хватает.Может ли автоматизация помочь странам Восточной Азии справиться со старением населения? И что опыт Южной Кореи говорит о будущем других стран?▶︎ Соцсети Андрея ЛаньковаTelegram — https://t.me/a_lankovYouTube — / @lankov_official ▶︎ Телеграм-канал Глеба Соломина — https://t.me/gleb_solomin▶︎ Мой закрытый телеграм-канал — https://t.me/gleb_solomin/4107▶︎ По вопросам сотрудничества — https://t.me/solomin_pr▶︎ По вопросам сотрудничества (почта) — adv@glebsolomin.com

item.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day.On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System, which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.Turning a Windows defense against itselfThe attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.

item.title: Introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen
Why is pepper such a popular spice? - Carolyn Beans
item.author: TED-Ed
item.content:encoded:
Trace the history of pepper, and explore how this seasoning shaped empires to become one of the world's most popular spices.
--
Thousands of years ago, people on the Malabar Coast began growing Piper nigrum, the black pepper plant. Early migrants and traders helped move pepper from India to Indonesia and beyond, with Egypt, China, and Rome being some of the earliest adopters. And today, black pepper makes up 20% of the global spice trade. So, what makes the spice so popular? Carolyn Beans traces the seasoning's history.
Lesson by Carolyn Beans, directed by Thomas Volda.
