item.title: Siemens Building Automation and Energy Products
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: On October 21, 2026, the PHP project and security researchers disclosed two critical, unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in the core PHP language runtime known as "php2shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines, and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Siemens is actively monitoring the situation and assessing the implications of these vulnerabilities on our portfolio. Because this evaluation is ongoing, our findings are subject to change as new technical details and vendor updates emerge. We will publish updated findings, guidance, and remediation recommendations as soon as they become available. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.The following versions of Siemens Building Automation and Energy Products are affected:AMIS TS vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)blueplanet 360 NX3 M6 WM OD IISX vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)blueplanet 360 NX3 M6 WM OD IISX - S vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)Energy Engage V2.0SP9 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)Energy Engage V3.1SP1 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)Heliox Rapid vers:all/* ()Local Monitoring bt-monitoring-vm vers:intdot/<20261103 (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)Spectrum Power 3 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109619)Spectrum Power 4 vers:all/*, vers:all/*, vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)Spectrum Power 7 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)Spectrum Power TG vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)Critical Infrastructure Sectors: EnergyCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: GermanyPHP uses longjmp() for out-of-memory (OOM) errors to exit the current context and abort handling of the request. Some contexts may not properly account for this scenario and leave request memory in an uninitialized state before performing an allocation. The subsequent request cleanup procedure may read or branch on this memory. Multiple OOM strategies can consistently trigger this condition and lead to remote code execution (RCE).Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableblueplanet 360 NX3 M6 WM OD IISXProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is plannedProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedUpgrade PHP version to V8.1.34 release 6blueplanet 360 NX3 M6 WM OD IISX - SProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableLocal Monitoring bt-monitoring-vm < V20261103Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedUpdate to V20261103 or later versionSpectrum Power 4 using Nagios or ZabbixProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableSpectrum Power 4 with Web Office Portal V3.0, V3.1 and V3.2Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableSpectrum Power 4 with HISViews V1.0Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableSpectrum Power 7 using IHM (NagiosXI)Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedRed Hat released a PHP security patch for RHEL 8 and 9Spectrum Power TG which are based on Microsoft Windows using the WebConsole and WebQuery componentsProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedUpgrade PHP version to V8.5.12PHP has various global state that temporarily points into request memory. In some scenarios, global state may not be correctly reset, or may be repopulated after being reset. The global state may then refer to request memory even after it has been freed. Subsequent requests may read or branch on this stale state before it is fully initialized. Multiple strategies can trigger this condition and produce remote code execution (RCE).Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableblueplanet 360 NX3 M6 WM OD IISXProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is plannedProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedUpgrade PHP version to V8.1.34 release 6blueplanet 360 NX3 M6 WM OD IISX - SProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableLocal Monitoring bt-monitoring-vm < V20261103Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedUpdate to V20261103 or later versionSpectrum Power 4 using Nagios or ZabbixProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableSpectrum Power 4 with Web Office Portal V3.0, V3.1 and V3.2Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableSpectrum Power 4 with HISViews V1.0Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableSpectrum Power 7 using IHM (NagiosXI)Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedRed Hat released a PHP security patch for RHEL 8 and 9Spectrum Power TG which are based on Microsoft Windows using the WebConsole and WebQuery componentsProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedUpgrade PHP version to V8.5.12Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableblueplanet 360 NX3 M6 WM OD IISXProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is plannedProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedUpgrade PHP version to V8.1.34 release 6blueplanet 360 NX3 M6 WM OD IISX - SProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableLocal Monitoring bt-monitoring-vm < V20261103Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedUpdate to V20261103 or later versionSpectrum Power 3 using IHM (NagiosXI) running on Red Hat Enterprise Linux version (RHEL) 7Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedRed Hat released a PHP security patch for RHEL 7Spectrum Power 4 using Nagios or ZabbixProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableSpectrum Power 4 with Web Office Portal V3.0, V3.1 and V3.2Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableSpectrum Power 4 with HISViews V1.0Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedCurrently no fix is availableSpectrum Power 7 using IHM (NagiosXI)Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedRed Hat released a PHP security patch for RHEL 8 and 9Spectrum Power TG which are based on Microsoft Windows using the WebConsole and WebQuery componentsProduct Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedUpgrade PHP version to V8.5.12Siemens ProductCERT reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.Operators of critical power systems (e.g. TSOs or DSOs) worldwide are usually required by regulations to build resilience into the power grids by applying multi-level redundant secondary protection schemes. It is therefore recommended that the operators check whether appropriate resilient protection measures are in place. The risk of cyber incidents impacting the grid's reliability can thus be minimized by virtue of the grid design. Siemens strongly recommends applying the provided security updates using the corresponding tooling and documented procedures made available with the product. If supported by the product, an automated means to apply the security updates across multiple product instances may be used. Siemens strongly recommends prior validation of any security update before being applied, and supervision by trained staff of the update process in the target environment. As a general security measure Siemens strongly recommends protecting network access with appropriate mechanisms (e.g. firewalls, segmentation, VPN). It is advised to configure the environment according to our operational guidelines in order to run the devices in a protected IT environment. Recommended security guidelines can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/gridsecurityCISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.Advisory Conversion DisclaimerThis ICSA is a verbatim republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-166980 from a direct conversion of the vendor's Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF) advisory. This is republished to CISA's website as a means of increasing visibility and is provided "as-is" for informational purposes only. CISA is not responsible for the editorial or technical accuracy of republished advisories and provides no warranties of any kind regarding any information contained within this advisory. Further, CISA does not endorse any commercial product or service. Please contact Siemens ProductCERT directly for any questions regarding this advisory.2026-10-26Updated the Known not affected listAdded AMIS TS, Energy Engage V2.0SP9, Energy Engage V3.1SP1, Spectrum Power 3, Spectrum Power 4, Spectrum Power 7 and Spectrum Power TG to Affected Products and updated the list of known not affectedUpdated Known Not Affected and Known Affected Products listInitial CISA Republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-166980 advisoryLegal Notice and Terms of Use

item.title: Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Palo Alto Networks has published on a vulnerability in PAN-OS related to the Node2Shell vulnerability. This advisory lists the related Siemens Industrial products affected by this vulnerability. Customers are advised to consult and implement the workarounds provided in Palo Alto Networks' upstream security notifications. The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 are affected:RUGGEDCOM APE1808 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical ManufacturingCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: GermanyA buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream. Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Palo Alto Networks PAN-OSProduct Status: known_affectedUpgrade to corresponding available PAN-OS version. Contact customer support to receive additional patch and update information.Siemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA.CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.Advisory Conversion DisclaimerThis ICSA is a verbatim republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-898633 from a direct conversion of the vendor's Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF) advisory. item.title: Siemens Industrial Edge Management
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Siemens is currently assessing the impact of Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) on Industrial Edge. Please check your Industrial Edge Management (IEM) setup: - No Management Applications installed: No action is required. Although the affected Brotli library is included in the IEM software stack, the affected functionality is not used or exposed. The same applies to IEDK. - Management Applications installed: Follow the specific mitigations until a fix is available. - Device Applications installed: Follow the specific mitigations until a fix is available. For Siemens-managed services, Industrial Edge Hub and Industrial Edge Management Cloud, appropriate Firewall/WAF protection has already been implemented. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.The following versions of Siemens Industrial Edge Management are affected:Cloud Connector Configurator vers:intdot/<1.24.3 (CVE-2026-111497)Common Configurator (CC on IEM) vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)Common Configurator on Device (CC on Edge) vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)Data Flow Monitoring vers:intdot/<3.0.18 (CVE-2026-111497)Databus Configurator vers:intdot/<4.0.1 (CVE-2026-111497)DataXess Configurator vers:intdot/<1.5.7 (CVE-2026-111497)Edge OPC UA Server Configurator vers:intdot/<2.3.10 (CVE-2026-111497)Flow Creator Configurator vers:intdot/<1.15.1 (CVE-2026-111497)Industrial Edge Hub vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)Industrial Edge Management Cloud vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)Cloud Connector ConfiguratorCritical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical ManufacturingCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: GermanyA buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream. Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.Cloud Connector Configurator < V1.24.3Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V1.24.3 or later versionIndustrial Edge Management CloudProduct Status: known_affectedVulnerability fixed on central cloud service starting 2026-10-28; no user actions necessaryCommon Configurator (CC on IEM)Product Status: known_affectedUninstall all Management Applications and protect your IEM instance with a Firewall/WAF until a fix is availableCurrently no fix is availableCommon Configurator on Device (CC on Edge)Product Status: known_affectedStop Common Configurator on Device (CC on Edge) until a fix is availableCurrently no fix is availableData Flow Monitoring < V3.0.18Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V3.0.18 or later versionDatabus Configurator < V4.0.1Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V4.0.1 or later versionDataXess Configurator < V1.5.7Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V1.5.7 or later versionEdge OPC UA Server Configurator < V2.3.10Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V2.3.10 or later versionFlow Creator Configurator < V1.15.1Product Status: known_affectedUpdate to V1.15.1 or later versionProduct Status: known_affectedVulnerability fixed on central cloud service starting 2026-10-29; no user actions necessarySiemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA.CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. item.title: Siemens Desigo, Gridscale
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions.The following versions of Siemens Desigo, Gridscale are affected:Desigo CC family V8 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)Desigo CC family V9 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)Gridscale X DSA vers:intdot/>=5.3|<5.4 (CVE-2026-111497)Gridscale X PSS®E vers:intdot/<36.8.0 (CVE-2026-111497)Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Information TechnologyCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: GermanyA buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream. Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedInstall the latest .NET security updates via Windows Update.Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedInstall the latest .NET security updates via Windows Update.Gridscale X DSA >= V5.3 < V5.4Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedUpdate to V5.4 or later versionGridscale X PSS®E < V36.8.0Product Status: known_affected, known_not_affectedUpdate to V36.8.0 or later versionSiemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA.Operators of critical power systems (e.g. TSOs or DSOs) worldwide are usually required by regulations to build resilience into the power grids by applying multi-level redundant secondary protection schemes. item.author: Александр Панчин
item.content:encoded:

item.title: Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?
item.author: BrianKrebs
item.content:encoded: The cybercrime group has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.The head of Qilin goes by the handle “,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to , a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: .Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user on the Russian cybercrime forums and two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including , , and . Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address .The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by , the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user , recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses and . IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.Further reading: , an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

item.title: Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities
item.author: BrianKrebs
item.content:encoded: did another four-digit patch drop today, releasing updates to fix almost 1,100 security vulnerabilities in its operating systems and supported software. This month’s Patch Tuesday addresses 63 critical flaws — including a zero-day in — and comes amid important security updates from other software makers, including , , and .Image: Shutterstock.com. Diorama by @zepp1969.November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of .Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in , , and . Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined., an instructor at the , noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”Google this week released Chrome , which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of out today () resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited., vice president of product management at , said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished applying operating system updates. As ever, if you experience any issues installing this month’s bundle of love from Microsoft, please drop a comment about it in the space below.

item.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows.The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.

item.title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Hackers are actively exploiting a recently discovered critical vulnerability that allows them to log in to privileged accounts on many Linux systems, multiple researchers are reporting.The vulnerability, tracked under the name *sshole, arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and a code library known as musl. Linux systems that use both of these packages and meet certain other requirements can be hacked to give unauthenticated access to high-privilege accounts in a matter of seconds. *sshole became publicly known last Thursday and quickly stoked concerns it could lead to widespread compromise of Linux machines. Four days later, the prediction shows signs of becoming real.Attackers conducting "mature intrusions"Security firm Greynoise said Monday that honeypots it maintains in Southeast Asia have come under attack by a group it’s tracking as GT10. The group conducted “mature intrusions" into the systems, which Greynoise uses to detect attempted or successful attacks in real time. Greynoise subsequently gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims and some of the tools used in the campaign. A backdoor the group is using in the attacks contains Chinese language comments and appears to be generated with the use of AI.

item.title: Chainalysis says hackers stole credentials and tokens for all of its customers
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis said that hackers have obtained sensitive personal information—including names, usernames, password hashes, and live tokens—for all of its users following a breach of its network security.The accomplishment could be a major coup for the attackers. Both Chainalysis and publicsources have revealed a long list of high-profile customers, including government agencies such as the FBI, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, and the US Air Force, as well as private companies such as Microsoft, Coinbase, and Barclays. It's unclear if the data theft exposed customers to additional threats.We regret to inform you...Last Friday, Chainalysis said it had been the target of a cybersecurity incident in October that was similar to the hacks of other platforms during the same month. The external actor used AI agent-assisted offensive techniques to gain unauthorized access to Chainalysis systems and internal tools. An email the company sent to affected customers said some “non-sensitive customer data, such as user IDs, full names, email addresses, and organization role labels for users provisioned on our platform were accessed.” It's not clear why the company considered such information "non-sensitive."

item.title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password.The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.One connection, works every time, needs no retriesThere are two other conditions necessary for successful exploitation. First, a system must have at least one user account that’s accessible using a password that is hashed using the SHA256 or SHA512 functions. Second, the target system account must be configured to be passwordless, by way of specifying a "*" in the password field in /etc/shadow, the Linux file where password hashes are stored. Passwordless accounts are commonly used for accounts that use certificate-based authentication. This setting is common for certain types of accounts.

This 11-episode course will teach you how to identify, develop, and share your best ideas, while mastering essential communication skills along the way.

item.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
item.author: BrianKrebs
item.content:encoded: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.The security firm said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.The proxy tracking company said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called , a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder is a Russian man whose hosting firm was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

item.title: Hackers exploited iOS and Android flaws to infect phones
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: Hackers possibly linked to the Kremlin exploited previously patched iOS and Android flaws in an attempt to hack visitors of multiple websites, including one celebrating the 250th anniversary of American independence, researchers said Wednesday.The attackers, which the researchers assessed with “moderate to high confidence” were part of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service, targeted other sites, many with links to that country’s ongoing war against Ukraine. The attacks began when iPhone or Android users visited one of potentially hundreds of different sites. JavaScript injected into the traffic then profiled the device. The final payloads, tailored to the type of platform visiting, attempted to steal browser cookies and, in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords and full mobile device data.One of the impersonated sites was america250.org, belonging to a non-partisan group of lawmakers, business executives, and at least one former member of the Trump administration. The attackers registered america250[.]holiday and used it as a reverse proxy to america250.org. The imposter website delivered content from the real one but added malicious JavaScript into it.

item.title: VMware releases vSphere Express for virtualization on up to 128 cores
item.author: Scharon Harding
item.content:encoded: After alienating many long-time small- to medium-sized business (SMB) customers, Broadcom’s VMware is trying to appeal to its smaller customers.Today, the virtualization company announced vSphere Express, a lower-end virtualization offering for organizations that require “cost-effective essential virtualization.”vSphere Express comes after many customers reported that VMware was pushing them to VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), the flagship private cloud bundle that has many features SMBs don’t need and is expensive. Some SMB users have reported that VMware sales representatives previously told them that vSphere Standard, VMware's prior entry-level virtualization offering, wasn’t available anymore.

item.title: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: The hackers who stole billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from the Binance exchange spent months working on the theft and used both social engineering and novel malware in the process, the company said Tuesday.The heist, which both the FBI and the TRM Security firm attributed to North Korean actors, initially targeted $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance wallets. The exchange has since frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of that sum. Binance said it has set aside funds required to cover the loss and provided this link to a Proof of Reserves page. The $6.34 billion represents the biggest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft.Advanced persistent threatBinance said the people behind the heist began no later than June and continued until last Thursday, when they successfully compromised an engineer's laptop and withdrew assets from several wallets. Like just about every organization that suffers a public, high-consequence hack, Binance said the threat actor was sophisticated and resourceful.

item.title: UEFI bootkit infected fully patched Windows machines. Is Microsoft to blame?
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: In 2023, malware tracked as BlackLotus became the first publicly documented in-the-wild UEFI bootkit capable of bypassing Secure Boot on fully updated Windows 11 systems. With the industry-wide chain-of-trust mechanism subverted, the malware was able to run malicious code before Windows was fully loaded and many security defenses were operational.Microsoft had already patched the vulnerability that BlackLotus exploited in 2022. In 2023 and 2024, Microsoft issued additional updates. The first added a new certificate that no longer trusted the vulnerable boot managers. The second provided the means to revoke trust in the digital certificate used to sign older vulnerable Windows boot managers. The organizations infected by the new bootkit, which is tracked under the name BlackX, had installed all of these patches. So how did they fall victim?Before discussing the incident further, a brief review of BlackLotus and UEFI malware is in order. Short for Unified Extensible Firmware Interface, UEFI is firmware that runs immediately after a computer is turned on. One of its main jobs is to load system configuration settings, identify and initialize hardware components, and prepare the computer to start its OS.

item.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
item.author: BrianKrebs
item.content:encoded: said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include , also known as , which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based . In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called , which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.Another provider linked to the botnet was , a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company . In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include , , , , and.Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including , a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand by a publicly traded company in China called , concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.Synthient founder told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service . In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from who found the popular TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was mentioned in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers [Linus Tech Tips said in a statement shared with Synthient that it has since updated the video to explicitly frame the product as a scam and have removed all associated affiliate links].The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

item.title: ИИ ЗАБЕРЁТ твою работу к 2027 | Экс-директор Google X
item.content:encoded: В новом выпуске - разговор с Мо Гавдатом, бывшим директором по развитию бизнеса Google X, предпринимателем и автором бестселлеров об искусственном интеллекте и будущем человечества. Мо работал в Google в период активного развития нейросетей, участвовал в развитии технологических проектов и сегодня исследует, как искусственный интеллект может изменить нашу жизнь.Поговорили о том, почему искусственный интеллект может превзойти человеческий разум гораздо раньше, чем мы ожидаем, действительно ли современные нейросети способны мыслить и какие опасности несёт стремительное развитие ИИ. Мо объяснил, почему главная угроза может исходить не от самих машин, а от людей, которые используют их для достижения собственных целей, и почему искусственный интеллект способен изменить мировую экономику.Обсудили, какие профессии могут исчезнуть первыми, стоит ли сегодня получать высшее образование и как подготовиться к будущему, в котором искусственный интеллект будет выполнять значительную часть интеллектуальной работы. Мо рассказал, какие навыки помогут людям оставаться востребованными, почему важно использовать нейросети для развития собственного мышления и какие возможности открываются перед предпринимателями.

item.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
item.author: Dan Goodin
item.content:encoded: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident.The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorion said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account.In search of cloud credentials“It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorion CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorion has more details here.

item.title: What if you didn’t brush your teeth for a year? - Justin Merritt
item.author: TED-Ed
item.content:encoded:
Trace the impact that not brushing or flossing can have on your teeth, gums, microbiome, and overall health over time.
--
At any given time, your mouth is maintaining a delicate balance between hundreds of microbial species, which is why dentists agree that you should brush twice and floss once every day. But what if you just… didn’t? If you stopped doing any oral hygiene, how long would it take for your mouth to get messy? Justin Merritt investigates how not brushing can impact your health over time.
Lesson by Justin Merritt, directed by Lee Oz, Eliška Oz, Oz Animation.

item.title: Siemens Mendix SAML Module
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Mendix SAML module contains an authentication bypass vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to gain unauthorized access by replaying a valid SAML assertion in IdP-initiated authentication flows. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions.The following versions of Siemens Mendix SAML Module are affected:Mendix SAML (Mendix 10 compatible) vers:intdot/<4.2.4 (CVE-2026-89209)Mendix SAML (Mendix 11 compatible) vers:intdot/<4.2.4 (CVE-2026-89209)Mendix SAML (Mendix 9 compatible) vers:intdot/<3.6.29 (CVE-2026-89209)Mendix SAML (Mendix 10 compatible)Authentication Bypass by Capture-replayCritical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Information TechnologyCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: GermanyAffected versions of the module do not properly protect against SAML assertion replay in IdP-initiated authentication flows. This could allow unauthenticated remote attackers to gain unauthorized access to the application by replaying a valid SAML response.Mendix SAML (Mendix 10 compatible) < V4.2.4Product Status: known_affectedDisable IdP-initiated SSOUpdate to V4.2.4 or later versionMendix SAML (Mendix 11 compatible) < V4.2.4Product Status: known_affectedDisable IdP-initiated SSOUpdate to V4.2.4 or later versionMendix SAML (Mendix 9 compatible) < V3.6.29Product Status: known_affectedDisable IdP-initiated SSOUpdate to V3.6.29 or later versionSiemens ProductCERT reported this vulnerability to CISA.As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurityFor further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisoriesThe use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.Advisory Conversion DisclaimerThis ICSA is a verbatim republication of Siemens ProductCERT SSA-137528 from a direct conversion of the vendor's Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF) advisory. item.title: Hitachi Energy CoreTec Product
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Hitachi Energy is aware of OS command injection and Dirty Frag vulnerabilities that affect CoreTec product versions listed in this document. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could result in impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability of the product. Please refer to the Recommended Immediate Actions for information about the mitigation/remediation.The following versions of Hitachi Energy CoreTec Product are affected:CoreTec5 vers:CoreTec5/<=3.4.0, 5.0.0 (CVE-2026-13162, CVE-2026-43284)CoreTec4 vers:CoreTec4/<=3.4.0 (CVE-2026-13162)Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection'), Write-what-where ConditionCritical Infrastructure Sectors: EnergyCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: SwitzerlandAn OS command vulnerability exists in CoreTec product that allows authenticated users with certain roles to execute arbitrary system commands with full control over the device. The vulnerability exists in the configuration daemon's time synchronization handler, which is responsible for setting the system timezone. When processing timezone configuration updates, the daemon constructs a shell command by concatenating user-supplied input without any sanitization or validation.CoreTec5 versions 3.4.0 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedUpdate to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0CoreTec4 versions 3.4.0 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedUpgrade to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0Follow general mitigation factorsA vulnerability exists in the IPsec ESP subsystem (esp4) of the Linux kernel used in CoreTec5 that allows a local unprivileged user to escalate privileges to root. The flaw exists in how the kernel handles memory pages when processing ESP encrypted network packets. An attacker can craft a packet that causes the kernel to decrypt data directly into memory pages it does not own, including cached copies of privileged operating system binaries. When one of those binaries is executed, the attacker's injected code runs with root privileges. In CoreTec5, the vulnerable ESP component is compiled in kernel as a built-in and is present at boot time allowing a local user to exploit it.CoreTec5 versions 3.4.0 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedUpdate to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0CoreTec4 versions 3.4.0 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedCoreTec5 versions 3.4.0 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedUpdate to CoreTec5 version 5.0.0Ritesh Kumar Kalle, Subhojeet Mukherjee, Hishamudeen of the Cybersecurity Research group, Hitachi India R&D Center reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.The information in this document is subject to change without notice and should not be construed as a commitment by Hitachi Energy. Hitachi Energy provides no warranty, express or implied, including warranties of merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose, for the information contained in this document, and assumes no responsibility for any errors that may appear in this document. This document and parts hereof must not be reproduced or copied without written permission from Hitachi Energy and the contents hereof must not be imparted to a third party nor used for any unauthorized purpose. All rights to registrations and trademarks reside with their respective owners.For additional information and support please contact your product provider or Hitachi Energy service organization. For contact information, see https://www.hitachienergy.com/contact-us/ for Hitachi Energy contact-centers.General Mitigation FactorsRecommended security practices and firewall configurations can help protect a process control network from attacks that originate from outside the network. Such practices include that process control systems are physically protected from direct access by unauthorized personnel, have no direct connections to the Internet, and are separated from other networks by means of a firewall system that has a minimal number of ports exposed, and others that have to be evaluated case by case. Process control systems should not be used for Internet surfing, instant messaging, or receiving e-mails. Portable computers and removable storage media should be carefully scanned for viruses before they are connected to a control system. Proper password policies and processes should be followed. Additional information on Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices can be found in the Hitachi Energy “Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity Best Practices” Cybersecurity Notification. item.title: Hitachi Energy TRO600 series products
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Hitachi Energy is aware of multiple vulnerabilities that affect the TRO600 series product versions listed in this document. These vulnerabilities can be exploited for remote code execution (RCE) to carry out further attacks and disclosure of sensitive information. Please refer to the Recommended Immediate Actions section for information about the mitigation/remediation.The following versions of Hitachi Energy TRO600 series products are affected:TRO600 vers:TRO600/<=9.2.1.6, vers:TRO600/<=9.1.1.0, 9.2.2.1, 9.1.2.0 (CVE-2026-10756, CVE-2026-106087)Improper Restriction of Communication Channel to Intended Endpoints, Missing Authentication for Critical FunctionCritical Infrastructure Sectors: EnergyCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: SwitzerlandTRO600 contains a vulnerability that allows an authenticated attacker to bypass network access restrictions and access services intended to be reachable only from localhost. By leveraging port forwarding, an attacker can interact with locally bound ports and services, resulting in unauthorized access to sensitive functionality and confidential information, and causing availability impact.TRO600 version 9.2.1.6 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedUpdate to version 9.2.2.1TRO600 contains an arbitrary file read vulnerability. An unauthenticated attacker can exploit this vulnerability to read or download arbitrary files on the affected device, including sensitive configuration files and password data, resulting in the disclosure of sensitive information.TRO600 version 9.2.1.6 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedTRO600 version 9.1.1.0 and priorProduct Status: fixed, known_affected, recommendedFixed in version 9.1.2.0.
